key_points: The unsigned lead editorial, "The Open Society," argues that India's historic tradition of intellectual tolerance, traced from Rammohun Roy through Tagore and Gandhi, grounds the newly formed Movement for Cultural Freedom's resistance to totalitarian regimentation.

The "Notes" section criticises a Hind Mazdoor Sabha delegation's attendance at Communist China's May Day celebrations, questions the government's excuse for postponing an international peace congress in Delhi, and condemns a West Bengal proposal to remove British-era statues from the Calcutta Maidan as "tampering with history."

"Masterpieces of the 20th Century" reports on a five-member Indian delegation, led by Sir Rustom Masani, to the Congress for Cultural Freedom's Paris exposition, alongside honorary presidents Croce, Dewey, Jaspers, Madariaga, Maritain, and Russell.

"Our Tasks" records the Committee's first Annual General Meeting and Executive Committee, and the Bombay Committee's syndication of Sydney Hook's and Robert Guillain's articles to Indian-language newspapers.

Viswamitra's satirical "Exhibit One" mocks the Soviet Art Exhibition in Bombay as gaudy, Stalin-worshipping propaganda, noting a canvas that pictorially distorted Stalin's and Mao Zedong's relative heights.

The issue closes by reprinting the Indian Congress for Cultural Freedom's "Declaration on Cultural Freedom" of 31 March 1951, which frames modern totalitarianism as uniquely dangerous for seeking to dictate truth itself, not merely its expression.

Sidney Hook's tribute "Salute To John Dewey" recalls Dewey's philosophy of experience, his 1937 chairmanship of the international commission that cleared Trotsky of the Moscow trial charges, and calls his thought the most distinctive expression of the American liberal faith.

The "Notes" section criticises an Indian goodwill delegation's naive reporting from Communist China, defends the UN's refusal to forcibly repatriate Korean War POWs, criticises Finance Minister C. D. Deshmukh's evasiveness on Soviet claims, and condemns Indian law requiring inter-communal marriage partners to renounce their religion.

Ka. Naa. Subramaniam's "Freedom and the Arts" reports on the Paris International Exposition of the Arts, arguing that a decade of Soviet experience dispelled the illusion that artistic experimentation was akin to the communist social revolution, and calls for an All-Asian writers' conference.

P. Y. Deshpande's "Revolt and Human Fellowship," delivered at the same Paris exposition, argues that the modern spirit of revolt against blind tradition is compatible with, not opposed to, human fellowship, distinguishing it sharply from Marxist dogma.

Philip Spratt reviews Michael Polanyi's "The Logic of Liberty," summarising Polanyi's argument that liberty cannot be defended as an absolute in itself but must flow from other absolutes such as truth, justice and tolerance.

A notice proposes a Yusuf Meherally memorial library built from his own book collection, and a short piece praises a Bombay Child Art Exhibition for the spontaneity and freedom of children's creative work.

Philip Spratt's "After Twentysix Years" recounts his return to Europe after 26 years to attend the Paris arts exposition, defending modern art and music against both Stalinist and "lowbrow" charges of decadence.

The "Notes" section criticises the US McCarran Act's exclusion of former Communist trade unionist Raja Kulkarni, rebuts V. K. Krishna Menon's dismissal of Chinese forced labour with Chinese Communist press evidence, and opens coverage of J. B. H. Wadia's warning that government film censorship could extend to direct state control of production.

Tambimuttu's "The Poet and the Challenge of the Times" rejects Marxist literary criticism that reads the modern poet's individualism as bourgeois decadence, citing Lorca, Yessenin and Mayakovsky as poets destroyed by state pressure on artistic freedom.
A reader's letter from Raman K. Desai praises the debut issue's "The Open Society" and criticises state deference to religious sentiment in an ostensibly secular India.

Ka. Naa. Subramaniam reviews Robert Guillain's "Revolution in China" and Edward Hunter's "Brain Washing in Red China," comparing the latter favourably to Orwell's 1984 as documentary rather than fiction.
M. R. Masani appeals for entertainment-tax exemption for amateur theatre, and a note criticises judging standards at a child-art exhibition.
"The Green Dean," a satirical poem by Sagittarius reprinted from the New Statesman and Nation, mocks Cold War alarmism about Chinese "germ warfare" claims.

Jayaprakash Narayan's "Incentives For Goodness" argues that materialist philosophy, including the dialectical materialism he once embraced, cannot supply a rational incentive for individual goodness, and that social reconstruction requires non-material grounding for ethics.

The "Notes" section cites a rediscovered Athenian law against dictatorship to criticise India's Preventive Detention Bill, reports the McCarran Act's exclusion of Raja Kulkarni and Alberto Moravia from the US, and describes Soviet "LitAg" propaganda tactics operating through Indian journalism.

K. D. Sethna's "Sri Aurobindo and Man's Future" surveys Aurobindo's life and his concept of the "Supermind," while Frank Moraes's tribute to Ananda Coomaraswamy praises his synthesis of East and West across many disciplines.

Michael Padev reviews David Mitrany's "Marx Against the Peasant," summarising its thesis that Marxist theory has waged a consistent ideological war against peasant interests despite tactical alliances during revolution.

A review section covers Herbert Philbrick's "I Led 3 Lives," Matyas Rakosi's "How We Took Over Hungary" (introduced by Jayaprakash Narayan while fasting in Poona), and J. B. H. Wadia's review of Sidney Hook's "Heresy, Yes — Conspiracy, No!," which distinguishes Communism-as-heresy from Communism-as-conspiracy and criticises McCarthyist excess.
"Russia At The Olympics" recounts alleged Soviet manipulation of medal counts at the 1952 Helsinki games and quotes sports critic A. F. S. Talyarkhan questioning Soviet amateurism.

Bertram D. Wolfe's "Soviet Technique Of Historiography" (part one) argues that Soviet history-writing serves as a political weapon, purging disfavoured figures such as Trotsky, Bukharin and the historian M. N. Pokrovsky into "unpersons."

The "Notes" section defends Louis Fischer's right to criticise Vice-President Radhakrishnan, eulogises Gandhian thinker K. G. Mashruwala, praises General Naguib's Egyptian land reform, and exposes "International Student Relief" as a Communist front rivalling the genuine World University Service.

Purshottam Tricumdas reports on the International Congress of Jurists in Berlin, which documented East German rule-of-law violations including the abduction of lawyer Dr. Linse, and describes his unsuccessful push to broaden the Congress's condemnation to South Africa, Tunisia and Algeria.

A review section covers Walter Kolarz's "Russia and Her Colonies" on Soviet suppression of non-Russian nationalities, Louis Fischer's "The Life and Death of Stalin," a Socialist Union pamphlet regrounding British socialism in ethical values, and Aneurin Bevan's "In Place of Fear," praised for its critique of laissez-faire capitalism but faulted for naivety about Soviet intentions.
A reader's letter from J. D'Souza, S.J. praises Jayaprakash Narayan's "Incentives for Goodness" as a welcome return to the spiritual foundations of Indian culture.
M. P. T. Acharya's short note, "Stalin's Annual Income," itemises Stalin's stated official earnings at roughly one million roubles a year.

Philip Spratt's "Priorities" surveys Liberalism, Marxism and Gandhism as ideologies combining an ethical ideal with a self-interested economic theory, and recommends an Indian party stress the ethical ideal over elaborate economic theory.
S. R. Mohan Das's "Principles And Incidentals" dissects what ideology means for a political party, warning that implementing methods can wrongly ossify into first principles themselves.

A running "Freedom FIRST?" debate pits Prof. M. L. Dantwala, who argues hunger rather than any deficit of ideals makes India's poor vulnerable to Communism, against M. R. Masani, who defends the priority of non-material values and dignity while insisting both must be pursued together.

An unsigned piece reports on a scandalous Soviet play, "Sins of the Commissars," which exposed sexual and moral corruption among Communist Party elites despite official denunciation by Pravda and Bolshevik.

"M.R.A." defends the Moral Re-Armament movement's Bombay visit against both Communist and traditionalist Indian criticism, crediting its meetings with dissolving class distinctions into shared moral equality.

"Ferry to Nowhere" and "Bull In A China Shop," both reprinted from the New York Times, use the plight of a stateless traveller and a bookshop encounter with Soviet delegate Jacob Malik as symbols of Cold War tyranny and censorship.
An unsigned review of Woodrow Wyatt's "Southwards from China" credits Wyatt's on-the-ground access but faults his neglect of Gandhi's role in containing Communism on the subcontinent.

An unsigned editorial reproduces the Congress for Cultural Freedom's appeal to the UN Secretary-General demanding investigation of the Prague show trial, condemning its use of "Zionism" as an accusation against mostly Jewish defendants as a revival of Nazi-style incitement.

The "Notes" section eulogises Sane Guruji's Antar-Bharati inter-cultural movement, criticises Krishna Menon's Korea peace resolution as appeasement after rejection by the USSR, China and Korea itself, and reports Dr. Satyanarain Sinha's clearance of A. K. Gopalan's forgery charge.
Aamir Ali's "Siddhartha Gautama, The Buddha" presents the Buddha as a pragmatic ethical teacher who refused metaphysical speculation and asserted the equality of all castes.

Prof. A. V. Hill's presidential address, excerpted as "Is this Neutrality?," uses India's First Five-Year Plan population data to probe whether medical relief from disease without parallel education and development creates a net ethical harm.

Book reviews cover Hemingway's "The Old Man and the Sea," UNESCO's "What Is Race?," praised as a scientific rebuttal of racial prejudice, and Michel Padev's "Dimitrov Wastes No Bullets" on the Petkov trial.

Letters to the editor include Shankar Raj's critique of Moral Re-Armament as substituting vague talk of "absolutes" for genuine ethical rigor, and J. B. H. Wadia's complaint about All India Radio's film-music policy.
A report covers Francois Bondy's visit to the Committee's Bombay and Madras chapters, and the closing press digest notes Vinoba Bhave's remark on leaders who cannot control their own minds.

Bertram D. Wolfe's "Tito And Stalin—I" analyses the 1948 Tito-Stalin split through six interpretive frames, from Stalin's fear of an independent Balkan Federation to Titoism as a heresy claiming a return to "primitive Leninism."

The "Notes" section disputes Attlee's claim that Europe rather than Asia is the Cold War's centre of gravity, criticises the in-camera Rawalpindi Conspiracy trial verdict, and criticises the near-boycott of Nehru's Gandhian Seminar by communist states.

Sampurnanand's "The Tasks Of Our Leadership" attributes Indian corruption to the abrupt, unassimilated transplant of Western democratic institutions onto an unreformed caste-based society, and calls for reinterpreted spiritual values as the basis for moral education.

Zafar Futehally's "An Unrepentent Spy" examines British scientist Alan Nunn May's 1946 conviction for passing atomic secrets to the USSR, quoting May's own claim that he still believed he had "acted rightly."

Prof. Edwin D. Dickinson's "Geneva Convention And U.N. Stand" argues, from precedent including Vyshinsky's own legal writing, that states retain unlimited competence to grant asylum to unwilling Korean War POWs.
A.S.P. reviews Whittaker Chambers's "Witness," framing it as testimony that vindicates Chambers's decision to testify against Alger Hiss.
Letters to the editor criticise Major-General S. S. Sokhey's pro-Soviet public statements and warn that a Cominform "Doctors for Peace" campaign is recruiting Indian medical professionals.

Prof. G. D. Parikh's essay on academic freedom argues that institutional autonomy and improved academic standards are compatible goals, recommending an Inter-University Board and University Grants Commission over direct state control.

The "Notes" section profiles Reinhold Niebuhr's election as honorary president of the Congress for Cultural Freedom, defends Eisenhower's Formosa "liberation" policy, and treats the Kashmir Praja Parishad agitation with qualified sympathy despite its communal composition.

J. B. H. Wadia's rejoinder to Sampurnanand argues that once a secular state allies with an authoritative religion the alliance inevitably drifts toward authoritarianism, proposing "liberal secularism" as the safeguard for individual liberty.

"Demosthenes' Reproach" recalls Toynbee's and Minoo Masani's shared use of Demosthenes's warning against Athenian complacency as an analogy for democracies unprepared against Hitler and, now, Soviet Communism.

Bertram D. Wolfe's "Tito And Stalin—II" documents Soviet economic exploitation of Yugoslavia through unequal joint-stock companies and argues Tito's defiance cracked the myth of Kremlin infallibility.

K. D. Sethna reviews two Arthur Goodfriend photo-essay books, praising their attempt to counter Communism's pseudo-religious appeal with wisdom drawn from the Upanishads, Buddha, and other traditions.

Asoka Mehta's "Stalin," written just after Stalin's death, argues Stalin sought to erase individuality into a "mass-man," using Brecht's Die Massnahme against Toller's humanist tragedy to illustrate the pattern, and calls for cultural freedom as the antidote.

The "Notes" section backs Congress-Praja Socialist Party cooperation while insisting international communism remains the primary democratic threat, and supports banning communist party members from government and teaching posts.

A condensed transcript of a Tokyo roundtable, "The Intelligentsia In Modern Society," features Minoo Masani, Francois Bondy, Herbert Passin and Japanese panelists debating why 20th-century intellectuals have proven vulnerable to totalitarian co-option; Masani argues British colonial rule created an unrepresentative "new Brahmin" intelligentsia that Communists now target.

A report on the Bombay meeting "After Stalin" records M. R. Masani calling Stalin "the most efficient and ruthless embodiment of an evil system," while Asoka Mehta warns that a "hot war" is already underway in Korea.
Adam Adil's rejoinder to J. B. H. Wadia defends Indian religious tradition's historical tolerance, arguing India's social degradation stemmed from economic self-interest rather than religion itself.
A reader's letter from M. Kerkera describes Communist lawyers displacing non-Communist counsel in Industrial Courts as part of a strategy to infiltrate white-collar trade unions.
A condensed review of Carsun Chang's "The Third Force in China" is credited as the most impressive condemnation yet written of India's international policy toward China.

Philip Spratt's "The Scientist's Responsibility" argues scientific men are unusually vulnerable to Communist recruitment, documenting the World Federation of Scientific Workers as effectively Communist-controlled and India's Association of Scientific Workers as drifting toward sympathetic coverage of Communist positions.

The "Notes" section reports the Congress Working Committee's ban on members joining Communist "Peace" front conferences and criticises V. K. Krishna Menon's election to the Rajya Sabha as a possible "Trojan camel" toward a Cabinet post.

An unsigned editorial, "Godspeed," argues India's UN intervention on Korean POW repatriation weakened the moral clarity of the Western position, urging the UN Command to unilaterally release unwilling prisoners if negotiations stall.

Prabhakar Padhye's essay on the role of social reform argues Indian freedom-fighters and social reformers made mirror-image errors of subordinating one cause to the other, and warns today's champions of economic equality repeat the mistake by assuming redistribution alone will dissolve caste inequality.

M. V. Pradhan reviews Ernst and Loth's "Report on the American Communist," questioning whether its psychological framework of Party recruitment applies to India, where economic inadequacy rather than personal psychology draws the unemployed middle class to Communism.
Sidney Hook's letter argues Senator McCarthy has become a liability to America's international reputation for hounding reformed ex-Communists rather than investigating real threats.
A notice records the Indian Committee for Cultural Freedom's tea party with Adlai Stevenson during his Bombay visit, attended by M. R. Masani, J. R. D. Tata and other prominent figures.

P. Kodanda Rao's "Bilingualism For India" argues English should not be treated as a "foreign" language, proposing "vertical bilingualism" — the regional language for arts and administration, English for sciences and higher and international purposes.

The "Notes" section reads the East German and Czechoslovak workers' riots as exposing the falsity of Soviet propaganda, and criticises Health Minister Rajkumari Amrit Kaur for praising Soviet medicine uncritically.
An unsigned editorial, "Cutting The Gordian Knot," defends Syngman Rhee's unilateral release of Korean War POWs as consistent with the voluntary-repatriation principle the UN itself had endorsed.
Bertram D. Wolfe's memoir "Memories Of Yusuf Meherally" recalls Meherally's relationships with Jinnah and Gandhi and his softening view of British rule over time.

An unsigned survey, "Is Krishna Menon Pro-Communist?," traces Menon's political trajectory from Theosophist India League founder through the 1935 Comintern United Front shift to his controversial UN conduct, inviting readers to judge for themselves.

Philip Spratt reviews James Burnham's "Containment Or Liberation?," endorsing Burnham's argument that mere containment cannot defeat Soviet expansionism and that a political offensive focused on Europe is required.
Prabhakar Padhye reviews George Fischer's "Soviet Opposition to Stalin" on the Vlasov movement, and R.H. reviews Steinbeck's "East of Eden" as an explicit rejection of moral relativism.
The unsigned editorial "Freedom's Opportunity" analyses Beria's fall after Stalin's death as an opportunity for the free world to support captive peoples rather than pursue Big Four appeasement.

Michael Polanyi's "Protests And Problems" previews the Hamburg "Science and Freedom" conference, arguing that denouncing totalitarian control of scholarship requires clearer principles of intellectual liberty than presently exist, and criticises the Soviet imposition of Lysenko's biology on the Academy.

An editorial, "The Essence Of Democracy," rebuts Jayaprakash Narayan's criticism of party-based parliamentary opposition, invoking E.F.M. Durbin's "The Politics of Democratic Socialism" to defend organised opposition as essential to democracy.

Bertram D. Wolfe's "Meherally, Gandhi & The C.S.P." recounts how the Congress Socialist Party detected and expelled Communist infiltrators in the 1930s, crediting Gandhi's moral influence for the party's relative immunity to corruption, and narrates Wolfe's own conversion to admiration of Gandhi.

"The Need To Identify" defends the bulletin's practice of naming suspected Communists and fellow-travellers as distinct from McCarthyism, and reports the dismissal of Prabhakar Padhye from Navashakti for attending a discussion on "The World after Stalin."
A review section covers Arthur Koestler's autobiography "Arrow in the Blue" and Hector Hawton's "The Feast of Unreason" on Existentialism.

Letters to the editor debate Einstein's refusal to testify before congressional committees, and J. C. Daruvala protests the cancellation of D. F. Karaka's passport as a violation of freedom of travel.

An editorial, "Another Landmark," previews the Committee's second Annual General Meeting in Madras, inaugurated by C. Rajagopalachari, recapping the 1951 Bombay Congress and the resulting Declaration on Cultural Freedom.

The "Notes" section argues for a BBC-style autonomous broadcasting corporation for All India Radio, frames Mossadegh's fall in Iran as a defeat for Soviet expansion, and criticises British Labour figures for a double standard admitting Communist China's legitimacy while condemning Franco's Spain.

Francois Bondy reports at length on the Hamburg Congress on Science and Freedom, where Sydney Hook argued scientific freedom is inseparable from citizenship, geneticists documented Lysenkoism's damage, and Friedrich Hayek grounded scientific freedom in the "omnipresence of ignorance."

A reprinted exchange, "The Universality Of Human Values," pits R. H. S. Crossman, who argues Communism can still be a "liberative force" outside Europe, against M. R. Masani, who rebuts him by citing Jayaprakash Narayan, Lohia and Asoka Mehta as Asians pursuing change while resisting Soviet and Chinese imperialism.

The Indian Committee for Cultural Freedom's Annual Report, "A Year of Achievement," records the founding of Freedom First, international representation on the Congress's Executive Committee, and total membership of 495 as of August 1953.
R.H. reviews Sartre's play "Lucifer and the Lord," judging it "rambling and ill-constructed" and questioning Sartre's assumed causal link between atheism and social revolution.

C. Rajagopalachari's inaugural address "True Freedom" argues Indian culture rests on self-control rather than freedom-as-licence or state-regulation, drawing on the Isa Vasya Upanishad and Bhagavad Gita, and rejects relativism about truth as common to both Hitlerism and Communism.

Dr. Sampurnanand's presidential address "The Neuroses of the Indian Intelligentsia" diagnoses a pervasive uncertainty and rootlessness among Indian intellectuals, contrasting India unfavourably with Russia's cultural continuity through revolution, and calls for a Vedanta-rooted universalist culture to fill the spiritual vacuum.
The Annual General Meeting adopted seven resolutions spanning Bhoodan, forced labour, the Asian communist threat, solidarity with victims of totalitarian tyranny, and cultural freedom for Adivasis.
The issue also carries a review of D. F. Karaka's biography of Nehru and a "Notes" column commenting on Cold War propaganda and Indira Gandhi's remarks on the USSR.
A short report covers ICCF activities including a reception for Dr. Harry Gideonse.

R. Srinivasan's "Freedom And Discipline In Music" argues codified rules in Karnatic music enable rather than restrict improvisation, citing Leopold Stokowski's praise of Indian music's flexibility relative to Western reproduction-bound performance.

The "Notes" section welcomes Kazakh refugee defectors into Kashmir, criticises state funding of theatres as inviting bureaucratic censorship of the arts, and reports that only 19 of 921 Chinese POWs, or 2 per cent, chose repatriation to Communist China.

Philip Spratt's "The New Serfdom" reviews the 1953 ILO/UN report on forced labour, finding the Soviet Union's use of forced labour for both political punishment and economic production the worst offender, though noting some forced labour existed even in Spain, South Africa and the US.
M. Bhaktavatsalam's welcome address to the ICCF's Madras conference argues Gandhi's insistence that means be as pure as ends is the strongest defence against "ideological germ-warfare."

Faiz Noorani reviews Frank Moraes's "Report on Mao's China," praising its exposure of communist thought control while criticising Moraes's lapse into providing intellectual cover for Indian neutralism.

A review of the inaugural issue of Encounter, edited by Stephen Spender and Irving Kristol, highlights Nicolas Nabokov's essay on Soviet music and Denis de Rougemont's somewhat patronising portrait of India.

Santha Rama Rau's letter disputes a prior pseudonymous review of Perspectives, and the formal Rules of the Indian Committee for Cultural Freedom, adopted at the Madras conference, are reproduced in full.

Narie Oliaji's "Has Art A Purpose?" rejects Proudhon's utilitarian view that art must serve humanity's uplift, preferring Zola's definition of art as transformation rather than imitation, and praises Shakespeare for never taking political sides.

The "Notes" section urges sympathetic treatment of Assam's Dafla tribesmen, welcomes Ramon Magsaysay's election in the Philippines, and reports the US Army's tally of 29,815 victims of Communist Korean War atrocities.

An anonymous contributor's "The Limits Of A United Front" condemns the Praja Socialist Party's Travancore-Cochin seat-sharing arrangement with Communists as the "thin end of the wedge" toward blurring democratic-communist moral distinctions.

Bruno Shaw's "The Saga Of Wang Ti-chiu" narrates a young Chinese POW's defection from Communist indoctrination, framing the roughly 16,000 Chinese and 6,300 Korean POWs who refused repatriation as proof Communism could not hold its soldiers' loyalty.

J. B. H. Wadia's "The New Humanism: A Plea" criticises the ICCF's own conference speeches for urging acceptance of traditional restraints, proposing M. N. Roy's Radical Humanism, centred on the sanctity of the individual, as cultural freedom's proper programme.
Faiz Noorani's "Nothing Left For Communists To Destroy?" argues democracy's key advantage over dictatorship is that it can be voted out, urging patience over a protest vote for Communism.
A review section covers a Soviet Science symposium showing politically distorted genetics research, Carsun Chang's "The Third Force in China," and Karl Jaspers's "Tragedy Is Not Enough."

C. Rajagopalachari's "Hindu Philosophy In A Modern State" reads the Gita's doctrine of Karma-Yoga as the spiritual basis for a regulated, non-competitive modern economy, and distinguishes Karma from fatalism as "the truest charter of freedom and initiative."

The "Notes" section criticises India's UN abstention on the Committee on Forced Labour's report on Soviet practices, links student indiscipline to Communist exploitation of unrest, and highlights roughly 400,000 West German, Japanese and Italian nationals still held in Soviet territory.

An unsigned appreciation, "A Postscript On Eugene O'Neill," surveys O'Neill's restless movement between dramatic styles, judging "Mourning Becomes Electra" his closest approach to true tragic purpose.
T. V. Subba Rao's "Freedom Of Self-Expression" uses the Carnatic composer Tyagaraja to argue that true artistic freedom operates within, not against, inherited tradition.

Faiz Noorani reviews 'Vivek's' "India Without Illusions," praising its forthright realism about India's professed neutrality, while Aziz Madni reviews Raja Hutheesing's "Window on China" as a detached, non-propagandistic account of two visits to Mao's China.
The issue notes the founding of the Ceylon Committee for Cultural Freedom, inaugurated in Colombo on 17 November 1953.
Rex Berry's profile of Dylan Thomas, who had recently died, defends his poetic obscurity as a product of rigorous compression rather than lack of control.

John S. Connor's essay on the new humanism traces Western Liberalism's rise and its blind spots, arguing Marx synthesised Hegel, Feuerbach and Ricardo into Communism as Liberalism's chief challenger, and frames "New Humanism" as an attempt to revive a philosophically bankrupt pragmatic liberalism.

S. M. Shakoor's "The British Guiana Crisis" gives an insider account of Cheddi Jagan's communist-led People's Progressive Party capturing the colony's trade unions and Assembly, prompting the British government to suspend the constitution.

The "Notes" section endorses Ceylon PM Kotelawala's call for an Asian collective-security pact, condemns Bombay's restriction of English-medium school admissions as unconstitutional "educational apartheid," and reports leaked CPI correspondence exposing the "United Democratic Front" as a Leninist tactic to destroy, not ally with, socialist parties.

A review section covers a Soviet Cultural Delegation's disappointing ballet performance in Bombay, painter Shiavax Chavda's exhibition, and Melvin Voorhees's "Korean Tales," criticised for crude generalisations about "Oriental" peoples.
"Books in Brief" notes new titles on Baudelaire, unpublished Yeats correspondence, and the final volume of Churchill's Second World War memoirs.

Dr. Sampurnanand's essay argues India's vulnerability to Communism stems from a spiritual and moral vacuum, criticising the confusion of secularism with the absence of any faith and calling Gandhi the last to have successfully revived an authentically Indian philosophy of life.

The "Notes" section reports Professor S. N. Agarwal's challenge to the CPI to prove the "Communist Conspiracy at Madurai" documents forged, frames the Travancore-Cochin election as a defeat for Communist-aligned forces, and welcomes Senator McCarthy's political decline as proof democracies cannot fight totalitarianism with totalitarian methods.
Rex Berry's "Hemingway—The Strange Old Man" satirically portrays Hemingway's public "tough guy" persona against his private, churchgoing side.

Kobita Sarkar's "Style In The Cinema" surveys national cinematic traditions and profiles directors including Chaplin, Hitchcock, Orson Welles and the Italian neorealists as exemplars of personal directorial style.

Professor Harold H. Fisher's "Three Kinds Of Communist Colonies—II" argues foreign Communist parties constitute a distinct "third type" of colony more tightly controlled than traditional national colonies, and predicts Chinese Communism will eventually strain against Soviet dominance.
The issue reproduces the American Committee for Cultural Freedom's "Ethics Of Controversy" statement deploring McCarthyist trends, listing ten standards of ethical public discourse.

Prabhakar Padhye reviews Klaus Mehnert's "Stalin Versus Marx," tracing twelve elements by which Stalin revised Marxist doctrine, while a review of Kathleen Nott's "The Emperor's Clothes" defends liberal humanism against neo-scholastic Catholic critics.

Prabhakar Padhye's lead essay rebuts the charge that the Indian Committee for Cultural Freedom is a Western/American stooge organisation, arguing its criticism of Indian "moral neutralism" reflects principle, not pro-American bias, and noting the Committee declined financial contributions from the Paris-based international movement.

The "Notes" section argues Soviet objections to US hydrogen bomb tests are opportunistic, and reports the UN's withdrawal of consultative status from the Communist-aligned Women's International Democratic Federation.

Further notes discuss the Colombo Conference, an officially admitted Chinese famine affecting roughly 200 million people, and honour Jayaprakash Narayan's renunciation of Marxism for Vinoba Bhave's Bhoodan Yagna movement.

Yatin Gaznavi's "W. H. Auden: A View" surveys Auden's poetry on his 1953 Bollingen Prize, arguing he uniquely absorbed Freudian and Groddeckian psychoanalysis rather than merely adopting fashionable posture.
Dr. James T. Shotwell's poem "The Way," read at the Carnegie Endowment International Center's dedication, calls for global unity and justice transcending national loyalties.

Zafar Futehally reviews two David Rousset pamphlets on Soviet police-state and forced-labour methods, and a review of "Communist Conspiracy At Madurai" describes a secret CPI "Tactical Line" document proposing violent overthrow disguised as a "Government of Democratic Unity."
The American Committee for Cultural Freedom's May Day statement calls for lifting the Iron Curtain while affirming it is "morally monstrous" to equate American conditions with Soviet totalitarianism.

V. B. Karnik's "Two Crusades Or One?" rebuts Nehru's characterisation of the Cold War as a symmetrical clash of two fanatical crusades, arguing free nations share no common economic system but are united only by commitment to liberty against totalitarianism.

The "Notes" section credits U Nu of Burma as the Colombo Conference's quiet anti-communist hero, condemns the India-China Tibet treaty as "The Tibetan Sell Out," and welcomes the US Supreme Court's school desegregation ruling.

R. B. Joshi's report on the P.E.N. Third All-India Writers' Conference at Chidambaram criticises its crowded format and challenges Nehru's call for "one literature" as contrary to creative writing's rootedness in particular experience.

Prabhakar Padhye's "The Committee And The Arts" defends the autonomy of aesthetic experience against totalitarian instrumentalisation of art, citing writer Krishna Chandra as an artist hollowed out by ideological service.

Professor Theodor Litt's "Science And Moral Responsibility," delivered at the Hamburg Conference, argues scientific objectivity is not morally neutral, since social inquiry inevitably shapes the society it studies.

Yatim Ghaznavi reviews Sartre's scenario "In The Mesh," summarising Sartre's view that submitting one's will to party, religion or law denies one's freedom, while arguing Sartre conflates freedom with unmitigated licence.
The issue also records news of the Hamburg music prize winners and the American Committee's protest against the denial of a passport to playwright Arthur Miller.

V. B. Karnik's "Sapping The Foundation" criticises the Congress Working Committee's proposed constitutional amendments to Article 31 as executive encroachment on judicial review of compensation and tribunal oversight.

Two readers debate why Indian intellectuals remain suspicious of the ICCF's pro-Western stance despite historical India-US intellectual ties, one citing self-interested Western anti-communism, the other tracing warm ties from Vivekananda to the Indian Constitution's debt to US jurisprudence.
Sophia Wadia's "Aims And Activities Of P.E.N." defends the All-India P.E.N. Centre's record since its 1933 founding, citing its 1940 editorial defence of Nehru's free speech while imprisoned.

Yatim Ghaznavi reviews Albert Camus's "L'Homme Revolte" (The Rebel), summarising Camus's argument that no philosophical precept can justify "crimes de logique" such as assassination and politically justified terrorism.
T. R. Fyvel's "The Broken Dialogue," abridged from Encounter, uses the Harry Dexter White espionage case to diagnose a broader Anglo-American perception gap over internal security since 1945.

V. B. Karnik's "Threats To Freedom In The Free World" argues colonialism, especially French rule in Indo-China and British action in Kenya, and McCarthyism both weaken the free world's anti-communist cause by handing propaganda advantages to Communists.

Daphne Whittam's "A Prime Minister Makes A Movie" recounts Burmese PM U Nu's anti-communist propaganda film "The People Win Through," noting it portrays its central Communist character sympathetically as a sincere, misguided idealist.

Upton Sinclair's "Democrats With A Small 'd'" recounts his decades of civil-liberties activism and warns that American Communists now pose as small-"d" democrats infiltrating genuine civil liberties organisations.

Ruben D. Villatoro's "Red Dictatorship In Guatemala" describes how Communists built a "veritable communist trade union dictatorship" under President Arbenz, and recounts his own torture and forced deportation after challenging its Soviet funding.

A reader signing as X.Y.Z. argues Indian "moral neutrality" toward the Cold War reflects a deep-seated collectivist habit of mind rather than mere strategic calculation, conceding the ICCF's values are foreign imports worth spreading nonetheless.

A review of Robert C. North's "Moscow and the Chinese Communists" traces Lenin's 1920 programme to co-opt Asian nationalist movements, and quotes Mao Zedong rejecting any "third way" or neutrality between Soviet and "imperialist" camps.

Malcolm Muggeridge's "The Art Of Non-Conforming" argues the mid-twentieth century is marked by credulity and re-enslavement rather than enlightenment, holding that Fascism, Nazism and Communism alike attack the individual's integrity, and that non-conformity is the root of humour.

Philip Spratt's autobiographical "The Dream He Lost" recounts his journey from British Communist Party organiser and Meerut Conspiracy Case defendant to disillusionment, concluding the Soviet refusal to sustain the wartime alliance was "the biggest crime" even the Soviet government committed.

Denis de Rougemont's "The Anxiety Of Modern Man" argues that the collapse of inherited moral codes leaves individuals susceptible to totalitarian movements offering relief from the burden of choice, citing Koestler's correspondents who joined the Communist Party for its discipline.

The "Notes" section criticises China's Chou En-lai for backing Nepalese rebel Dr. K. I. Singh despite pledges of non-intervention, and reports academician N. R. Phatak's account of Indian delegates' poor conduct at Communist-sponsored conferences.

Gopal Krishna reviews Arthur Koestler's "The Invisible Writing," praising its psychological explanation for the false confessions at the Moscow Trials and framing the book as illuminating civilisation's struggle against totalitarian barbarism.
"Croebos" satirises Soviet sports diplomacy, and a brief item reports Carl Rowan's Bombay address on "A Free Press In A Free Society."

V. B. Karnik's "A Free Or Regulated Press?" assesses the Press Commission's report, endorsing improved journalists' pay but rejecting extension of the Industries (Development and Regulation) Act to newspapers as the most objectionable route to government control.

The "Notes" section criticises Mao's accelerated farm collectivisation even as Yugoslavia decollectivises, and welcomes the newly signed South-East Asia (Manila) collective-defence pact against Communist expansion.

Yatim Ghaznavi's "Arthur Rimbaud: Le Voyant," marking Rimbaud's birth centenary, analyses "Le Bateau Ivre" as the archetype of his major themes and links his eventual poetic silence to a near-mystical sense that no expression suffices for absolute truth.

Nissim Ezekiel's "Breaking The Human Spirit" reviews Igor Gouzenko's novel "The Fall of a Titan," a fictionalised account of Maxim Gorky's disillusion with Communism, praising its "blandly prosaic" realism for conveying pervasive rather than dramatic fear.
R.V.L. reviews Czeslaw Milosz's "The Captive Mind," dwelling on Milosz's concept of "Ketman," outward conformity concealing inward resistance under Soviet-aligned regimes.
A.K.W. reviews Lydia Kirk's "Postmarked Moscow" on daily Soviet life and the restricted conditions faced by Western diplomats in Moscow.

Nissim Ezekiel's profile of Stephen Spender traces his shift from 1930s socialist-leaning poetry to his editorship of the anti-communist journal Encounter, defending the ethical continuity between both phases of his career.

The "Notes" section reports Nehru's parliamentary charge that Indian Communists are tied to foreign interests, and a Ford Foundation-sponsored team's recommendation to improve Indian teachers' pay and job security.

Bertram D. Wolfe's "Strange Case Of Diego Rivera" recounts Rivera's repeated expulsions from and readmissions to the Communist Party, his hosting and rupture with the exiled Leon Trotsky, and Trotsky's eventual assassination by Stalinist agents.
M. K. Argus's satirical "A Parliamentary Report From Moscow" mocks the gullibility of British MPs on a Supreme Soviet-sponsored trip to Moscow.

G.D.P. reviews James Burnham's "The Web of Subversion" on communist-infiltrated US government networks, while questioning whether Burnham's narrow factual scope avoids taking a position on McCarthyism.
Zaffar Futehally reviews Herbert Carleton Mayer's "New Footprints of the Trojan Horse," endorsing its argument that free societies fall to internal infiltration rather than external invasion.
A reader's letter warns that the newly formed "All India Association of Democratic Lawyers" in Calcutta is a front for the Paris-based International Association of Democratic Lawyers.

Stephen Spender's "Thoughts Arising From An Incident" reflects on being accused of betraying the Spanish Republican cause for criticising Communist fabrication of evidence, arguing intellectuals should assume good faith across political camps and defending the Congress for Cultural Freedom's positive cultural programming.

The "Notes" section records President Rajendra Prasad's warnings against executive overreach into judicial functions, and reports the attack on socialist leader Asoka Mehta in Kashmir under National Conference one-party rule.

Nissim Ezekiel's "The Case Of Comrade Adib" exposes Times of India columnist Sham Lal's pseudonymous "Adib" column as selectively quoting and misrepresenting anti-Communist writers including Salvador de Madariaga, Hemingway and Bertrand Russell.

Writing as "Ashad," an essay on Ilya Ehrenburg's "The Writer and His Craft" argues Ehrenburg cannot acknowledge that political control of literature, not merely excessive industrial themes, is the root cause of Soviet writing's decline.

Principal G. R. Dalvi reviews M. R. Masani's "The Communist Party of India — A Short History," arguing that opposition to Communism must be grounded in a scientific, humanist social philosophy rather than religion or nationalism alone.
An unsigned obituary for Soviet prosecutor Andrei Vyshinsky traces his role in the Moscow show trials following Kirov's murder, which sent many of Lenin's former colleagues to death or exile.

Laeeq Futehally reviews Frank Rounds Jr.'s "A Window on Red Square" on everyday Moscow life under constant surveillance, and Faiz Noorani reviews Aubrey Mennen's "Rama Retold" as an unsuccessful burlesque of the Ramayana.

Charles Morgan's presidential address to the XXVI International PEN Congress in Amsterdam reflects on the rarity of peace for his generation and the writer's obligation to bear witness, invoking the Centre of Writers in Exile as PEN's especial charge.

The "Notes" section rebuts the false "bread or freedom" choice via Ignazio Silone, praises a Gandhian-style unarmed peace mission used to quell rebellion in Tunisia, and criticises the enacted defamation-of-public-servants clause in the Criminal Procedure Code Amendment Bill.

V. B. Karnik's "The Prime Minister And Communists" defends and extends Nehru's condemnation of Indian Communists as anti-national, arguing Indian communism is an instrument of an internationally directed, Moscow-controlled apparatus.

An unsigned piece, "Real Wages In Soviet Russia," summarises Janet G. Chapman's statistical study concluding Soviet workers in 1952 stood roughly at pre-1917-revolution parity, blaming forced collectivisation and neglected consumer-goods production.

Stephen Spender's "The Writer And Freedom" engages Marxist critic George Lukacs, defining artistic freedom as the "vital margin" separating a socially responsible artist from being reduced to a mechanical instrument of ideology.

A report, "Mr. Nabokov In India," covers Nicolas Nabokov's Bombay and Delhi visit, including his press conference on the "conformist tendency of modern intellectuals" and meeting with Prime Minister Nehru.

Letters to the editor debate whether the Congress for Cultural Freedom is more than "intellectual opportunism" and criticise Principal Dalvi's dismissive review of Gandhism and the Bhoodan Movement as anti-communist forces.

The unsigned lead article "The Problems of Cultural Freedom in Asia" (by Prabhakar Padhye) previews the Rangoon Conference on Cultural Freedom in Asia (17-20 February 1955) and argues Asian intellectuals need positive democratic alternatives such as Gandhism, Radical Humanism and Buddhist Socialism, not just anti-communist polemic, to counter communism's appeal.

A "Notes" column praises Nehru's Indian Science Congress address for defending scientists' independence, treats the Djilas-Dedijer Yugoslav trials as a tragic curdling of decentralisation into orthodoxy, dismisses Rajagopalachari's call for unilateral US nuclear disarmament as naive, and relates Mrinalini Sarabhai's account of restricted freedoms on a dance tour of East Germany.

A news report names India's six-member delegation to the Rangoon conference (Jayaprakash Narayan, M. R. Masani, Asoka Mehta, Eric da Costa, Ram Singh, Laxmanshastri Joshi) with Prabhakar Padhye serving as General Secretary.

Karl A. Wittfogel's centrepiece essay, "The Historical Position of Communist China: Doctrine and Reality," draws on suppressed Marx and Lenin writings on "Oriental despotism" to argue Communist China is not a proto-socialist society but a new form of "general (state) slavery" run by a monopoly managerial bureaucracy.

Nissim Ezekiel announces the launch of Quest, a new bi-monthly arts-and-ideas journal sponsored by the Indian Committee for Cultural Freedom, intended to complement Freedom First with a more ambitious literary and cultural mandate.

A "C.C.F. News" column reports on Congress for Cultural Freedom activities worldwide, including an Ernst Reuter memorial lecture series in Berlin and a Preuves meeting in Paris where Andrzej Panufnik and Czeslaw Milosz testified on artistic repression in Communist Poland.

Four book reviews cover U Nu's Burma Under the Japanese (V.B.K.), Celina Lu Zanne's Heritage of Buddha (Madan Lal Sharma), Rorty and Decter's McCarthy and the Communists (Faiz Noorani), and R. N. Carew Hunt's Marxism: Past and Present (Gopal Krishna).

Letters to the editor debate the Committee's anti-communist orientation, with J. K. Kotewal defending continued vigilance and J. Dubashi disputing a prior article's Soviet real-wages statistics, met by an editorial correction of a units error.
The closing 'With Many Voices' page collects topical quotations from Rajagopalachari, Stalin, Vinoba Bhave, S. Radhakrishnan and others on Soviet planning costs and Cold War politics.

U Ba Nyunt, Mayor of Rangoon, opens the Conference on Cultural Freedom in Asia with an inaugural address, "Culture And Freedom," arguing culture cannot flourish without freedom and warning the Welfare State's expansion of planning risks becoming 'a new form of imperialism.'

An unsigned report on the Rangoon conference lists thirty-five delegates from twelve countries and records M. R. Masani's argument that co-existence may be possible between states but not between the cultures of democracy and communism, alongside Jayaprakash Narayan's keynote on Bhoodan as voluntary social action.

Messages of support to the conference from Lin Yutang, Sir Arthur Wijeyewardhene, Kotaro Tanaka, Han Suyin and Bertrand Russell are reproduced, urging the Congress for Cultural Freedom to remain free of party affiliation and stressing Asia's spiritual traditions.

A 'Notes' column reads Malenkov's fall and Bulganin's rise as evidence Khrushchev has had to placate army interests, praises a 150-signatory Telugu writers' declaration for parliamentary democracy, and satirises a new 'United Marxist Party' in Bombay for claiming independence from Moscow while remaining pro-Soviet.

S. S. Vasan, President of the Film Federation of India, argues in a reproduced speech, "Problems Of The Indian Cinema," that Indian cinema's slow artistic progress owes to low economic standards and mass tastes, and proposes reforms including reduced admission tax and liberalised censorship.

Yatin Gaznavi's essay-review of Jacques Maritain's Man and the State argues political conflict lies less in competing lists of rights than in the hierarchy of values by which they are ordered, while explicitly dissenting from Maritain's claim that only the Church can handle 'matters of intelligence.'

Three reviews cover R. P. Masani's Education for World Understanding (Adam Adil), Tadeusz Wittlin's Reluctant Traveller in Russia on two years in Soviet forced-labour camps (Laeeq Futehally), and a Czechoslovak Industries Exhibition in Bombay.

I.C.C.F. News reports a Calcutta send-off tea party for delegates departing to Rangoon and a Poona Group lecture series on Maharashtra's nineteenth-century reform trends, covering Agarkar, Shinde and Phuley.

'With Many Voices' closes with press quotations including Clement Attlee comparing Russian foreign policy to Tsarist imperialism and Sir John Kotelawala crediting America's atom bomb with keeping 'free Asia' free of war.

Prof. Hannan Ezekiel's lead essay, "The Dangers Of Physical Planning," warns that P. C. Mahalanobis's 'physical planning' model for the Second Five Year Plan carries an inherently totalitarian tendency, citing D. R. Gadgil's fear that the National Sample Survey could 'exterminate all parallel agencies.'

Sir John Latham, President of the Australian Committee for Cultural Freedom, argues in "The Free Spirit Of Man" that tolerance of opposing opinion is essential to progress, since any regime claiming infallibility treats dissent as heresy leading to labour camps and liquidation.

A 'Notes' section welcomes Congress's defeat of the Communist Party in the Andhra elections despite the Communists retaining 31.6% of the vote, reports Sir Mirza Ismail's speech on communist infiltration, and rebukes New Statesman editor Kingsley Martin for saying he would have voted communist in Andhra.

An unsigned report on a British Ministry of Defence booklet, "Communist China And Prisoners Of War," documents the mistreatment and 're-education' of 978 British POWs held by Communist China during the Korean War, noting only 40 were judged genuine converts.

Martin S. Dworkin's "George Orwell On The Screen," reprinted from the New Leader, criticises the Halas and Batchelor animated film of Orwell's Animal Farm for its Disney-influenced style and 'heavy' narration, judging it more effective propaganda for Europeans unfamiliar with Soviet history than for readers of the book.

Reviews cover Manes Sperber's novel Journey Without End on Jewish resistance in a doomed Polish village (N.E.), C. Groves Haines's The Threat of Soviet Imperialism featuring George F. Kennan (M.B.S.), and Karl Barth's Against the Stream, whose 'narrow path between Moscow and Rome' the reviewer judges untenable given Soviet capacity for terror.
C.C.F. News previews the Congress for Cultural Freedom's Milan conference on 'The Future of Freedom' (September 1955) and a Paris exhibition of paintings by Indian artist Laxman Pai.

I.C.C.F. News reports the Committee's new Bombay office and a members' meeting at which M. David Rousset described evidence of slave labour camps in Communist China and plans for an Asian tribunal of inquiry.

'With Many Voices' includes Ambedkar's remark comparing the Constitution to a temple now occupied by 'devils' and Salvador de Madariaga's warning that ordinary Russians, not the regime, hold the moral claim on Western sympathy.

The unsigned editorial 'Towards A Communist Pattern?' alleges the Second Five Year Plan's drafting team under Mahalanobis is dominated by Iron Curtain economists, quoting Jayaprakash Narayan's charge that its 'seven authors... are all men from behind the Iron Curtain,' and criticises V. K. R. V. Rao's proposed National Labour Force as a possible precursor to forced labour.

Guy J. Pauker's essay 'Sardar Panikkar -- A Gifted Opportunist,' abridged from World Politics, portrays K. M. Panikkar as an opportunist whose Asia and Western Dominance was written to flatter Asian audiences seeking to accommodate Soviet and Chinese power, quoting Nehru's remark that Panikkar 'will be Communist in Peking and a champion of freedom in Washington.'

Yatim Ghaznavi's essay 'Literature And Belief' argues twentieth-century fiction suffers an 'erosion of the imaginative soil' as science and psychoanalysis annex territory once held by religion, finding even Graham Greene and Evelyn Waugh incapable of 'full-blooded doubt.'

Reviews cover Max Beloff's Soviet Policy in the Far East (Aziz Madni), a Ford Foundation report on its India-supported activities (R.H.), and Ignazio Silone's novel A Handful of Blackberries about a disillusioned Italian communist party worker (Laeeq Futehally).
Letters to the editor debate Dr. Kalidas Nag's foreword to a poetry translation and propose forming 'The Friends of Democratic Nations' to counter communist propaganda domestically.

A news report describes Justice U Chan Htoon of Burma's Supreme Court touring Bombay under I.C.C.F. auspices, linking Buddhist revival in Burma, Thailand and Ceylon to resistance against communism and materialism.
C.C.F. News notes the Italian Association for Cultural Freedom's Rome meeting and a Hamburg lecture series including Siegfried Landshut on 'Karl Marx in our Time.'

'With Many Voices' closes with quotations from Lal Bahadur Shastri and Master Tara Singh on communism, alongside the ICCF membership enrolment form and the masthead naming editor V. B. Karnik and printer Prabhakar Padhye.

V. B. Karnik's lead essay 'Bandung: A Step Towards Integration' argues the Bandung Conference of twenty-nine Asian-African nations became an unexpected rebuke of communism despite fears it would become a pro-communist or anti-Western platform, with China under Chou En-lai playing a conciliatory rather than propagandistic role.

A 'Notes' section praises trade unionists who refused Chinese May Day invitations, criticises the Congress Working Committee's move toward stricter film censorship, endorses Vinoba Bhave's and Morarji Desai's calls for education free of state control, and reports the persecution and deportation of Kalmuck Buddhists in the USSR.

Hasan Muhammad Tiro's report on communist infiltration in Indonesia warns that Premier Ali Sastroamidjojo's government has postponed elections while purging anti-communist officers and pardoning 1948 Madiun coup plotters into ministerial posts.

An unsigned piece and a companion account by Edward Hunter, author of Brain-Washing in Red China, describe the communist campaign that forced Dr. Lin Yu-tang to resign as founding Vice-Chancellor of Nanyang University in Singapore, followed by deadly student rioting.

A review signed 'N.E.' praises Maria Yen's The Umbrella Garden for its firsthand, unembellished account of student life in Red China, tracing the arc from benign early discipline to mandatory 'communal living' and government-assigned graduate jobs.

'Bandung: As Others See It' surveys international press reaction, quoting New York Times correspondents Tilman Durdin and Robert Aldon on Krishna Menon's private criticism of Nehru's handling of the conference and Burma's U Nu's quietly effective role.

Letters to the editor cover a Bombay meeting on Muslim political withdrawal since 1947 (Zafar Fatehally) and an idiosyncratic call for Indian disengagement from Asian geopolitics grounded in 'spiritual doctrines' (Raman Desai).
'With Many Voices' closes with Chester Bowles on Asian revolutions being led by frustrated middle-class intellectuals and Arthur Koestler's chastened line that 'we can at best hope for a reprieve.'

The unsigned editorial 'Let There Be No Mistake' defends Freedom First's earlier criticism of the Mahalanobis Plan Frame now that primary documents are available, citing B. C. Roy's and B. R. Shenoy's dissenting notes, and rejects Congress General Secretary Shriman Narayan's charge that the Committee is a capitalist mouthpiece.

Prof. W. Arthur Lewis's reprinted 'A Socialist Economic Policy' argues Britain's inherited socialist tools -- progressive taxation, economic controls, nationalisation -- have reached the limits of their usefulness and calls for redistributing property ownership more broadly instead of further nationalisation.

Prabhakar Padhye's 'Planning For Freedom' questions whether a one-party-dominated legislature can meaningfully approve the Plan rather than merely rubber-stamp it, while welcoming cottage-industry provisions as a decentralising counterweight to heavy industry.

A review signed 'N.E.' of George N. Schuster's Religion Behind the Iron Curtain documents systematic persecution of religion across the Soviet bloc, quoting a condemned man's son's 1952 letter and Cardinal Mindszenty's final scribbled note to his mother.

A statement drafted by Sir John Latham for the Australian Committee for Cultural Freedom on obscene-literature legislation argues censorship is undesirable in principle except for customs control of imports, recommending court prosecution over an administrative Board of Review.
The 'Notes' section covers Soviet-Yugoslav relations, home rule in Tunisia, Chinese payment-in-kind labour policy, and debates over textbook shortages and the English-language question.

The unsigned editorial 'At The Post' announces that this is the last issue of Freedom First published under the Indian Committee for Cultural Freedom banner, continuing instead under the Democratic Research Service as the new journal Quest takes over the literary and cultural brief.

A 'Notes' section warns against Great Power deals over Asian nations made without their elected representatives, argues Vietnam-wide elections would be meaningless unless northern voters can freely oppose Ho Chi Minh, and recounts the Kerala 'Tactical Line' controversy over a leaked Communist Party document.

Arthur Koestler's 'The Trail of the Dinosaur -- I,' reprinted from Encounter, charts humanity's growing destructive power against a stagnant moral curve and argues atomic superiority cannot deter limited, camouflaged local aggression.

The unsigned 'Planning And Democracy' takes issue with Nehru's reported remark that democracy's 'structure' might need reconsidering if it obstructs planning, insisting democracy must come first and planning second, only as a means to a better life.

J. G. Tewari's 'The Danger In Indo-China' argues the Nehru-Bulganin declaration's call for prompt Vietnamese elections, without adequate safeguards against a Communist-controlled North holding 13 million people, plays into Communist strategy to conquer the whole country.

Sudhir Hendre reviews Robert St. John's Through Malan's Africa, describing apartheid South Africa's brutal inequality and tracing discriminatory legislation against Natal Indians from an 1892 poll-tax to the 1946 Ghetto Act.

'With Many Voices' closes on N. V. Gadgil's quip linking planning to rising unemployment and a West Bengal Congress leader's statement that a violence-prone party flying 'a foreign flag' has no right to exist in India.

Nissim Ezekiel's 'Our Concern For Africa' argues India's condemnation of colonialism substitutes moral indignation for genuine political understanding, pointing to Indians' own persistent colour consciousness toward Africans living in India.

Zafar Futehally's report previews the Congress for Cultural Freedom's international conference on 'The Future of Freedom' in Milan (12-17 September 1955), naming attendees including Raymond Aron, J. K. Galbraith, Hayek and India's M. R. Masani, B. R. Shenoy and Amlan Dutta.

A 'Notes' section questions arbitrary Indian passport refusals, condemns escalating violence in Morocco and Algeria, argues hartals are increasingly inappropriate against an elected government, reports Jayaprakash Narayan's condemnation of the August 1955 Patna police firings, and honours Goa satyagrahis killed by Portuguese authorities.

Edward Shils's 'Intellectuals And Politicians In America' traces the historical estrangement between American intellectuals and politicians from the Republic's founding through McCarthyism, concluding the episode set back but did not reverse a century-long healing of the rift.

Arthur Koestler's 'The Trail of the Dinosaur -- II' examines the long-term decline of religious faith since the Copernican revolution, warning nuclear and bacteriological weapons will soon decide whether humanity 'goes the way of the dinosaur.'
A letter from Prabhakar Padhye argues bread and freedom form a unity rather than a false dichotomy, pressing Freedom First to recognise 'economic freedom' as integral to its concept of liberty.
I.C.C.F. News reports the opening of the Congress for Cultural Freedom's Asian office in New Delhi, headed by Padhye, and lectures by Kodanda Rao and Edward Shils.

'With Many Voices' quotes Eisenhower on never trading freedom 'for the pottage of a false peace' and communist leader P. Ramamurthi crediting Nehru's foreign policy to Lenin's thesis of peaceful co-existence.

V. B. Karnik's lead essay 'A Tactic Or A New Policy?' weighs whether the post-Stalin Soviet 'thaw' is genuine or tactical, citing the Austrian Treaty and Geneva summit against Khrushchev's own warning that the smile does not mean abandoning Marx and Lenin.

A 'Notes' section welcomes South Vietnam's new republic under Diem, endorses Nehru's sympathetic approach to North-East Frontier tribal peoples while warning of Chinese infiltration, and criticises a proposed National Book Trust as risking political favouritism over private publishing.

M. R. Masani's report on the Congress for Cultural Freedom's Milan conference details debates on planning versus freedom, contested claims about Soviet economic progress, and his own intervention pressing Western delegates on solidarity with underdeveloped countries.

An unsigned report on Indonesia's first general election describes a dangerously fragmented result -- Nationalists, Masjumi, Nahdatul Ulama and Communists near-even -- warning a nationalist-led coalition reliant on communist support could produce a Soviet-satellite 'people's democracy.'

'History In The Making In Soviet Russia' reproduces the 1954 and 1955 Soviet Encyclopedic Dictionary entries on Malenkov side by side, showing his biography cut from 108 to 53 lines after his resignation, and compares the practice to Orwell's 1984.

Reviews cover Philip Spratt's Blowing Up India, tracing his path from Comintern agent implicated in the Meerut Conspiracy case to disillusioned anti-communist writer (Aziz Madni), and Dagobert Runes's The Soviet Impact on Society, arguing communism reproduced capitalism's worst features once implemented (M.B.S.).
'With Many Voices' includes Picasso dismissing Soviet painting as monotonous and militaristic, and Acharya Kripalani's self-description as 'a paralysed socialist.'

V. B. Karnik's lead article 'Let Us Know Who Kisses Us And Why' criticises the Indian government's elaborate, state-orchestrated reception of Bulganin and Khrushchev, objecting to the 'cynical use... of children as instruments of diplomacy' and the Soviet leaders' attacks on Western democracies during their Parliament address.

A 'Notes' section endorses Vinoba Bhave's view that states reorganisation is chiefly administrative, condemns the twelve deaths in police firing during the Samyukta Maharashtra agitation, and disputes Rajkumari Amrit Kaur's claim that China's health services outpace India's.

Bertram D. Wolfe's 'Peaceful Co-Existence' dissects the term as Soviet 'Newspeak' masking simultaneous internal purges and external world conquest, tracing its origins to Trotsky's 1917 peace programme and Lenin's opportunistic use of peace rhetoric.

M. B. Shah's 'Philosophy Of Freedom' traces freedom's historical emergence through liberalism, arguing democracy's failure to realise the Declaration of the Rights of Man in practice fuelled fascism and communism, and calls for a 'positive freedom' via Erich Fromm and M. N. Roy.

W. Z. Laqueur's 'The Double Think And Double Talk,' reprinted from The New Leader, contrasts Bulganin and Khrushchev's public praise of Gandhi with Soviet textbooks that still call him a 'traitor,' tracing Soviet experts' opportunistic reversal on Nehru.
Laeeq Futehally's light essay 'Our New Hobby' wryly observes Bombay's new enthusiasm for Nature excursions to spots like Powai Lake and a boom in domestic gardening.
I.C.C.F. News reports Nicolas Nabokov's November 1955 tour of India and the Committee's Annual General Meeting scheduled for 17-18 December in Bombay.
'With Many Voices' quotes Anthony Eden arguing free elections cannot be held while Germany's communist system must be preserved.

M. A. Venkata Rao's 'The Challenge Of The Visit' reads the Bulganin-Khrushchev tour of India and Burma, alongside a Soviet 'Nyet' at Geneva and a hydrogen bomb test, as one calculated Soviet peace offensive that risks blurring the moral distinction between Gandhian Congress values and Bolshevik practice.

Asiaticus's 'China Enters Stalinism' traces escalating Chinese Communist campaigns from 1951 film criticism through the 1955 Hu Feng affair, citing 271,074 arrests and concluding China may eventually exceed Soviet-era terror given its greater backwardness.

An unsigned 'Notes' section urges investigation of an Indian reportedly detained in the Vorkuta labour camp, praises the two Lok Sabha members, N. C. Chatterjee and H. V. Kamath, who alone protested the Soviet visit, and criticises a Bombay High Court ruling that passport denial is non-justiciable.

An unsigned report on the I.C.C.F.'s Third General Meeting (17-18 December 1955) records addresses by Asoka Mehta and Nicolas Nabokov and four resolutions, including disapproval of mobilising schoolchildren during the Soviet visit.

'What Would The Marshal Have Said?' describes the cancelled Bombay Press Guild reception for Bulganin and Khrushchev and a combative Rangoon press exchange challenging the Soviets on Panchashila's applicability to their own satellites.

Philip Spratt reviews Gabriel Almond's The Appeals of Communism, highlighting its finding that Communist propaganda emphasises tactical discipline (94%) far more than ideal 'goal qualities' (6%) in canonical texts.

A report details Nicolas Nabokov's December tour of Madras, Bangalore, Mysore and Bombay, and a reader's letter from S. S. Bankeshwar accuses Nehru of a double standard on US versus Soviet military aid and weapons tests.

V. B. Karnik's editorial 'Where Is India Heading?' uses a Times of India editorial on the Congress Amritsar session to warn that the shift from 'socialistic pattern' to 'socialist structure,' adopted without debate, risks one-party totalitarian drift.

A 'Notes' section rebuts a Blitz allegation that the Democratic Research Service instigated the Samyukta Maharashtra riots, criticises a new Copyright Bill for halving the copyright term to 25 years, and reports Austria's success in expelling the communist-aligned World Federation of Trade Unions from Vienna.

Bertram D. Wolfe's essay on the post-Stalin 'collective leadership' of Khrushchev, Bulganin, Malenkov, Molotov and Beria argues the Soviet system's lack of any legitimate succession mechanism makes collective rule an inherently unstable interregnum.
Alex Atkinson's satirical mock travel-brochure 'Come To Sunny Russia,' reprinted from Punch, lampoons Soviet tourism propaganda against the real drabness and surveillance of Moscow life.

An item on the PEN International controversy quotes President Charles Morgan's 1955 questions about whether a Soviet PEN centre could ever be genuinely free of state control, and his refusal to admit writers who are 'instruments of tyranny.'

Reviews cover Sister Cecilia, an escaped Slovak nun's memoir of Czechoslovak communist persecution (A.A.), the launch of the new magazine The Ambassador edited by Sudhir Hendre, and Walter Lippmann's The Public Philosophy, which the reviewer connects to the Indian idea of raja dharma.
I.C.C.F. News reports a Martha Graham seminar, a lecture by Prof. W. S. Woytinsky on the world economy, and a reception for four visiting Japanese women writers.

The unsigned editorial 'Stalin: A Vindication' marks the third anniversary of Stalin's death, arguing the Soviet leadership's own denunciation of Stalin vindicates the journal's earlier criticism while naming Khrushchev, Bulganin, Mikoyan and Molotov as his willing accomplices.

V. B. Karnik's 'Wait And Watch' argues the 20th CPSU Congress rejected Stalinism while retaining Leninism, counselling a cautious middle path between naive trust and reflexive dismissal of Soviet reform.

Franz Borkenau's 'How Mao Bluffed Dulles,' from the New Leader, argues the 1955 Formosa crisis was a deliberate bluff to mask Mao's internal 'Second Revolution' of agrarian collectivisation, and predicts China will deal with Russia and the West on near-equal terms within a decade.
Richard Mowrer's 'The Soviet Woos Franco Spain' documents Soviet efforts since 1954 to court Franco's Spain via prisoner releases and trade, aiming to detach Spain from US economic dependence.

A 'Notes' section reports Jayaprakash Narayan's election as Honorary Chairman of the Congress for Cultural Freedom alongside Bertrand Russell and Jacques Maritain, and a Soviet circus defector's eyewitness testimony of Russian military participation in the Korean War.

Reviews cover M. A. Venkata Rao on Nicolai Hartmann's Ethics, and a Hague brochure on 'Law in Communist China' based on Father Andre Bonnichon's testimony describing a system where arrest itself is treated as proof of guilt.
Four Bombay I.C.C.F. members' letter protests the government's handling of the Bombay/Samyukta Maharashtra dispute; the editor replies defending the journal's neutrality on the dispute's merits.

M. A. Venkata Rao's 'Two Thousand Five Hundred Years' marks the Buddha's 2500th anniversary, reading his rejection of external authority as a contrast to totalitarian states that mould the individual mind.

A 'Notes' section recounts the hostile British reception of Bulganin and Khrushchev's 1956 UK visit, reports the collapse of Singapore student emigration to Communist China after early arrivals discovered repression, and dismisses the Cominform's dissolution as a hollow gesture.
S. R. Tikekar's 'Copyright Bill: Author's Viewpoint' criticises the new Bill for halving the copyright term to 25 years and vesting commissioned works' copyright in employers rather than authors.

'The End Of Equality In U.S.S.R.' cites Mikoyan's admission of a 62-to-1 income disparity between scientists and average Soviet workers to argue regulated capitalism has achieved more equality than Soviet-style planning.
Nabakishore Das's 'Prospects Of Democracy In India' warns that caste hierarchy and illiteracy, documented via 1951 Census figures, threaten Indian democracy absent a genuine opposition party.

A review of the symposium Why I Oppose Communism traces Minoo Masani's contribution recounting disillusionment with the USSR after the 1936 Purges, alongside M. A. Venkata Rao's review of Bertrand Russell's Human Society In Ethics And Politics.
A reader's letter cites Raymond Garthoff's How Russia Makes War to add further evidence of Soviet military pay disparities between privates and generals.

V. B. Karnik's 'Verdict On China' reports an international Brussels commission's findings, corroborated by 89 released Catholic missionaries, that forced labour in Communist China is economically embedded and 'reform through labour' constitutes 'a true concentrationary system.'

M. A. Venkata Rao's 'Neogy Upsets The Apple Cart' details Planning Commission member K. C. Neogy's dissent, alongside B. R. Shenoy and C. N. Vakil, warning that deficit financing near Rs. 1200 crores would generate serious inflation.

A profile of visiting American novelist James T. Farrell situates him in the naturalist tradition of Dreiser and Sinclair Lewis, noting his refusal to let Marxism dictate his individual judgment despite earlier Trotskyite associations.
'Operation Lullaby' analyses the CPI's Fourth Congress at Palghat as mirroring 1930s Popular Front tactics, warning of growing Congress tolerance toward the CPI as a legitimate opposition.

V.B.K.'s review of Alwin H. Scaff's The Philippine Answer to Communism recounts President Magsaysay's 'all-out force and all-out friendship' defeat of the Huk rebellion via the EDCOR resettlement programme.
A correspondent's report on an I.C.C.F. seminar in Poona covers Maharashtra's casteism and liberal heritage, with M. R. Masani forcefully countering claims that liberalism was 'dead and gone.'

A four-page supplement, 'Social Democrats In Communist Jails,' reproduces a letter to Khrushchev and Bulganin from international socialist leaders including Julius Braunthal, Norman Thomas and A. Philip Randolph, demanding release of over 350 imprisoned socialists and trade unionists across the USSR and Eastern Europe.

The unsigned editorial 'Only A Handful' rebuts Nehru's claim that only a 'handful' of critics disagree with non-alignment, arguing Indian foreign policy applies a double standard by staying silent on Soviet purges while condemning Western colonialism.

A 'Notes' section reports renewed persecution of Milovan Djilas despite Tito's Moscow rapprochement, profiles new Soviet Foreign Minister Dmitri Shepilov's earlier letter instructing Indian communists to avoid embarrassing Indo-Soviet diplomacy, and covers U Nu's surprise resignation in Burma.

G. S. Bhargava's 'The Double Standard In Action,' abridged from The New Leader, diagnoses Indian intellectuals' selective outrage -- fury at the Rosenberg executions but silence on Beria's execution -- and links Nehru's Soviet tilt to managing domestic communists.

Ida Dhami's 'Whither Algeria?' surveys the Algerian independence crisis, noting nine million indigenous Algerians against roughly one million French colons, and warns of Soviet or Egyptian exploitation if no settlement is reached.

Adam Adil's 'Can Socialists & Communists Cooperate?' examines talks between Jayaprakash Narayan, Asoka Mehta and CPI's Ajoy Ghosh, citing the 1948 Czechoslovak coup and the deaths of Jan Masaryk and President Benes as the definitive warning against united fronts with communists.

A letter from S. R. Mohan Das corrects an earlier note on the INTUC's stance on the right to strike, and I.C.C.F. News reports James T. Farrell's Bombay and Delhi visit, including a long interview with the Prime Minister.
'With Many Voices' quotes Ajoy Kumar Ghosh admitting the 'cult of personality' around Nehru is well developed in India, alongside Eisenhower calling communism 'a gigantic failure.'

V. B. Karnik's 'The Indictment Of Stalin' surveys global reaction to Khrushchev's secret speech, arguing the condemnation is self-serving since it excuses earlier purges of Trotsky and Bukharin and offers no pledge of civil liberties or habeas corpus.

K. K. Sinha's 'The Guilty Men And Their System' argues Stalin's crimes were the structural product of Leninist party dictatorship, predicting reverence will simply transfer to a new 'Great Pupil of Lenin.'

M. A. Venkata Rao's 'The Poznan Portent' treats the June 1956 Polish workers' revolt as proof of Soviet planning's failure, tracing the unrest to bread shortages, suppressed nationalism, and the retention of roughly two million Poles in Soviet labour camps.

Solidarity statements from European intellectuals including Albert Camus, Karl Jaspers, Arthur Koestler and Ignazio Silone, and from prominent Indians including Sophia Wadia and B. R. Shenoy, demand an end to repression of the Poznan workers' leaders.

A 'Notes' section criticises Congress President U. N. Dhebar's remark equating loyalty to Nehru with not opposing his wishes, links it to C. D. Deshmukh's resignation speech, and endorses C. Rajagopalachari's warning about an uncritically adulatory Indian press.

'With Many Voices' quotes K. M. Munshi lamenting that no university teaches Gandhi's or Ramakrishna's philosophy, and Frank Moraes warning Soviet strategy is shifting from coexistence to popular fronts.

V. B. Karnik's 'Strange If True' argues that even limited electoral 'adjustments' between the PSP and Communist Party would inevitably escalate into a united front, invoking the 1930s Congress Socialist Party precedent and Burma's AFPFL experience as cautionary parallels.

A 'Notes' section reports Chinese incursion into Burmese territory, criticises the Madhya Pradesh Niyogi Committee report on Christian missionaries as 'reckless,' and reveals C. D. Deshmukh's resignation disclosures on unconstitutional cabinet decision-making over Bombay's reorganisation.

An unsigned report traces Indonesia's post-election cabinet formation, in which the Communist Party (P.K.I.) became Asia's second-largest despite ultimately being excluded from the resulting government.

M. A. Venkata Rao's piece on the planned Asian Writers' Conference questions whether a unified 'Asian Mind' exists, arguing the Moscow-aligned sponsors intend the Delhi conference as a communist 'Front' or 'communication belt.'

Eugene Lyons's 'An Open Letter To A Fellow-Traveller,' addressed to novelist Howard Fast, presses him to recognise his response to Khrushchev's revelations as 'a cry for help' rather than a genuine break from communism.
M. A. Venkata Rao reviews Klaus Mehnert's Stalin versus Marx, concluding Soviet ideology's shift to national conservatism amounts to 'a new Fascism -- a strange meeting of extremes.'
'With Many Voices' quotes Nehru saying no one in a communist country can raise their head against Party decisions, and K.P.S. Menon noting India has 'followed your (Soviet) example' economically.

An exclusive interview has Jayaprakash Narayan deny any ideological sympathy for the CPI while defending a narrowly tactical electoral seat-adjustment as a safeguard against near one-party Congress rule, explicitly ruling out any united front.

'Fresh Light On Communist Machinations' describes the Democratic Research Service's disclosure of secret CPI Fourth Congress documents revealing internal 'frustration and cynicism' and continued fealty to Moscow even after de-Stalinisation.

V. B. Karnik's 'The Danger To Democracy' welcomes JP's clarification but criticises his suggestion that communists be allowed to govern a state democratically, since once in power they entrench themselves and end free elections.

M. A. Venkata Rao's 'Behind U Nu's Resignation' attributes the Burmese leader's surprise retirement to disillusionment with Soviet and Chinese embassy interference rather than his stated reason of party purification.

A translated Soviet article by Yu. P. Nasenko, reproduced as evidence of Moscow's own analysis, dismisses Indian socialists' 'democratic socialism' as cover for hostility to Marxism and alleges American funding of the 1951-52 Socialist election campaign.

'A Misleading Report' criticises an Indian delegation's report on Chinese agricultural collectivisation for taking propaganda at face value while its own text admits middle and upper farmers were eliminated 'through terror and coercion.'

The 'Notes' section covers a communal riot linked to a republished book, film censorship of the American documentary 'With These Hands,' and the Punjab Special Powers Press Act's pre-censorship provisions.

M. A. Venkata Rao's 'Homage To Hungary' argues the Hungarian uprising went further than Poland's protests by rejecting the entire one-party communist system, recounting Soviet suppression of Budapest demonstrators and appeals to Nehru from Ference Nagy and Western intellectuals.

V. B. Karnik's 'Asian Socialist Conference' argues Asian socialists can pursue industrialisation without sacrificing civil liberties, rejecting the claim that totalitarian methods are necessary, and citing Nazi Germany and Stalinist Russia as counterexamples that never produced democratic societies.

An unsigned 'Soviet Economy And Its Problems' marshals Pravda, Khrushchev, Bulganin and Mikoyan's own admissions of falling livestock numbers, chronic housing shortages and consumer-goods scarcity to indict Soviet central planning.
