Adam Adil's 'Situation In South Africa' documents the forced removal of over 100,000 non-whites, including 22,000 Indians, from Johannesburg under the Group Areas Act, with losses to Indian traders estimated at over £22 million.

A 'Notes' section reads the Sino-Nepal Treaty as extending Chinese influence at India's expense and criticises Nehru for supporting a restrictive new Punjab press bill despite his own democratic history.
Reviews cover Walter Laqueur's Communism and Nationalism in the Middle East and the anthology From Darkness to Light, drawing on the Upanishads, the Gita and modern Indian thinkers.

A reader's letter signed 'Politicus' argues India's Single Member Constituency system risks squeezing out moderate parties, leaving only Congress and the Communist Party viable and risking 'hanging democracy by its own rope.'

The unsigned editorial 'D.R.S. Answers The P.M.' rebuts Nehru's Parliamentary charge that the Democratic Research Service and I.C.C.F. are communist-front organisations, detailing the DRS's 1950 founding under Sardar Patel's blessing and reproducing Jayaprakash Narayan's public defence of its record.

'India And Hungary' criticises the Government's slow, equivocal response to Soviet intervention in Hungary, singling out V. K. Krishna Menon's UN vote alongside the Soviet bloc as damaging India's moral standing.

Soetan Sjarir, former Prime Minister of Indonesia, delivers 'Russian War Against Hungary' at a Bombay public meeting, condemning the Soviet crackdown as classical imperialism and urging Asian vigilance against 'Red imperialism.'
An unsigned report describes the formation of the Indian Committee for Solidarity with Hungary under Jayaprakash Narayan's presidency, who demands Krishna Menon's recall from the UN.

'A Call For Healthy Insight,' a joint statement by writers including Ram Singh and Sudhindranath Datta, argues India's intelligentsia refuses on ideological grounds to recognise Soviet imperialism even while vigilantly opposing Western colonialism.

A letter signed 'T.M.' argues Nehru's shift toward satyagraha rhetoric on Hungary is more authentic than invoking Panchshila, likening the latter's non-interference logic to Cain's 'Am I my brother's keeper' evasion.

V. B. Karnik's 'The Beginning Of The End' surveys the Soviet crushing of the Hungarian revolution, quoting Milovan Djilas's judgment that it may mark 'the beginning of the end of Communism generally,' and criticises the free world's failure to back Imre Nagy's appeal.

A 'Notes' section reports Soviet student unrest in Moscow and Leningrad as a ripple effect of Hungary, Bombay Education Minister Shantilal Shah's opposition to state control of the film industry, and a tribute to the recently deceased B. R. Ambedkar.

M. A. Venkata Rao's 'Copyright Bill' reports the Joint Select Committee's restoration of the copyright term to fifty years, while criticising the Bill's vesting of commissioned works' copyright in commissioning parties rather than authors.

'Mr. Djilas And Marshal Tito' reports Djilas's secret trial and three-year sentence for his New Leader article on Hungary, with international protest from the American Committee for Cultural Freedom and Tito's own biographer Vladimir Dedijer.

'Saadi' defends the Democratic Research Service against Nehru's charge of being 'propagandist rather than a search for truth,' contrasting Nehru's own eulogy of Stalin with the DRS's five-year record of warnings later vindicated.

A correspondent's report on the Delhi Asian Writers' Conference describes it as nearly wrecked by communist-versus-anti-communist tensions, with Rajaji arguing art's purpose is to create beauty, not propaganda.

'Echoes Of The Hungarian Revolution' compiles international statements, including Denis de Rougemont's refusal to normalise relations with anyone who 'justifies' Budapest and Norman Thomas's criticism of Krishna Menon's UN vote.
Francois Bondy's first-person 'A Moment In Budapest' recounts conversations with Hungarian writers, including Julius Hay and Tibor Dery, on the eve of the Soviet crackdown.

V. B. Karnik's editorial 'General Election' predicts India's 1957 poll will change little given popular indifference and hero-worship, warning fifteen unbroken years of Congress rule risks strengthening totalitarian tendencies within a nominally democratic system.

A 'Notes' section reports apartheid crackdowns in South Africa under the Group Areas and Suppression of Communism Acts, and protests the Preventive Detention Act arrests of about twenty-five Praja Socialist workers in Ahmedabad.

Manes Sperber's 'The West Has Lost The Right To Weep,' reprinted from The New Leader, delivers a bitter indictment of Western passivity during the Hungarian revolution, invoking Rosa Luxemburg's thesis on the spontaneity of the masses.

'Saadi''s essay '"We Are All Stalinists"' dissects Khrushchev's continued praise of Stalin as a 'model communist,' reporting a secret Comintern-successor directive instructing all Communist Parties to defend Soviet action in Hungary.
An international cable to Tito, signed by figures including T. S. Eliot, Albert Camus and Indians Jayaprakash Narayan, M. R. Masani and B. R. Shenoy, demands Milovan Djilas's release.
A. B. Shah reports on a Karachi seminar on 'Religion and Freedom,' where participants debated whether Islam or any religion can guarantee individual political and cultural freedom.

M. A. Venkata Rao's 'Officialising The Cooperatives?' opposes Minister K. D. Malaviya's call to officialise cooperatives, citing comparative evidence that forced collectivisation nowhere raised agricultural output above pre-revolution levels.

V. B. Karnik's 'Back To Stalinism?' argues Soviet de-Stalinisation was never genuine liberalisation but a tactical retreat forced by near-collapse of control after Hungary and Poland, quoting Khrushchev's own admission that he does 'not separate Stalinism and Stalin from Communism.'

G. F. Hudson's 'The Paradox Of Jawaharlal Nehru,' condensed from Commentary, dissects a 'double standard' in Nehru's foreign policy -- harsh on Suez, muted on Hungary -- while still affirming Nehru's 'basic devotion to liberal principles.'

'The Truth About Poland' extensively quotes Gomulka's October 1956 Central Committee report admitting the Six Year Plan's failure and attributing the Poznan riots to genuine grievances rather than foreign incitement.

Extracts from Oscar Lange's Zycie Gospodarcze article, introduced as the economist who advised Mahalanobis on India's Second Plan, detail Poland's 'disintegration of the national economy' and propose a nine-point emergency programme including 'further democratization.'

B. K. Desai reviews Peter Fryer's Hungarian Tragedy, praising Fryer's firsthand account of 'three and a half days of freedom' while faulting his continued loyalty to a Communist Party he intends to 'reform from within.'
Franklin A. Lindsay's counterfactual 'What Might Have Happened In Hungary,' from Free Spirit, imagines a UN Observation Commission and decisive Western intervention averting the Soviet crackdown.
A 'Notes' section welcomes Indian government moves against communist-front organisations, university autonomy calls from John Matthai and Vinoba Bhave, and marks the birth of the Republic of Ghana.

M. A. Venkata Rao's 'Kerala: The Cockpit' assesses the CPI's Kerala election victory, winning 60 of 126 seats, as reflecting disgust with Congress and PSP misgovernment rather than ideological conversion, warning of the psychological danger of lending communism respectability.

A 'Notes' section reports renewed Soviet-Yugoslav tension, alleges communist infiltration of the AICC's Economic Review, and describes a Bulgarian youth organ's attack on Ghana's Kwame Nkrumah as evidence of a coordinated communist campaign against new states.

Ida Dhami's 'Signor Nenni's Change Of Heart' reports Italian socialist leader Pietro Nenni's break from a decade-long communist alliance following Khrushchev's revelations and the Hungarian and Poznan uprisings.

'Saadi''s survey of student discontent behind the Iron Curtain documents unrest in East Germany, Hungary, Poland and the USSR, concluding that Marxism and Communism are 'obviously losing their appeal to the Soviet students and intelligentsia.'

Raja Kulkarni surveys parliamentary democracy's fragile state across Asia -- Sukarno's 'Guided Democracy' proposal in Indonesia, Thailand's contested elections, Burma's Karen insurgency -- and frames Kerala's communist government as the decisive test case for the Indian constitutional framework.

B. K. Desai reviews Bertram D. Wolfe's Six Keys to the Soviet System and Khrushchev and Stalin's Ghost, summarising Wolfe's argument that the real twentieth-century question is 'total state or limited state' and that Khrushchev's speech selectively omitted the Hitler-Stalin pact and Katyn.
Short obituaries mourn Philippine President Ramon Magsaysay, credited with defeating the Huk insurgency through land reform, and former Bombay Chief Minister B. G. Kher.

V. B. Karnik's 'The Elections And After' reviews the 1957 general elections, attributing the CPI's stronger showing -- capturing Kerala and gaining seats in Bengal -- not to communist strength but to the 'confused, supine and divided' state of India's democratic forces.

An extract from Wolfgang Harich's smuggled memorandum, 'Testament Of A Party Rebel,' describes an East German reformist faction seeking to shed the party's residual Stalinism and calling for elections with real choice, written shortly before his arrest and ten-year sentence for treason.

M. A. Venkata Rao praises the Patel-Rana Dissenting Note on Chinese 'agricultural cooperatives,' which argues Chinese collectives strip peasants of proprietorship through manufactured 'voluntary' accession following prior land-reform terror.

Writing as 'Ekalavya,' an essay on communist 'mis-education' documents Soviet-bloc textbooks' indoctrination of hatred toward 'Anglo-American imperialists' and warns the same methods could reach Kerala's newly communist-run schools.
A 'Notes' section reports Aneurin Bevan's candid criticism of Soviet and Chinese collectivisation's countryside discontent and a wave of British Communist Party resignations after Hungary and Poland.
'With Many Voices' closes with a satirical mock dinner-invitation from A. K. Gopalan's Kerala communist government to leading industrialists, 'and Harakiri soon thereafter.'

V. B. Karnik's 'Party, Government And The People' critiques Nehru's claim that India occupies a middle position between Communist party-state fusion and Western parliamentary democracy, warning that identifying government with Congress would be 'a step in the direction of totalitarianism.'

Leszek Kolakowski's 'What Is Socialism?,' smuggled from the banned Polish paper Po Prostu, builds a long ironic catalogue of what socialism is 'not' -- a police state, a system with more spies than nurses -- before its deliberately anticlimactic close, 'socialism is a good thing.'

A 'Notes' section describes new Second Plan taxation and deficit financing, the USSR's 1957 decree freezing repayment of state bonds as a de facto default, and the arrests of Indonesian writers Takdir Alisjahbana and Mochtar Lubis without charges.
M. A. Venkata Rao reviews Kwame Nkrumah's autobiography Ghana on the occasion of Ghanaian independence, describing his thought as 'an amalgam of Marxist specialism and Mazzinian nationalism.'

Hans Edward Teglers's interview with Yugoslav politician Vladimir Dedijer has him argue Marx today would write Das Kapital against Soviet exploitation of its own people, concluding the Soviet experiment's lesson is 'how not to do it.'

C.C.F. News reports plans for a 1959 East-West Music Festival in Tokyo and reiterates protests over the Indonesian writers' arrests, while an article on Indian cooperative farming warns against following the Chinese collectivisation model.

V. B. Karnik's 'Mao's Flowers And Weeds' analyses Mao's 'Hundred Flowers' speech, noting Mao's own admission that his security forces liquidated 800,000 people between 1949 and 1954, and reads the slogan as freedom only 'with leadership.'

A 'Notes' section condemns the paralysis of French policy after 34 months of war in Algeria and praises the UN Investigating Committee's report establishing that Soviet intervention in Hungary was 'massive armed intervention' unrequested by the Hungarian government.

Adam Adil's two-part 'Philosophy Of Freedom' surveys the idea of liberty from Plato through Locke and Mill, arguing economic freedom should accompany but not be a precondition of political freedom, quoting Gaitskell's rejection of that doctrine as 'dangerous nonsense.'

J. H. Oldenbroek's message marks the fourth anniversary of the 1953 East German workers' revolt, recounting how 274 cities rose against imposed pay differentials and pervasive surveillance before Soviet tanks crushed the uprising.

M. A. Venkata Rao's 'Educational Policies In Kerala' warns that the communist government's proposed textbook nationalisation risks rewriting history along Marxist-Leninist lines and disparaging figures like Shivaji as 'communal.'

A reprinted correspondence between Soviet critic Ivan Anissimov and Ignazio Silone ends with Silone declaring 'a dialogue between us is impossible' given Soviet censorship, after pressing Anissimov on the unresolved death of Maxim Gorky and disappeared writers.

V. B. Karnik's 'Whither Bhoodan?' questions whether the Bhoodan movement's evolution into Gramdan, whole-village land gifts, risks drifting toward Soviet-style collectivisation, citing Vinoba Bhave's remark that he might accept 'the communist way' if non-violence fails.

A 'Notes' section rebuts a libel republished by Blitz alleging foreign funding of the Democratic Research Service and M. R. Masani, and reports growing complaints of lawlessness under Kerala's communist ministry led by E. M. S. Namboodiripad.

The United Nations Special Committee's report on Hungary, reprinted in full, concludes the 1956 uprising was a spontaneous national revolt, not fomented by Western or reactionary forces, and finds evidence Soviet troop movements began before the Hungarian government's request.
Paul Ignotus's firsthand account, 'The Hungarian Revolution,' recalls Hungarian writers' central role in the uprising and catalogues fellow writers arrested, imprisoned or disappeared afterward.

M. A. Venkata Rao's 'On The Chinese Road!' argues India's cooperative-farming push mirrors Communist China's collectivisation, which transferred control of the harvest from peasant to state, contrasting this with Denmark's ownership-preserving cooperative model.

A statement by Kerala's Private Schools' Rights' Defense Committee opposes the communist government's plan to nationalise 'badly run' private schools, comparing the approach to Hitler's Germany and Mussolini's Italy.

A letter from Rev. T. Mascarenhas rebuts Venkata Rao's suggested equivalence between Catholic school doctrine and communist indoctrination, defending Catholic schools' constitutional right to operate without compelling outsiders.

Adam Adil's 'Ten Years Of Freedom' takes stock of a decade of Indian independence, warning against the personality cult fostered by a Films Division documentary on Nehru and against the drift toward 'statism' via cooperative-farming proposals he calls disguised collectivisation.

A 'Notes' section welcomes the averted post-and-telegraph strike but criticises the Essential Services Maintenance Bill, and reports K. M. Munshi's warning that proposed tax tribunals represent totalitarianism entering with 'padded feet.'

Excerpts from Milovan Djilas's smuggled manuscript The New Class contrast bourgeois revolutions' gains in civil rights with communist revolutions' gains accruing only to the ruling bureaucracy, and document 20,000 cases of 'socialist property' theft in Yugoslavia in 1954.

V. N. Rudin's 'The Split In The Kremlin?' analyses Khrushchev's July 1957 purge of the Molotov-Malenkov-Kaganovich faction, concluding power has shifted to the 318-member Central Committee, diluting central Soviet authority.
R. S. Panday marks Malaya's independence on 31 August 1957, crediting British rule with infrastructure and stability while noting the economy's dependence on rubber and tin.
A Democratic Research Service discussion on the Kerala Education Bill warns it could enable 'nationalisation of education from the back-door' and communist indoctrination.

V. B. Karnik reviews three books on the Hungarian Revolution -- Michener's The Bridge At Andau, Mikes's The Hungarian Revolution, and Barber's A Handful Of Ashes -- quoting a passage accusing Nehru of moral cowardice for his silence during the crisis.

Writing as 'Jupiter,' an essay titled '"Kerala Communists Are Different..."' argues the claim is a deliberately cultivated Communist strategy rather than fact, since the CPI has mirrored every twist of Soviet policy including de-Stalinisation and Hungary.

James Critchlow's 'Ilya Ehrenburg Rebels' describes Ehrenburg's essay 'Lessons of Stendhal' as the strongest public challenge to Communist cultural dictatorship since Stalin's rise, defending dissident writer Vladimir Dudintsev.

V. B. Karnik's 'Our Vote On Hungary' condemns India's UN abstention on the Hungary resolution, rejecting the government's comparison to Suez since England and France, unlike the USSR, complied with UN resolutions.

Adam Adil's 'Our Language Problem' surveys the Hindi-versus-English dispute following the Official Language Commission's report, noting fifty MPs sought a 25-year postponement and quoting Rajagopalachari's proposal that both languages serve jointly.

A 'Notes' section welcomes an apparent government retreat from Chinese-style collectivisation toward voluntary 'service cooperatives,' and reports B. R. Shenoy's and K. M. Munshi's warnings at a Bombay welfare-state symposium against 'equivocal slogans' concealing Marxian dogma.

Extracts from Kodanda Rao's press statement dispute the Official Language Commission majority's characterisation of English as 'foreign,' arguing bilingualism serves the public better than the majority's proposed trilingualism.
Two readers' letters debate the West German election's implications for reunification and press Adam Adil to name which Indian language should replace English if not Hindi.

V. B. Karnik's lead essay, "A Dream Becomes A Nightmare," marks the fortieth anniversary of the Bolshevik Revolution by tracing four decades of disillusionment with Soviet rule, from the Constituent Assembly's dispersal and the Moscow Trials to Khrushchev's secret speech and the crushing of Hungary, and locates the root of Soviet tyranny in Marxist-Leninist doctrine itself rather than in Stalin alone.

The unsigned Notes section reports Milovan Djilas's further imprisonment for The New Class and Stevan Dedijar's parallel persecution, and credits Freedom First's own earlier warnings for the AICC's dismissal of H. D. Malaviya from its Economic Review over alleged communist bias.

Melvin J. Lasky's "No, I Could Stand It No Longer" uses East German writer Alfred Kantorowicz's September 1957 flight to West Berlin to survey a broader gallery of Communist defections, from Bertrand Russell in 1920 to Arthur Koestler in 1938, and wonders how long new believers in Ghana, Ceylon and Kerala will take to reach their own breaking point.

Adam Adil's "Polish Road To Socialism" reports that the gains of Poland's October 1956 liberalisation are being rolled back under Gomulka's own warnings to the Party's liberal wing and the closure of independent papers such as Po Prostu.

M. A. Venkata Rao reviews William Sargant's Battle for the Mind, framing Communist regimes' scientific exploitation of psychological and physiological weakness, including police interrogation methods that produce false confessions, as more dangerous to human freedom than atomic weapons.

A contributed report argues the West Bengal bank employees' strike was engineered by Communist-controlled union leadership seeking to rehabilitate the Party's standing among organised labour after its July setbacks, naming AIBEA office-bearers as communists or fellow travellers.

R. S. Pandey's "Segregation In South Africa" details the 1950 Group Areas Act's displacement of over a million non-whites and the proposed Separate University Education Bill, contrasting South Africa's trajectory with school desegregation enforcement at Little Rock.

The issue closes with an I.C.C.F. News report on a Bombay protest meeting against the South African bill and the Indian tour of Hungarian writers George Paloczi-Horvath and Paul Tabori, alongside a "With Many Voices" column of press quotations on Sputnik and Soviet policy.

M. A. Venkata Rao's lead essay, "The Challenge Of The Sputniks," argues the Soviet satellite launches have shattered Western military containment strategy, criticises Rajagopalachari's proposed nuclear ban as naive, and calls for a Point Four-style global partnership plus an intensified "crusade for democracy."

The Notes section links the purge of Marshal Zhukov to the Sputnik launches as evidence of persisting Soviet political primitivism, reports Communist China compelling token "democratic parties" to self-remould under the Hundred Flowers crackdown, and welcomes President Ngo Dinh Diem's visit to India as a corrective to assumptions about the Soviet bloc.

Further Notes items warn that G. M. Sadiq's new Democratic National Conference in Kashmir shows communist leanings, condemn the Dravida Kazhagam's calls to burn the Constitution, and catalogue the new Communist government's failures in Kerala after six months, including stalled investment and an alleged rice-deal fraud.

Richard Lowenthal's "Another Turn Of The Wheel," condensed from Commentary, reads Khrushchev's defeat of his presidium rivals as the reassertion of party-machine rule over the Soviet state rather than genuine de-Stalinisation, and warns the informal amnesty for Stalin-era crimes is breaking down.

Thomas P. Whitney's "Humanist Specter In Eastern Europe" traces a growing current of "socialist humanist" writing across the Soviet bloc, citing Adam Wazyk's poetry and Vladimir Dudintsev's Not by Bread Alone, as a serious internal challenge to Leninism that the Party's own journal Kommunist felt compelled to attack.

Aziz Madni reviews Imre Nagy's smuggled memoir On Communism as a devoted communist's defence of his "New Course" against rival Matyas Rakosi, while V.B.K. reviews K. K. Sinha's Towards Pluralist Society, noting its "triangular state" proposal echoes M. N. Roy's ideas on partyless democracy.

The issue closes with I.C.C.F. and D.R.S. news of a Patna conference and a seminar on "Russian Revolution and Human Freedom," alongside a "With Many Voices" column quoting Clement Attlee, Eisenhower and Khrushchev on Sputnik, Zhukov and Kerala.

V. B. Karnik's "A Significant Conference" reports on the ICCF's fourth Patna conference, where a seminar on "The Democratic Alternative" questioned whether centralised Second Plan-style planning is compatible with democracy and floated Bhoodan-based decentralisation as a synthesis of liberalism and Gandhism.

Max Lerner recounts a visit to the wife of imprisoned Yugoslav dissident Milovan Djilas in Belgrade, describing her modest, guarded life and Djilas's prison conditions, including developing arthritis and restricted reading.

An unsigned Notes item argues the Moscow summit of twelve communist parties failed to suppress "national communism," citing Yugoslavia's refusal to sign its declaration, while a companion item argues Communists are exploiting Indonesia's West Irian crisis to seize Dutch enterprises.

Further Notes praise Union Minister Morarji Desai's candid criticism of communist-ruled Kerala's illegal "Cell Courts," and respond to a Lok Sabha revelation of a Harijan boy's murder in Uttar Pradesh by arguing untouchability persists despite constitutional abolition.

Howard Fast, in an extract from The Naked God, recounts his break with the American Communist Party over the killing of Soviet Jewish writers David Bergelson and the poet Itzik Feffer, while insisting he retains faith in socialism despite rejecting Party dogma.

Adam Adil's profile "The Passionate Sceptic" traces Bertrand Russell's path from Hegelian influence to founding the analytic movement, his disillusionment after an 1920 visit to Soviet Russia, and his 1955 campaign against the hydrogen bomb.

A correspondent's detailed report on the Patna conference covers Mrs. Rukminidevi Arundale's presidential address on the danger of politicising art, the conversion of the journal Quest into a quarterly, and closing addresses by M. R. Masani and Jayaprakash Narayan on individualism versus collectivism.

B. K. Desai reviews Louis Fischer's Russia Revisited, crediting it with tracing disillusionment across Eastern Europe toward the Polish and Hungarian uprisings and closing on Fischer's cautious optimism that "freedom must win."

The closing "With Many Voices" column quotes Jayaprakash Narayan calling parliamentary democracy a failed experiment in India and Shriman Narayan describing communalism and communism as "two facets of the same...phenomenon."

V. B. Karnik's "Emotional Integration" argues Indian national unity, forged mainly by shared opposition to British rule, remains superficial, citing the states-reorganisation dispute, the Hindi-English controversy, Ramnad riots and Naga and Jharkhand separatism, and calls for forward-looking economic development rather than appeals to a shared past.

The Notes section reports secret trials and executions of 1956 Hungarian revolutionaries including children, catalogues corruption and fund under-utilisation in Kerala's Communist ministry, and welcomes a $225 million US loan as narrowing India's foreign-exchange gap while criticising Krishna Menon's "impertinence" toward the West.

B. K. Desai's "Afro-Asian Solidarity Conference" reports on the December 1957 Cairo gathering as evidence of Soviet Russia positioning itself as leader of Afro-Asian nationalism, noting the Indian delegation was entirely communists or fellow-travellers.

Adam Adil's "Guided Tourism In China" describes how Maoist China stage-manages nearly identical itineraries for foreign visitors, including a suspiciously rehearsed "model jail," while barring access to Tibet, border regions and forced-labour camps.

A report on the ICCF's three-day Bangalore seminar on "Education for Democracy" covers addresses by M. A. Venkata Rao on history's role in democratic education and Philip Spratt on how totalitarian states control thought across education and the sciences.

Leon Dennen's "The Revolt Is Rising" casts Vladimir Dudintsev's Not By Bread Alone, denounced by Khrushchev as "unhealthy" and "obnoxious," as the first post-Stalinist novel to indict the one-party system itself, situating Dudintsev among purged writers Pilnyak, Olesha and Babel.

An unsigned report on "The Affair Of Dr. Zhivago" traces Moscow's reversal on publishing Boris Pasternak's novel and the Union of Soviet Writers' ruling that its "cumulative effect casts doubt on the validity of the Bolshevik Revolution," recalling the earlier arrest and execution of Boris Pilnyak.
The closing "With Many Voices" column quotes Asoka Mehta criticising Kerala's Communist government and Cambodia's Norodom Sihanouk warning against underestimating communism after Hungary.

R. V. Murthy's "Lessons Of The L.I.C. Episode" reviews the Chagla Commission's finding that the Life Insurance Corporation's purchase of Mundhra-controlled shares was rushed through without consulting its Investment Committee, and argues for breaking up state monopolies like the LIC to restore competition and honour C. D. Deshmukh's earlier assurance against using LIC funds to control private industry.

The Notes section recounts Mao's "Hundred Flowers" campaign followed by a purge of over 100,000 alleged rightists, condemns French bombing of the Tunisian village Sakhat Sidi Youssef, and notes the new Soviet Encyclopaedia cutting Stalin's coverage from 87 to 5 pages.
Further Notes criticise US envoy Henry Cabot Lodge's warmth toward V. K. Krishna Menon as poor diplomacy, and mourn Maulana Abul Kalam Azad, praising his Al-Hilal journalism and Quran translation.

B. K. Desai's "Tragedy Of India-China Friendship" portrays the India-China Friendship Association as a communist front lent legitimacy by Congress politicians including Krishna Menon, detailing resolutions backing Red China's UN seat and a cultural-show stand collapse that injured Bombay schoolchildren.

Adam Adil's "Crisis In Indonesia" analyses President Sukarno's inclusion of Communists in the Djuanda cabinet, the resulting rival Sumatran government under Sjafruddin Prawiranegara, and proposes ending collaboration with Communists, adopting federalism, and equitable revenue distribution.

Hugh Seton-Watson's "Populist Spirit In East Europe" singles out Milovan Djilas as unique among communist officials for criticising the essence of communist power itself, tracing how the new intelligentsia communist regimes educated became the "bitterest critics" driving the 1956 Polish and Hungarian revolutions.

The Congress for Cultural Freedom's Paris declaration expresses solidarity with intellectuals under totalitarianism, naming Tibor Dery, Julius Hay and Djilas among the imprisoned, and links their struggle to Little Rock and the South African Treason Trial.

The closing "With Many Voices" column quotes rebel Indonesian premier Sjafruddin Prawiranegara comparing admitting Communists to government to "injecting sickness into one's body" and closes with the issue's statutory ownership statement.

Dinu Randive's "One Year Of Failure" reviews the first year of E. M. S. Namboodiripad's Communist ministry in Kerala, detailing an eviction-staying Ordinance benefiting ruling-party sympathisers, the release of prisoners convicted of violent underground activity, and hardening ministerial rhetoric defending the use of "lathis or even worse tear gas."

V. B. Karnik's "Communist Party Of India — A Transformation?" argues the CPI's new draft constitution and talk of "socialism through peaceful means" is tactical, since Article XIV's principle of Democratic Centralism still subordinates the base to central directives and the Preamble commits the party to Marxism-Leninism and the experience of the USSR and China.

Sutan Sjahrir's "The Background Of Indonesia's Crisis," reprinted from The Socialist Call, attributes Indonesia's post-independence chaos to nationalism's insufficiency as a governing creed once independence was won, calling for a new national "directive" grounded in social justice and rational economic planning.

"Kerala Under Communism" catalogues the Ministry's underspending of its own Plan allotment, proliferation of Communist-stacked "people's committees," and specific corruption allegations including the Andhra rice deal and a book-supply contract for the Education Minister's son.

The same feature documents rising unemployment, numerous lathi-charge incidents, and a run of local elections showing Communist losses, alongside a comparison showing Communist Ministers' effective pay exceeded that of their Congress and PSP predecessors despite "Spartan life" rhetoric.

B. K. Desai's "Double-Talk at Amritsar" shows the CPI's new constitution, adopted at its Fourth Congress, lifts language nearly verbatim from the 1957 Moscow Declaration, and that General Secretary Ajoy Ghosh's own writings concede "peaceful transition" is only a tactical possibility, not a genuine commitment.

Istvan Vizinczei's "A Hungarian Writer's Story" recounts literary life under Communist patronage and repression in Hungary, profiling fellow writers Istvan Eorsi and Jozsef Gali, and his own escape after the 1956 Revolt despite Gali's charge that leaving was cowardice.

An unsigned report on Paul Robeson's sixtieth-birthday celebrations, organised simultaneously in twenty-six countries, describes Indian Communists enlisting figures including Chief Justice M. C. Chagla onto organising committees, and cites the NAACP's own journal The Crisis distancing itself from Robeson's Soviet-aligned politics.

An editorial note defends an earlier Freedom First item criticising US Ambassador Henry Cabot Lodge's "hugging handshakes" with V. K. Krishna Menon, reporting wide American press pickup and Lodge's on-record dismissal of the charges as "ridiculous."

An unsigned piece traces Boleslaw Piasecki's path from pre-war Polish Falangist to Stalinist ally, using his later opposition to Gomulka's liberalisation as a case study in the ideological kinship between Nazism and Communism.

A note reports the Bombay Praja Socialist Party's "Hungary Fights for Freedom" exhibition, inaugurated by Jayaprakash Narayan, who contrasted the end of Western imperialism in Asia with the more "sinister" Soviet imperialism shown in Hungary.

I.C.C.F. News covers Melvin Lasky's April tour of India, including meetings with Jamini Roy, Satyajit Ray and C. Rajagopalachari, while the closing "With Many Voices" quotes Nehru suggesting the Amritsar resolution might make Communists "cease to exist as such."

V. B. Karnik's "Face The Facts" charges the National Development Council with retaining the Second Plan's Rs. 4800 crore target despite the Planning Commission's own finding that only Rs. 4360-4500 crores were realistically available, warning that deficit financing and stalling employment growth vindicate the Plan's early critics.

The Notes section credits Nehru for openly criticising the CPI's foreign-directed "thinking apparatus" and Soviet purges, reports the Communist candidate's narrowed Devicolam by-election win in Kerala, and criticises the Governor of Orissa for improperly declining to follow constitutional procedure in the Mahtab ministry affair.

Jayaprakash Narayan's address "Towards A Fuller Democracy" argues parliamentary democracy fails Lincoln's test of government "by the people" since party machines crowd out independents, and sets out a Gandhian-Sarvodaya vision of vertically decentralised, village-based direct democracy built from Gramdan upward.

Narayan cites the Bhoodan-to-Gramdan movement as evidence of the voluntary "inner change" he advocates, and envisions a partyless, consensus-based democracy modelled on Quaker meetings and Athenian assemblies, ultimately toward a non-national Sarvodaya world order.

B. K. Desai's "Tito And The Red Goliath" analyses the 1958 rupture between Tito's Yugoslavia and Moscow over Yugoslavia's draft programme, which denied Communist parties a monopoly on the path to socialism, while concluding that Titoism is "equally reprehensible" given Tito's own treatment of dissidents Djilas and Dedijer.

Stephen Spender's lead piece condemns the secret trial and execution of Hungarian Premier Imre Nagy and General Paul Maleter, joined by a Congress for Cultural Freedom statement, a Bombay citizens' homage signed by Asoka Mehta and M. R. Masani, and a Patna I.C.C.F. resolution calling the killings "the return of Stalinism."

The Notes section covers the AFPFL split in Burma, Nehru's declining to criticise either side of the Tito-Khrushchev rift, and criticises a new communist-backed "Congress for Disarmament and International Co-operation" in Stockholm, noting C. Rajagopalachari shared a platform with E. M. S. Namboodiripad at a preparatory conference.

V. B. Karnik's "An Alternative To The Congress" argues the Praja Socialist Party is India's only credible democratic alternative to Congress, quoting M. N. Roy's view that the true conflict is between totalitarianism and democracy, and Jayaprakash Narayan's letter explaining his break from party socialism toward Sarvodaya.

S. Sharangpani's "Communists On War-path" analyses E. M. S. Namboodiripad's warning that a united anti-communist front in Kerala risks civil war, arguing the Communist Party's own "united front" tactic aims to divide opponents rather than build genuine coalition.

Adam Adil examines General de Gaulle's plan to integrate Algeria with France, detailing the deep economic interdependence of the two countries and floating a wider French-Algerian-Tunisian-Moroccan federation to exploit Saharan resources.

A review signed "Sadi" covers Howard Fast's The Naked God, crediting it with documenting Communist infiltration of American unions while criticising Fast's "final understanding" as insufficient atonement, and noting his erasure from Soviet public life after his 1957 break with the Party.

Writing as "Atreya," a report on the Praja Socialist Party's Fourth Annual Convention surveys sharply divergent state attitudes toward alliances with Congress and Communists, from Kerala's uncompromising anti-communism to Maharashtra's accommodation, following Ram Manohar Lohia's defection and Jayaprakash Narayan's retirement.

B. K. Desai's "Aftermath Of Nagy Execution" traces the CPI Secretariat's twelve-day paralysis after Imre Nagy's killing, with P. C. Joshi's New Age columns shifting from apology to endorsement while dissenting communists like Santosh Chatterjee publicly objected despite a party directive to stay silent.

Notes accuse the Kerala Communist government of using nationalised textbooks for indoctrination, citing a text praising Soviet education and another glorifying the Russian and Chinese revolutions while omitting the Warsaw Pact, alongside Namboodiripad's warning that opposition could trigger civil war.

A companion item criticises Orissa Chief Minister Harekrushna Mahtab for demanding the replacement of three newspaper correspondents on an unproven charge, quoting opposition leader R. N. Singh Deo's characterisation of it as "high-handed administrative blackmail."

V. B. Karnik's "A Grave Mistake" argues the Anglo-American military intervention in Lebanon and Jordan violates non-interference and props up undemocratic regimes, invoking Lord Attlee's warning against propping up rulers lacking democratic legitimacy.

M. A. Venkata Rao defends the same intervention as a necessary counter to Soviet-Nasserite "indirect aggression," drawing an extended parallel to the "salami tactics" that sovietised Hungary and Czechoslovakia and applying the analogy directly to Kerala.

General Bela Kiraly's "A Kiss For Big Brother" recounts how Hungary's secret police scripted a supposedly spontaneous 1950 Budapest parade minute-by-minute, with children selected from Politburo families rehearsed to "spontaneously" kiss Party leaders.

A "News From Poland" brief reports the banning of Leopold Tyrmand's novel Seven Long Journeys and withdrawal of his passport under Gomulka's tightening cultural policy, alongside writer Marek Hlasko's exile to Paris.

Writing as "Atreya," "Kerala—A Lesson In Legend Building" catalogues seven communist "legends" built around Kerala's ministry, arguing state contracts channelled to party-controlled cooperatives constitute organised corruption and that killings of Congress and PSP workers by armed Communist jathas triggered Nehru's condemnation.

The Notes section reports Parliamentary alarm over Kerala lawlessness, rebuts the CPI's "autonomy" objection to Central inquiry by invoking Article 335, and highlights a 6.7 million ton food-grain deficit tied to historical under-investment in agriculture.

Further Notes frame the planned Tashkent Asian-African Writers' Conference as communist-dominated, and welcome the Magsaysay Foundation's inaugural award to Vinoba Bhave for his humility and critique of caste-based candidate selection.

M. R. Masani's "Towards Economic Democracy" argues no Parliament can democratically control comprehensive economic planning, and defines economic democracy through the worker's right to strike, the peasant's right to own land, and the investor's and consumer's freedom of choice, resting on free trade unions, free peasant proprietors and free enterprise.
Rev. T. Mascarenhas's "The Light Of Personality" argues, via Jacques Maritain's distinction, that socialism needs the relational language of "person" rather than the merely enclosed "individual."

The Review section covers John Gunther's Inside Russia Today, Barbara Ward's The Interplay of East and West, and D. R. Gadgil's pamphlet arguing the Planning Commission overreached its advisory mandate into policy-making.

A leaked letter from 23 Bengal CPI members accuses the Party leadership of acting as a Soviet satellite on the Yugoslavia dispute, timing its cable reversal to a Soviet withdrawal and Moscow Radio broadcast, and a companion item reports Amal Kumar Ganguli's resignation from the CPI over the same charge of subjugation to Moscow and Peking.

B. K. Desai's "From Amritsar To Kerala" traces the CPI's shift from confidence at Amritsar to a defensive mood by August 1958, citing police firings and the Kerala-Birla pact, and outlines a three-part strategy: deflecting blame for Kerala unrest, building anti-Congress fronts nationally, and fusing both narratives.

Notes recount a Parliamentary standoff that scuttled a promised debate on Kerala, with Acharya Kripalani charging the government is being "bullied" by the Communist Party, and praise Dr. Charles Malik's election as UN General Assembly President.

S. V. Raju's "Revolt In Occupied Tibet" documents sustained Tibetan rebellion against Chinese land reform in the Kanze Chou region since 1956, and reports a petition from the Dalai Lama's brother alleging the bombing of Litang village and over 4,000 deaths.

Roderick Macfarquhar's "Khrushchev-Mao Tse-tung Meeting" reads the July-August 1958 Peking summit as Khrushchev securing Chinese backing for disarmament overtures in exchange for abandoning conciliation toward Tito, amid China's harder line on the Lebanon-Jordan crisis.

Michael Polanyi's "The Impact Of Science" argues applying scientific exactitude to human affairs strips grounds for respecting one's fellow men, tracing a line from Bentham through Marx to Nietzsche that helped generate twentieth-century totalitarian violence.

Adam Adil reviews Massimo Salvador's Liberal Democracy as a defence of liberal ideas against the charge they are outdated "bourgeois" relics, highlighting Salvador's claim that intellectuals, not masses, direct history's "doers."

"Kerala Under Communism" reproduces an open letter from N. Sreekantan Nair of the Revolutionary Socialist Party detailing the killing of RSP members at Chandanathope, government favouritism toward an American company over an RSP cooperative, and a pattern of withdrawn prosecutions against communists.

V. B. Karnik's "A Lesson And A Warning" contrasts Burma's military takeover, which preserved parliamentary trappings, with Pakistan's outright abrogation under Iskander Mirza and then Ayub Khan, warning India shares the same cultural and economic conditions and that a "cult of personality" could itself threaten its democracy.

Notes criticise Kerala's Communist government for siding with a communist-led union in a plantation strike that ended in police firings killing four workers, and report continued persecution of Hungarian intellectuals two years after 1956, including disbarment of Budapest lawyers.

A correspondent's report on the Congress for Cultural Freedom's Rhodes seminar on "Representative Government and Public Liberties in New States" records the largest delegation being Indian, and notes international curiosity about India's democracy and Jayaprakash Narayan's partyless-democracy ideas.

Adam Adil's "'People's Communes' Of China" details how communes strip peasants of private property in exchange for wage labour and communal mess halls, with pay docked for insufficient ideological diligence, covering 99.98% of one province's households by August 1958.

S. Sharangpani's "India, Bhutan And China" surveys the Himalayan buffer states' historical treaty relationships, warning some Bhutanese show signs of ideological drift toward "red Tibet" as China builds roads and bases in southern Tibet, framing Nehru's first prime-ministerial visit to Bhutan as overdue engagement.

Ida Dhami's "France Bows To De Gaulle" analyses the September 1958 referendum's 80% approval of the Fifth Republic constitution, including a surprising 93% "yes" vote in Algeria, and notes the French Communist Party's losses including Maurice Thorez's defeat.

Dhami also reviews Robert Guillain's The Blue Ants, framing accurate understanding of Maoist China as a precondition for genuine Sino-Indian friendship and noting Guillain's argument that Chinese communism is an extension of, not a rival to, Russian communism.

The closing "With Many Voices" juxtaposes Pakistan's President Iskander Mirza defending his seizure of power as resting on "the sanction of my conscience" against RSS chief M. S. Golwalkar's comparison of Communist rule in Kerala to "foreign rule."

J. B. H. Wadia's lead essay denounces the Soviet campaign to vilify Boris Pasternak after Doctor Zhivago's publication and Nobel Prize, appeals to Indian writers' associations to protest, and closes naming Pasternak "the skylark of Russian literature."

Notes denounce Nehru's Bhopal speech on the "disease of giganticism" in planning as welcome self-criticism, while a Parliamentary debate exposed over 45% cost overruns at the simultaneously-built Hindustan Steel plants.

Writing as "Atreya," "The Tashkent Writers' Conference" alleges the Indian delegation to the Soviet-hosted conference was packed with communist and pro-Soviet writers who bypassed Union Minister Humayun Kabir as leader, provoking resignations, and that a permanent Colombo bureau was voted in over Indian objections.

Daniel Bell reports from a Congress for Cultural Freedom seminar in Vienna on "Workers' Participation in Management," contrasting British trade unionists' rejection of worker participation with German-Austrian co-determination and Yugoslav workers'-council systems, and citing Raymond Aron's thesis of "the End of the Age of Ideology."
A notice announces the December 1958 visits of Danish Social Democrat Frode Jacobsen, philosopher Sidney Hook, and novelist Arthur Koestler, author of Darkness at Noon.

Philip Spratt reviews newly available German archival documents indicating the Bolsheviks were financed mainly by German money in the six months before the October Revolution, and draws a contemporary parallel to Soviet subsidy of the Communist Party of India.

Raymond Postgate reviews The Soviet Cultural Scene 1956-1957 and Hyman Levy's Jews and the National Question, arguing the post-Stalin cultural "thaw" was minor and that prolonged exposure to Stalinist orthodoxy has left even sympathetic British communist intellectuals unable to think clearly.

A joint statement of Indian writers including Tarasankar Banerjee and Buddhadeva Bose condemns Pasternak's expulsion from the Soviet Writers' Union, joined by a separate protest from M. R. Masani, Sophia Wadia and others noting the Nobel Physics prize to Soviet scientists was accepted without controversy.

The closing "With Many Voices" quotes P. C. Joshi calling the "slander campaign" against Kerala's government the "greatest single danger to Indian democracy," alongside Nehru's own coinage of the "disease of gigantism."

S. R. Mohan Das's "The Spectre Of State Monopoly" argues Nehru's abrupt, unilateral decision to nationalise wholesale foodgrain trade, reversing the government's earlier rejection of the Asoka Mehta Committee's recommendation, reveals that policy in India is made by the Prime Minister's personal initiative rather than accountable process.

Kurt Gratz's "Weekend In Budapest" describes pervasive shortages, black-market currency arbitrage, and tightly guarded internal travel restrictions in Hungary two years after 1956, noting tourists become suddenly eloquent critics of the dictatorship only once across the Austrian border.

Notes survey the unstable post-monarchy situation in Iraq, where Communists have entrenched themselves in Defence, Press and Judicial departments, and read the removal of Soviet security chief Ivan Serov and Mao's resignation of the PRC chairmanship as milestones in shifting communist leadership, with Khrushchev privately calling China's communes "actually reactionary."

K. K. Sinha's "West Bengal—Problems And Prospects" analyses the CPI's rising dominance within West Bengal's "Leftist" bloc after the 1957 election, warning that unless democratic groups distinguish themselves on libertarian grounds, conditions favour a Communist takeover in the province.

Adam Adil's "Mao's Short-cut To Communism" details China's people's-commune system, including a militarised "Saturday-night system" limiting conjugal privacy and reports that elderly dead are processed into fertiliser in some Kwantung communes, concluding communes redistribute poverty rather than raise living standards.

"Life In East Germany," compiled from a Congress for Cultural Freedom refugee centre in West Berlin, documents professionals, a music professor, a lawyer, a clergyman, pressured to conform to Party expectations at the cost of their careers.
A digest reports the December visits of Frode Jakobson, Sidney Hook and Arthur Koestler, the last touring Bombay for a programme organised by Marathi, Gujarati and Hindi writers' bodies and the ICCF.

The closing "With Many Voices" quotes D. R. Mankekar warning the threat to Indian democracy comes "not from bullets but the ballot," and demographer S. Chandrasekhar describing China's communes as "a new colonialism."

V. B. Karnik's "The Spell Of Slogans" reviews Congress's Nagpur session, focusing on its agrarian resolution mandating cooperative joint farming and land ceilings by the end of 1959, noting U.P. Revenue Minister Charan Singh's forceful floor opposition and Nehru's dismissal of Congress President Dhebar's warnings on agriculture as "irrelevant."

Adam Adil's "West Asia In Turmoil" argues Iraq's revolutionary regime and Arab communists, not traditional monarchs, are the real threat to Pan-Arab unity, citing roughly 150 communists arrested in Egypt and 300 in Syria as a positive sign for regional stability.

K. A. Jelenski's "'Victory' At A Price" draws on a leaked Polish Communist Party plenary record to show Gomulka's post-1956 economic model survived neo-Stalinist attack only at the cost of cracking down on "revisionist" intellectuals, the same writers who had earlier denounced Stalinism's crimes.

An unsigned piece catalogues implausible Chinese production claims from the Great Leap Forward, quoting an internal directive that statistics must "serve the political struggle" rather than record reality, while a companion note on Chinese communes reports roughly 70% of output value is funnelled to state accumulation and taxes.

M. A. Venkata Rao's "Why 'Co-operative' Farming?" argues Indian land reform's push toward joint farming is designed to let the state seize the harvest, tracing a three-stage Chinese pattern from landlord liquidation to peasants reduced to supervised wage-hands, and proposes Rochdale- and Danish-style service cooperatives instead.

Ravi Prasad's "A Letter from Kerala: Subversion Of The Police?" scrutinises a Kerala government committee on the police's role in a "welfare state," prompted by a fatal 1958 strike-firing, suspecting proposals for a village police tied to panchayats are aimed at neutralising the police as a check on Communist Party activity.

M. R. Masani's "The Wrong Road" attacks the Nagpur resolution's joint cooperative farming as disguised Soviet-Chinese-style collectivisation, using comparative wheat and rice yield statistics to argue small farms already out-produce large ones and citing Yugoslavia's and Poland's abandonment of collective farming.

Masani quotes Aneurin Bevan warning India against the Chinese path and Jayaprakash Narayan's own admission that the Koraput gramdan experiment failed because peasants wanted their own land, defending Rajagopalachari, Narayan and K. M. Munshi as legitimate critics rather than deceivers of the peasantry.

Notes trace cooling Moscow-Cairo relations after Khrushchev criticised Nasser for arresting Arab communists, analyse General Ne Win's resignation in Burma, and report Julian Huxley's warning at a New Delhi population conference that India's growth is "explosive."

Ignazio Silone's "The Lesson Of Pasternak" frames the global outcry over Pasternak's persecution as proof of a transnational "Weltliteratur" community, condemning the Moscow Writers' Union's 800-strong condemnation of a novel none had read as more shameful than the Spanish Inquisition.

An unsigned report on new Soviet penal statutes notes reforms since 1953 alongside continuities, including retention of the death penalty for fleeing the USSR and criminalisation of "anti-Soviet propaganda" such as spreading "slanderous rumours."

Harry Goldberg's "What's Happening In China?" details the 1958 communisation of China's peasantry into people's communes, abolishing private plots and family life in favour of communal mess halls, and warns the total mobilisation is oriented toward external expansion, quoting Mao's 1940 remark that neutrality is "only a term for deceiving people."

An unsigned piece on "Communists And The Arab World" argues Soviet long-term interests favour a weak, divided Arab world over a strong unified state under Nasser, suggesting the USSR may covertly encourage Iraqi and Syrian factions opposed to merger.

Reviews cover Maulana Azad's posthumous India Wins Freedom, criticised for harsh, uncorroborated accusations against Sardar Patel, and A. D. Gorwala's Not in Our Stars, praised as a fearless critique of India's Soviet-leaning foreign policy.

An unsigned lead editorial, "Revolt In Tibet," argues the uprising against Chinese rule is a genuine, nationwide people's revolt, criticising Indian officialdom for suppressing early reports and Nehru's phrase "the Tibet region of China" as diplomatically evasive.

S. V. Raju's "Tibetan Crisis And Indian Policy" cites George N. Patterson's estimate of 200,000 guerrilla fighters against a 300,000-strong Chinese army, predicts the revolt will likely be crushed, and criticises India's refusal to let Parliament debate the issue.

S. R. Mohan Das's "The Cudgels For Co-operative Farming" argues criticism of the Nagpur resolution targets Nehru's sudden personal championing of joint farming, reading it as compensation for Congress's organisational weakness relative to the Communists after the loss of Kerala.

Adam Adil's "Communism In The Arab World" reports the failed Mosul revolt against General Kassim, noting Islamic clerical fatwas condemning communism and that Iraqi communists, though lacking broad popular support, are purging nationalists from the civil service and army.

Ravi Prasad's "Letter From Kerala" uses the state Police Department's own report to show murder cases rose from 173 in 1956 to 273 in 1958 and detection rates fell from 41% to 27%, tying this to the Communist ministry's liberal prisoner releases and withdrawal of 236 criminal cases in 1957 alone.

A companion report describes an Expert Committee under Kuruvilla Jacob finding hastily revised, religiously and socially offensive passages in Kerala's nationalised textbooks, and Jacob's subsequent resignation as the government's Honorary Educational Adviser.
A notice reports the formation of a Bombay Committee for Solidarity with Tibet on 27 March, chaired by Asoka Mehta with Frank Moraes as Chairman, calling for asylum for Tibetan refugees.

Bertram D. Wolfe's essay-review of Trotsky's Diary in Exile highlights Trotsky's admission that he and Lenin, not Stalin, ordered the execution of the Tsar's family, and his unchanged revolutionary certitude despite Stalin's persecution of his own family.

John Wain reviews Robert Conquest's anthology Poems from Behind the Iron Curtain, singling out Adam Wazyk's "Poem for Adults" and Gyula Illyes's "One Sentence on Tyranny" as surviving translation as considerable literary art.

V. B. Karnik's "Panchsheel And Tibet" argues the 1954 treaty was "born in sin" since India accepted Chinese suzerainty over Tibet in exchange for autonomy guarantees China had already broken, and warns Chinese ambition may extend to Nepal, Bhutan, Sikkim and Kashmir border areas.

A Committee for Solidarity with Tibet statement welcomes the Government of India's asylum for the Dalai Lama, rejects Chinese claims he was abducted, and concludes independence, not autonomy, is the only solution.

Notes describe a deliberate, government-directed Chinese propaganda campaign against India over Tibet naming Indira Gandhi among its targets, and use Kerala's new restrictive Education Act rules as evidence that communists in power become authoritarian regardless of their opposition-era conduct.

An unsigned correspondent's report on the Bombay City Conference of the Communist Party documents falling membership and declining sales of its Marathi weekly Yugantar, alongside heated internal debate over the Nagy execution.

M. A. Venkata Rao's "Green Against Red" contrasts Europe's peasant-smallholder "Green" revolutionary tradition, exemplified by Denmark's cooperative movement, with Leninist "Red" collectivism, arguing the Nagpur resolution abandons India's earlier promise of smallholder land reform for a coercive Soviet-style path.

An unsigned correspondent's account of the Calcutta Afro-Asian Solidarity conference describes non-communist delegates narrowly forcing the word "Tibet" into a resolution on imperialism over CPI objections, with the Women's Conference session reportedly surrounded by male delegates to block a Tibet resolution.

S. R. Mohan Das argues the CPI's Peking-aligned response to the Tibet crisis is consistent with its history as "an international conspiratorial movement," tracing its support for Pakistan's partition demand and its lockstep endorsement of every Kremlin policy shift.

Mironenko rebuts Khrushchev's Twenty-first Congress claim that there are no Soviet political prisoners, showing the 1953, 1955 and 1957 amnesties each excluded key political-offence articles and estimating over a million political prisoners remain of the roughly five million at Stalin's death.

Sal Tas's interview with newly freed Algerian nationalist Messali Hadj has him criticising the FLN as externally financed and proposing an independent Algeria in a Commonwealth-style "France-Maghreb" community, while S. Kabysh's factual survey documents rising compulsory work-day quotas on Soviet kolkhozes.

Writing as "Onlooker," "Where Is The Enthusiasm?" argues the Nagpur resolution's joint cooperative farming has met public indifference rather than enthusiasm, citing a listless All India Congress Committee meeting reported as "listless, inattentive and indifferent" with barely two dozen members present.

William Henry Chamberlin's "Why We Have A Cold War" rejects the view that the Cold War stems from American rigidity, laying blame on Soviet expansionism in Greece, Poland, Lithuania and Galicia, and invokes Tocqueville's scepticism about democracies' capacity for sustained foreign policy.

Notes defend India's asylum for the Dalai Lama while questioning restrictions on his movements, challenge Nehru's Lok Sabha defence of the Sino-Indian Tibet agreement, and discuss Rajagopalachari's petition against imposing Hindi as sole official language.
A brief tribute marks the death of US Secretary of State John Foster Dulles, praising his steadfastness against Soviet overtures.

An open letter dated 20 July 1956 from Thubten Nyenjik, Abbot of Gyantse Monastery, catalogues six years of Chinese occupation in Tibet, describing the bombing of Litang, forced labour on military roads, and Chinese-run schools offering only indoctrination.

A satirical piece compiles obsequious Pravda tributes crediting Khrushchev personally for achievements from agriculture to guided missiles, contrasting them with his own 1956 denunciation of Stalin's personality cult and closing that "the cult is dead, but long live personality."

A cable from the International Committee on Science and Freedom, signed by representatives of 296 universities in 52 countries, condemns South Africa's compulsory university segregation policy to Prime Minister Verwoerd.

A "News & Views" digest reports Radio Peking's admission that Chinese workers earn only about US$12.60 a month, the sentencing of eighteen East German students for treason, and 119,300 East Germans fleeing to the West in 1958, disproportionately young professionals.

The closing "With Many Voices" quotes Acharya Kripalani criticising the Panchsheel framework and China's People's Daily defending its conduct in Tibet, alongside Nehru's own acknowledgment that "autonomy" may carry different meanings for India and China.

V. B. Karnik's "A People's Upsurge" defends the anti-communist Kerala agitation as, in Nehru's own words after an on-the-spot visit, "essentially a people's upsurge," citing vote-share arithmetic showing the communist ministry won only 35% against a united 60% opposition, and calls for its resignation and fresh elections.

A special correspondent's report on the All-India Tibet Convention notes Nehru's dismissal of the gathering as a "wrong approach" before it was even held, yet records it drew over 1,700 delegates and a passionate Jayaprakash Narayan speech declaring "Tibet will not die."

Hemalata Acharya's essay on co-operative farming draws on a Programme Evaluation Organisation study of 22 societies to argue most were formed on government waste land or to evade land-ceiling legislation rather than from genuine cooperative conviction, and finds the programme's production and employment gains largely unrealised.

A contributed piece on the communist-organised Vienna Youth Festival reports 78 of 130 delegates at a preparatory Stockholm meeting were confirmed communists, and that all Austrian democratic youth organisations refused to associate with the event despite four million dollars in Soviet backing.

B. J. Fernandes's "Press In Bondage" contrasts the free press's ethic that "news is sacred, comment free" with Soviet doctrine that news must be organised propaganda, detailing the layered censorship of TASS, GLAVLIT and AGITPROP.

Raman Desai reviews Vladimir Nabokov's Lolita as a serious, artistically rigorous novel whose refusal of a softened ending gives it moral integrity, while M. R. Dalvi reviews A. D. Gorwala's Of Matters Administrative as a diagnosis of nepotism and inefficiency in Indian administration.

The closing "With Many Voices" quotes Nehru declaring "I fear nobody... I do not fear even god," met by C. Rajagopalachari's rejoinder invoking Old Testament psalms, and V. P. Menon's aphorism that "Communists and constitution are contradiction in terms."

Philip Spratt's "Communism Without Dictatorship" reports from Kerala on the "liberation war" against the Namboodiripad ministry, tracing its Education Bill controversy and Communist Party "cells" allegedly running a parallel administration, and concludes a communist government cannot function constitutionally without exercising terror.

Writing as "Apaksha," an essay on the newly formed Swatantra Party praises its Gandhian anti-statist programme and leadership under Rajaji and Masani, while judging its synthesis of Forum of Free Enterprise economics with Sarvodaya trusteeship incoherent given big business's poor record of honouring trusteeship.

A. Ranganathan's "The Right To Property" argues India's Constitution lacks an American-style Due Process Clause, and that the April 1955 amendment removing judicial review of compensation adequacy leaves private enterprise vulnerable to appropriation "at any price it desires."

Robert Guillain's report affirms Mao Tse-tung's personal authorship of China's people's communes despite the Central Committee's collectively-signed decision, detailing the disorganisation and failed blast-furnace campaigns that followed and Mao's subsequent, still-unresolved succession as President.

Hemalata Acharya concludes her field study of co-operative farming societies in Nasik district, finding a Tenant Farming Society succeeded where members had independent means while Collective Farming Societies largely failed from scattered plots and absentee members, concluding co-operative farming is "good in parts" rather than a panacea.

The closing "With Many Voices" quotes K. M. Munshi criticising the use of Section 144 in Kerala as evidence communists are uninterested in genuine order, and Mannath Padmanabhan demanding communists be barred from contesting elections elsewhere in India.

V. B. Karnik's "The Crisis And Its Lesson" reviews the Centre's dismissal of Kerala's Communist ministry, quoting Nehru's Rajya Sabha remark that the Communist Party "does not function in the soil of India" but has "ideological and mental contacts outside," and urges public vigilance rather than outright prohibition of the Party.

K. S. Chetty's profile of the Swatantra Party presents it as India's first party built on an original, non-Marxist philosophy, quoting Masani's attack on Congress's joint-farming and grain-monopoly policies and Sir Homi Mody's retort that even if Swatantra extended the Forum of Free Enterprise, "so what?"

A. V. Sherman's "The New Left In Britain" traces the post-1956 intellectual current formed by Communist Party members shocked by Hungary and Khrushchev's revelations, crediting its research on concentrated economic power while criticising its nostalgia and self-righteousness.

S. R. Mohan Das's account of the Bhilai Steel Project contrasts official publicity with skilled technicians housed in tents through extreme heat, describing AITUC's deliberate avoidance of organising there to protect the image of a Soviet-aided plant.

F. R. Allemann's "Visit To East Germany" reports a real if modest improvement in consumer goods alongside a purge of "politically unreliable" academics, finding rising living standards paradoxically sharpen resentment of the regime's continuing claims on private life.
The closing "With Many Voices" juxtaposes contradictory Nehru statements on Kerala's Communists and a satirical Khrushchev-Nixon exchange from Life Magazine.

B. K. Desai's "Dilemma Of Mr. Nehru" argues Nehru's China policy collapsed under the 1959 Tibetan uprising and border incursions, showing his 1954 legalistic acceptance of Chinese sovereignty over Tibet boomeranging into China's own claim over the McMahon Line.

An unsigned Notes item criticises India's passivity toward Chinese and North Vietnamese subversion of Laos, while a companion note welcomes President de Gaulle's new proposal offering Algeria a choice of secession, integration or self-government.

A profile under the byline "A Keralite" celebrates the 82-year-old Nair Service Society leader Mannath Padmanabhan, tracing his 1914 founding of the N.S.S., his reform of Nair inheritance customs, and his role organising the mass movement that toppled Kerala's Communist ministry.

Writing pseudonymously as "Democrat," an essay attacks Defence Minister V. K. Krishna Menon over the 1959 Defence Ministry crisis, cataloguing his communist associations since the 1930s League Against Imperialism and his pro-Soviet UN voting record on Hungary.

A reprint of the Tibetan government-in-exile's 1958 manifesto to Nehru describes the coerced "17-point agreement," confiscation of gold and grain, and the 1956 uprising in eastern Tibet met with bombing and destroyed monasteries.

Victor Zorza's essay, reproduced from the Manchester Guardian Weekly, examines a Soviet legal debate over "unearned income" from inherited savings, noting high officials' heirs can now live off interest alone in an officially egalitarian state.

The closing "With Many Voices" spans Nehru's assurance no army will be sent into Tibet, Indira Gandhi calling Indian communists "fifth columnists," and repeated demands from A. D. Gorwala and others for Krishna Menon's removal.

V. B. Karnik's "The Choice Before Praja Socialists" marks the PSP's silver jubilee by urging it to abandon class politics and rigid socialist doctrine, invoking M. N. Roy's dictum that the real choice is "between communism...and democracy," not shades of socialism.

Notes voice scepticism that Khrushchev's US visit will ease Cold War tensions, reprint a Hindustan Times editorial condemning Krishna Menon's UN conduct on Tibet as "appeasement, craven, humiliating, wicked," and report nine Indian policemen killed in a Chinese action in Ladakh.

B. K. Desai's "The Significance Of Labour Defeat" reads the Conservatives' decisive 1959 British election win as a rejection of doctrinaire socialism amid rising worker prosperity, contrasting Britain's stagnation under nationalisation with West Germany's free-enterprise prosperity.

S. R. Mohan Das's "Labour And The Third Five-Year Plan" characterises India's industrialising elite as "feudal and paternalistic," warning trade unions risk being confined to welfare functions rather than genuine collective bargaining under the new Plan.

S. P. Aiyar's "Democratic Planning And Publicity" criticises poor distribution of government publications and cites the Mundhra shares episode as symptomatic of unaccountable administration, proposing reforms including a parliamentary research bureau and cabinet rank for the Information Minister.

B. K. Desai reviews Tibor Meray's account of Imre Nagy and the Hungarian Revolution, portraying Nagy as a tragic reform communist who "preferred death for his convictions," while Aziz Madni reviews R. H. S. Crossman's The Charm of Politics.
The closing "With Many Voices" quotes C. Rajagopalachari calling the UN's handling of Tibet "indistinguishable from abetment of oppression" and R. K. Karanjia's effusive praise of Krishna Menon.

M. R. Masani's Lok Sabha speech, "An End To Appeasement," accuses Nehru of years-long suppression of facts about Chinese frontier activity, invoking Mao's 1948 remark that neutrality "is a fraud," and lists three demands: a trusted Defence Minister, frontier roads and airfields, and military parity with China.

S. Sharangpani's "India's Amazing Unpreparedness" documents the near-total absence of survey maps and roads on India's Himalayan frontier compared to China's completed Sinkiang-Tibet road, and details the October 20, 1959 Chinese attack in Ladakh against Indian police armed only with rifles.

Gilbert Jonas's "Burma Moves Toward The West" traces Burma's 1959 acceptance of $37 million in American aid to a Soviet Tass fabrication accusing pro-Western Rangoon newspapers of taking bribes, which provoked public fury and two Soviet defections.

Bertram D. Wolfe's "Communist Vulnerability" argues the free world's passivity, not communist strength, explains the West's failure to exploit the gap between original Bolshevik promises and their totalitarian inversion, framing communism as waging a single "protracted war."

A review of Saul Rose's Socialism in South-East Asia traces the fragmentation of the Congress Socialist Party as Masani rejected socialism, Patwardhan retreated to an ashram, and Jayaprakash Narayan drifted toward Sarvodaya, alongside a similar collapse of Burmese socialism under U Ba Swe and U Kyaw Nyein.
The closing "With Many Voices" quotes C. Rajagopalachari declaring non-alignment terminated "by the East" and G. B. Pant warning Indian communists could not be trusted against a communist aggressor.

V. B. Karnik's "Resist Aggression" argues Chou-En-lai's letters reveal Chinese designs on the whole Himalayan region, welcoming Nehru's Lok Sabha pledge that no cost is too great to defend India's honour while criticising government secrecy about recovering lost territory.

Notes praise Eisenhower's visit to India as a popular triumph correcting mutual misconceptions, and report Indonesia's ban on rural trade by resident aliens as targeting the ethnic-Chinese trading minority, risking civil strife.

Tibor Meray's "Peace Congress In Australia" portrays the Melbourne "Congress for International Cooperation and Disarmament" as effectively steered by Australian Communists, recounting J. B. Priestley's public protest over the conference's refusal to condemn Hungary's imprisonment of writers.

K. M. Munshi's "Chinese Expansionism" calls India's earlier belief in Sino-Indian friendship "self-deceiving gullibility," tying Chinese expansionism to control of oil, lead and copper in frontier regions and urging India to become "a nation in arms."

A report describes an Indian Committee for Cultural Freedom photograph exhibition on Kerala's "Liberation Struggle," inaugurated by Munshi, who credited the absence of a neighbouring communist army with the movement's success against the communist ministry.

A contributed piece on Soviet society describes Khrushchev acknowledging acute Siberian housing shortages, the nationwide extension of a hire-purchase credit system, and a controversial 1959 debate over taxing unearned inheritance income enjoyed by a Soviet "New Class."

M. Devadas Kini reviews Merle Fainsod's Smolensk Under Soviet Rule, using captured Party archives to argue Soviet communism produced a new bureaucratic ruling class and that collectivisation raised output only through coercive extraction from a peasantry stripped of freedom.

The closing "With Many Voices" juxtaposes Nehru's pledge to "negotiate, negotiate and negotiate to the bitter end" with Gen. Thimayya's revelation that 1957 proposals to secure the Sinkiang-Tibet road were rejected because the Defence Minister assumed Pakistan was the only real enemy.

V. B. Karnik's "Paramount Need" welcomes the thaw in India-Pakistan relations and argues China, not Pakistan, is now the paramount threat, criticising Nehru for rejecting Ayub Khan's proposal for joint subcontinental defence and quoting the Swatantra Party's call for a firm anti-China policy.

S. R. Mohan Das's "Russian Communists Are 'Different'" draws a parallel between Nehru's 1950 view that Chinese communism was benign and his 1959-60 claim that Soviet communism is now the more liberal one, citing an episode at Cairo's Afro-Asian Solidarity Committee where a Russian delegate blocked an Indian cable calling for Sino-Indian settlement.

A special correspondent's report on Kerala ahead of the 1960 elections describes the Communist Party's near-total isolation, with enquiry commissions substantiating corruption charges in cooperative societies and Toddy Tappers' Cooperatives.

J. B. Kripalani's "Menace Of Chinese Imperialism," styled as a foreword to the pamphlet Thought on China, recalls warning Parliament in 1950 about Chinese occupation of Tibet and argues aggression, like pain, needs no formal definition to be felt.

Francois Bondy's tribute to Albert Camus, written shortly after his death, recalls his wartime editorship of the Resistance paper Combat and his quiet interventions on behalf of imprisoned Algerians despite avoiding public pronouncements on Algeria.

A contributed study argues Soviet propaganda's cosmetic post-Stalin softening, more science and culture coverage, tolerance of internal policy debate, masks unchanged, aggressive messaging on foreign policy and the inevitable global triumph of communism.

The Review section covers A. D. Gorwala's Of Matters Administrative, "The British Road to Stalinism" on the declining British Communist Party's subservience to Moscow, and "Thought on China," crediting the weekly Thought with foreseeing Chinese aggression as early as 1950-51.

The closing "With Many Voices" quotes West German Chancellor Konrad Adenauer dismissing communism as belonging to "the hoary past" and a satirical Mysindia item comparing calls for Krishna Menon's removal to Cato's "Delenda est Carthago."

M. R. Masani's "A Climb Down" denounces Nehru's invitation to Chinese Premier Chou En-lai as a national humiliation, proposing instead a regional South and South-East Asian security organisation and insisting Chou En-lai be received only as a government guest, not an honoured guest of the Indian people.

Notes report former CPI functionary Tushar Pawar's disclosure that Maharashtra party leaders privately blamed India, not China, for border aggression, and cite BBC sources on continued mass executions in Hungary of 1956 uprising participants three years on.

An editorial note on Kerala's post-election crisis criticises the Congress High Command for nearly wrecking the winning United Alliance by seeking a single-party government, defending the Muslim League's role as representing a genuinely backward community.

S. R. Mohan Das surveys the surge of Soviet delegations to India culminating in Voroshilov's and Khrushchev's visits, arguing Soviet "peaceful co-existence" rhetoric masks an unchanged Marxist view of co-existence as "extension of the struggle between two social systems."

Philip Spratt's report on Kerala's mid-term election presents detailed results showing the United Front winning 94 of 126 seats against the Communist Party's 29, framing the "liberation struggle" as a moral reaction to lawlessness rather than simple class conflict.

Adam Adil analyses U Nu's landslide Burmese election victory following General Ne Win's military caretaker government, crediting the army with defeating the insurgency before warning that U Nu's now-unchecked majority removes healthy opposition checks.

Dr. C. Chandrasekhar projects China's population could reach 1,000 million by 1981, arguing population size interacts with resources and militarist nationalism, as in interwar Germany, Italy and Japan, to raise the risk of aggression.

The closing "With Many Voices" quotes V. K. Krishna Menon calling communists "servants of China" who should be "smashed," and Dr. K. Shridharani calling Khrushchev the "biggest salesman of Eisenhower."

V. B. Karnik's "Great And Grave Responsibility" frames the April 1960 Nehru-Zhou Enlai summit as a test of India's resolve, endorsing Rajagopalachari's proposal for a defensive regional alliance and insisting there can be no compromise on the traditional India-China boundary.

An Indian Committee for Cultural Freedom Discussion Group on Jayaprakash Narayan's thesis for reconstructing Indian polity meets in Bombay, with Narayan's closing reply arguing parliamentary democracy has proven inadequate in India and should not be blindly copied from the West.

A correspondent's report on the Swatantra Party's First National Convention at Patna records over 750 delegates adopting a 50,000-word Statement of Policy, "To Prosperity Through Freedom," and a resolution declaring solidarity with Tibet against Chinese "aggressive and imperialist communism."

Phiroze J. Shroff traces the failure of the League of Nations' lack of enforcement sanctions, evidenced by Japan's invasion of Manchuria and Italy's attack on Ethiopia, through to the founding of the United Nations and its International Court of Justice.

J. B. H. Wadia defends retaining English as an important second language in India, opposing a "closed vocabulary" built solely from Sanskrit roots and citing Panikkar's tribute to Burke, Sir William Jones and Macaulay.

A compilation of Nehru's own statements from 1949 to 1959 traces his shifting position on China and Tibet, from early confidence China sought no expansion to 1959 remarks calling talk of conflict "absurd" over "two miles of mountainous territory where no one lives."

Piloo Mody's "The Roof Has Fallen" argues India's 1950 rush to recognise Communist China and subsequent deference to Chinese "suzerainty" through the 1954 Panchsheel agreement effectively "sold the Tibetan people to their Han conquerors."
