Mieroszewski's "Russia And China—A Polish View," reprinted from the Polish monthly Kultura, argues Poland's national interest favours a strong, anti-Russian China as a counterweight to Soviet imperial dominance, framing the Sino-Soviet split as a historical-territorial dispute rather than a purely ideological one.

A review signed "Junius" of C. L. Sareen's "U.S.S.R. vs. Tarasov" recounts a defecting Soviet sailor's legal battle in Indian courts, praising the magistrates' rejection of fabricated Soviet evidence as a vindication of Indian judicial independence against Soviet pressure.

Gayatri Devi's Lok Sabha speech on the "Santhanam Committee Report on Corruption" argues the Committee's recommendations do not go far enough, calling for a broad statutory definition of corruption covering influence-peddling, disclosure of ministers' assets to an independent tribunal, and confiscation of unaccounted wealth as the penalty.

M. R. Masani's Lok Sabha speech on the "Dange Letters" presses the government to authenticate the disputed 1924 letters in which CPI leader S. A. Dange purportedly offered to serve as an intelligence agent for the colonial Governor-General, accusing the Home Minister of evading the question to avoid embarrassing Nanda or antagonising the Soviet Union.

An unsigned compilation, "When Thieves Fall Out....," assembles press reports of internal CPI accusations against chairman S. A. Dange, alleging he held undisclosed property through a nominee and received substantial funds from the Soviet-aligned World Federation of Trade Unions.

K. K. Sinha's "Crisis In Eastern India" describes an accelerating refugee exodus of non-Muslims from East Pakistan following the Khulna riots, reporting 4,000-5,000 crossings a day by mid-April 1964 and the inadequacy of the Dandakaranya rehabilitation scheme.

Raman Desai's "Kashmir—Past And Future" gives a long historical account of the 1947 accession, the UN plebiscite resolution, and Sheikh Abdullah's later advocacy for independence, concluding India must resist further Pakistani pressure even at the risk of war.

The closing "With Many Voices" column quotes C. Rajagopalachari calling "Congress socialism" a "South Sea Bubble" and Jayaprakash Narayan observing that "the freedom fighters of yesterday began so early to imitate the language of the imperialists."

S. R. Mohan Das's "Prohibition and Temperance" argues Maharashtra's newly liberalised liquor policy still conflates prohibition with temperance, proposing government-run beverage-and-food stalls and a state toddy monopoly with capped alcohol content as an alternative to both rigid prohibition and outright repeal.

New Zealand Ombudsman Sir Guy Powels's "Common Justice," reprinted from The Guardian, reviews his first 18 months in office handling 1,100 complaints through informal departmental cooperation, arguing liberty today is threatened more by the "suffocation" of an expanding welfare state than by external militant ideology.

M. R. Pai's "The Food Crisis—Who Is Responsible?" blames rising food prices on inflationary deficit financing under Soviet-style planning and gross inefficiency in state grain-handling, citing Rs. 12.38 crores in state-trading losses in 1962-63 and calling for treating agriculture as an industry rather than nationalising the grain trade.

"Forecast: Cloudy, Windy" compiles quotations from Asoka Mehta warning of an annual Rs. 100-crore tax increase and observing that industrial growth has failed to trigger corresponding agricultural growth.

V. B. Karnik's "Kashmir—A Plea For Fresh Thinking," written after Sheikh Abdullah's release, disputes that the Constituent Assembly's ratification or one-party state elections constitute genuine popular endorsement of accession, and urges either full integration via abrogating Article 370 or a region-by-region ascertainment of Kashmiri popular will.
The closing "With Many Voices" column quotes C. Rajagopalachari calling India's "adventure with democracy" an "expensive disappointment" while crediting Nehru alone with securing Indo-Pak sacrifices.

Purshottam Trikamdas's memoir "Jawaharlal Nehru As I Knew Him" offers a candid, unsentimental account spanning 1917 to the mid-1950s, recalling Nehru's 1957 admission of responsibility for SEATO's formation and his troubling idolisation of V. K. Krishna Menon, while concluding "with the end of his life, an era has ended."

Y. N. Sukthankar's "Nehru The Administrator" praises Nehru's prompt, non-dictatorial working style and credits him as the intellectual force behind key features of the Five-Year Plans, closing with Churchill's remark that Nehru had "conquered the three great enemies of mankind."

Robert Conquest's "The Fog Of Peace," adapted from a BBC broadcast, argues against relaxing vigilance toward the Soviet Union even amid talk of détente, using Soviet census data to argue Stalin's purges, not just the war, explain the USSR's postwar gender imbalance.

Surendra Mohan's "Consensus Or Conformity?" rebuts V. B. Karnik's earlier article, arguing consensus and conflict are intertwined and that manufacturing artificial unity risks leaving rising social conflicts unchannelled.

Rohit Dave's "The Budget Concessions" criticises the Finance Minister's budget as ineffective against black-market lending at 18-24% interest and the Reserve Bank's restrictive credit policy, calling for a comprehensive economic strategy rather than piecemeal tinkering.

Victor Frank's "The Case Of Joseph Brodsky" recounts the Leningrad trial and internal exile of the 24-year-old poet for "parasitism," highlighting Soviet writers' unprecedented public petition on his behalf as a sign of new dissent under Khrushchev.

The closing "With Many Voices" column, reacting to Nehru's death, opens with C. Rajagopalachari's tribute in Swarajya and includes Asoka Mehta's chariot metaphor of heavy industry and agriculture as the "two wheels" of development.

Raman Desai's "South Vietnam and Ourselves" argues Communist China has spent years fomenting civil wars around South East Asia's seaboard, calls for India to abandon panchsheel neutrality, and urges Indian foreign policy to align openly with the U.S., Cambodia, Laos, Vietnam and Malaysia against China.

A. G. Mulgaonkar's "After The Das Report" treats the Das Commission's findings against Punjab Chief Minister Pratap Singh Kairon as a turning point, proposing mandatory asset declarations for all political officeholders and referral of corruption findings to the President or Governors and statutory Commissions of Inquiry.

"Goldwater On Goldwater" reprints excerpts of Senator Barry Goldwater's Der Spiegel interview after his Republican nomination, in which he frames the Cold War as a struggle between "godless people and the people of God," claims Communists have broken 51 of 52 postwar agreements, and states the U.S. is already fighting "World War III... in Southeast Asia."

Raman Desai's sarcastic "Is Your Travel Necessary?" contrasts foreign-exchange privations on ordinary citizens with hospitality-funded foreign trips taken by officials like Bombay Chief Minister Naik, and calls for Indians to be allowed to retain pre-independence foreign-currency balances held abroad.

Dahyabhai V. Patel's "A Visit To Free China (June 1964)" reports on a delegation tour of South Vietnam and Taiwan, crediting Taiwan's land-reform programme with a claimed 369% rise in agricultural production since 1946 and urging Indian recognition of the Taiwan government.

V. B. Karnik reviews A. J. Fonseca's "Wage Determination and Organised Labour in India," crediting it with showing trade unions influence wage levels but exert no control over prices or employment, while noting Fonseca's inattention to wage-setting shifting from collective bargaining to tribunals.

The closing "With Many Voices" column includes Barry Goldwater's acceptance-speech line that "moderation in the pursuit of justice is no virtue" and William F. Buckley Jr.'s remark that under federal encroachment "States today are merely eunuchs."

M. R. Masani's "The Food Crisis" blames stagnant foodgrain output and rising prices on the Second Plan's priority for heavy industry over agriculture, criticises the government for scapegoating peasants and traders as hoarders, and calls for releasing buffer stocks, ending zonal restrictions and halting food exports.

A. G. Mulgaonkar's "Choosing The Leader" surveys three centuries of British prime-ministerial selection, from Walpole through the criticised 1963 "soundings" that produced Sir Alec Douglas-Home, to ask what precedent Lal Bahadur Shastri's unexpected rise offers for how Congress will choose future leaders.

N. S. Ranganath Rao opens a two-part essay, "Obscenity: Literature And Law," tracing the culturally relative history of obscenity regulation in English law from antiquity through the 1868 Hicklin test that Indian courts adopted, setting out the opposing arguments of free-expression and moral-restraint advocates.

Alexander Frater's satirical dialogue "Goulash And Ballet," reprinted from Punch, imagines Khrushchev and Mao privately coordinating a feigned Sino-Soviet rivalry for propaganda purposes while secretly planning a staged nuclear provocation.
The issue closes with "With Many Voices," a page of topical quotations from figures including President Johnson, Dean Rusk, G. L. Nanda and Asoka Mehta on world and Indian affairs.

Philip Spratt's "The Hindu Personality," delivered at the Indian Committee for Cultural Freedom's Poona seminar, argues from a Freudian perspective that the Hindu psyche is narcissistic rather than punitive, tracing this to Advaita Vedanta and indulgent child-rearing, and asks whether liberty can be made part of the ruling elite's ego-ideal.

Rohit Dave's "South East Asia And Ourselves" surveys the regional crisis in Laos, Vietnam and Malaysia after the Tonkin Gulf incident, rejecting both an all-out Indian military buildup and abandoning non-alignment for Western alliances, and calls for India to lead a regional response to Chinese expansionism.

"Russian Aid" reprints excerpts from the Chinese Communist Party's February 1964 letter to the CPSU rebutting Soviet claims of one-sided aid, detailing Chinese exports of grain and strategic minerals to the USSR and accusing Moscow of abruptly withdrawing 1,390 experts in 1960.

The "Without Comment" column reprints a Pravda article criticising the Communist Party of China for failing to hold regular Party Congresses and for the leadership deciding matters by "the directives of Mao Tse-tung" rather than its own Rules.

B. K. Desai's review of Peter Lyons's "Neutralism" argues non-alignment degenerated from a sound policy of avoiding military pacts into a dogma that blinded India to the communist threat, citing the Colombo powers' refusal to condemn Chinese aggression in 1962.

An unsigned piece, "China's Territorial Claims," documents Chinese expansionist doctrine and reproduces a 1954 Chinese textbook map showing claims on Ladakh, Nepal, Sikkim, Bhutan, NEFA/Assam and other neighbouring territories.

The closing "With Many Voices" column quotes C. Rajagopalachari denouncing the Fourth Plan's Rs. 22,000-crore outlay as "the nation's biggest enemy" and Sukarno describing himself as "a Communist, religious and nationalist as well."

V. B. Karnik's "Plus Ca Change--" analyses Khrushchev's October 1964 removal as a "palace revolution" engineered by a small circle of Communist Party leaders, with Kosygin taking the premiership and Brezhnev the party secretaryship, and warns a resulting Sino-Soviet rapprochement could reduce Russian willingness to support India against China.

A. G. Mulgaonkar's essay traces parliamentary privilege from Speaker Lenthall's 1642 defiance of Charles I through the Keshav Singh affair, in which the U.P. Vidhan Sabha's contempt powers clashed with the Allahabad High Court, prompting a Presidential Reference to the Supreme Court.

N. S. Ranganath Rao's second installment on "Obscenity: Literature And Law" argues India's Hicklin-derived obscenity test wrongly ignores authorial intent and judges books by isolated passages, and calls for admitting expert literary evidence as England's 1959 Obscene Publications Act does.

Raman Desai reviews A. G. Noorani's "The Kashmir Question," crediting its treatment of the U.N. Commission resolutions while criticising its disorganisation, and argues India should keep seeking agreement with Pakistan on frontier defence against China even at some sacrifice.

S. Natarajan reviews Charles H. Heimsath's "Indian Nationalism and Hindu Social Reform," praising its account of how the reform movement fed into nationalism while disputing R. C. Majumdar's thesis that 19th-century Hindus and Muslims lived in "water-tight" cultural compartments.

Leonard Schapiro reviews the anthology "Half-way to the Moon: New Writing from Russia," singling out Alexander Solzhenitsyn's "Matryona's Home" as its masterpiece and describing how Viktor Nekrasov's honest travelogue of the West reportedly led Khrushchev to suggest his expulsion from the Party.

M. R. Masani's editorial "The Bomb" argues China's atomic test is chiefly a political and psychological weapon, rejects an independent Indian nuclear deterrent as unaffordable, and urges India to seek a formal mutual-security understanding with the United States.

A. G. Mulgaonkar's essay, headed with Charles I's trial quotation, analyses the Supreme Court's advisory opinion in the Keshav Singh privilege dispute, which held that Indian legislative sovereignty, unlike Britain's, is subordinate to the Constitution and that High Courts' Article 226 jurisdiction cannot be ousted by a claim of privilege.

N. S. Ranganath Rao's third installment on "Obscenity: Literature & Law" proposes rewriting IPC Section 292 with a "taken as a whole" test, exceptions for bona fide literary and scientific work, and statutory Regional Boards with binding authority replacing the ad hoc Customs advisory panel.

A report on "Press Council" summarises an Indian Committee for Cultural Freedom seminar on the proposed Press Council Bill, including S. Natarajan's dissenting letter arguing press freedom is an internal professional responsibility that no external Council can secure.

A reader's letter to the editor defends A. G. Noorani's book "The Kashmir Question" against the journal's earlier unfavourable review, citing a favourable Observer editorial and objecting to the review's characterisation of Jayaprakash Narayan as "eccentric" for favouring a negotiated Kashmir settlement.

The closing "With Many Voices" column quotes Marshal Chen Yi on China's bomb and Fidel Castro on capitalism versus socialism, and closes with a signed note from M. R. Masani defending the journal's stance on Kashmiri self-determination even at the risk of "temporary unpopularity."

V. B. Karnik's "A Reminder" uses the defections of young Tadjik writer Aziz Oulougzade and, earlier, Svetlana Stalin to argue that fifty years of Soviet rule have failed to deliver the liberty the Revolution promised, showing the yearning for freedom cuts across Soviet class lines.

M. R. Hazaray's "Death Of Fourth Plan" blames the Planning Commission's own "doctrinaire dogmatists" for the Fourth Plan's collapse, tracing outlays rising from Rs. 3,360 crores in the First Plan to a targeted Rs. 21,350 crores, alongside unemployment backlogs rising from 5.3 to 25 million.

"Russia From Many Angles" compiles foreign press commentary marking the Revolution's fiftieth anniversary, including Louis Fischer on Russia's nationalist turn and a New York Times catalogue of Stalin's purges of Red Army officers.

Dilip Chitre's "Creativity In Crisis: Russian Story" argues Soviet writers under persecution, from Pasternak to Sinyavsky and Voznesensky, achieve a moral and creative intensity unmatched by Western "alienated" avant-gardes, and warns Indian writers against romanticising revolutionary mythology.

S. H. Deshpande's "Equality In Soviet Life" reconstructs Soviet income distribution from Western scholarship, tracing a hierarchy from a wealthy elite of artists and top officials down to forced-labour camp inmates estimated at several million under Stalin, and finds inequality has gradually narrowed since 1957.

A reprint from U.S. News & World Report, "Russian Revolution—A Balance Sheet," tallies the Revolution's fifty-year record, crediting the USSR with rising to second in world economic output and 95% literacy while estimating war, terror and famine cost the population 80 million relative to trend.
The closing "With Many Voices" column quotes Frank Moraes observing that "Communism is no longer a monolith" and C. Rajagopalachari on majority rule not being equivalent to democracy.

Adam Adil's "Recent National Conventions" surveys the PSP, SSP, Jan Sangh and Congress party conventions, criticising the SSP's withdrawal from the UP coalition cabinet as lawless and portraying the Congress Hyderabad plenary as a win for the party's right wing that avoided self-criticism over corruption.

M. D. Kini's "A Seminar On Liberalism" reports on a Poona seminar co-sponsored by the Indian Group of Liberal International, summarising talks by B. R. Shenoy, F. A. Mehta and others on planning's failures, and closing with M. R. Masani's argument that free economies like Taiwan and Israel grew faster than planned economies like India.

R. Srinivasan's "Liberty And Russian Revolution" traces how the Revolution's promise of freedom gave way under Lenin to Cheka terror and under Stalin to the 1937 purge that killed or exiled 70% of the Central Committee, arguing even Khrushchev's "welfare totalitarianism" left the underlying lack of freedom unaddressed.

V. B. Karnik reviews Gus Tyler's "The Labour Revolution," crediting its analysis of the American trade union movement's challenges from automation and Black workers' entry into the labour force, and its argument that unions are inherently political.

An unsigned report on the "Persecution Of Writers Under Communism" details the Soviet 'literary underground' trial sentencing Yury Galanskov to seven years' hard labour, alongside continuing concern over Sinyavsky and Daniel and Czechoslovak novelist Ladislav Mnacko's protest resignation from the Party.

The Reviews section covers A. G. Noorani's biography of President Zakir Husain, K. P. S. Menon's uncritically pro-Soviet Moscow ambassadorial diary, a U.S. Information Service booklet on the Peace Corps in India, and H. R. Pardiwala's balanced pamphlet on the Shiv Sena controversy.
The closing "With Many Voices" column quotes Frank Moraes and other commentators from January 1968 on Communist doctrine, the Naxalbari uprising, and the Soviet writers' trials.

M. D. Kini's "One Year Of Non-Congress Governments" surveys the coalition governments across North India, singling out West Bengal's gheraos and Naxalbari violence and Kerala's contempt-of-court conviction of Chief Minister E. M. S. Namboodiripad as failures, while praising Orissa's abolition of land revenue as the sole real gain for ordinary people.

Writing as "Emdeeke," the satirical column "Of Cabbages And Kings" mocks the proliferation of Indian political parties and Bombay street politics, including Bal Thackeray's promise to have Shiv Sena "sainiks" slap litterers clean.

The unsigned "Notes" section argues United Front coalitions collapsed from internal disunity rather than Congress subversion, and defends India's acceptance of the ICJ's Rann of Kutch arbitration award against M. C. Chagla's call for rejection on political grounds.

Writing as "Atreya," "'Little Summit' In New Delhi" analyses the January 1968 meeting among Kosygin, Tito and Indira Gandhi, arguing the Tashkent Agreement had permanently shifted Kashmir diplomacy from the West to the Soviet Union.

M. R. Pai's "The Image Of The Indian Economist" argues the profession's standing has fallen through careerism and political malleability, crediting B. R. Shenoy as the sole prophetic dissenter on the Second Plan Panel of Economists.

Adam Adil's "Withdrawal Of British Forces" examines Britain's 1968 decision to pull troops from east of Suez, noting Malaysia and Singapore's moves toward a NATO-style defence pact with Australia and New Zealand to fill the vacuum.
R. Srinivasan reviews a volume on "Higher Education In India" edited by A. B. Shah, praising Edward Shils's contribution while arguing education is too important to be left solely to academics.
V. B. Patankar reviews Keith Buchanan's "The South East Asian World," highlighting its concept of Southeast Asia as a "predeveloped region" whose progress was retarded by colonialism.

Writing as "Achyut Gandhi," a review of S. Vijayanand Bharathi's "Can Indira Accept This Challenge?" credits the book as a bold, objective survey of Indian politics since Independence, singling out its critical chapter on Nehru's "unscientific" dreams.
The closing "With Many Voices" column quotes Gulzarilal Nanda asserting that planning "never helps the peasants" and S. A. Dange threatening millowners who close mills with imprisonment.

M. R. Masani's "The Budget – A Gamble" rejects deficit financing versus taxation as a false choice, calling Bokaro a "White Elephant," comparing Hindustan Steel's poor capital efficiency against Tata Steel's, and proposing dual pricing so subsidised rations reach only the genuinely poor.

A. G. Mulgaokar's "The Speaker's Role" traces the erosion of the Speaker's impartiality to Nehru's failure to have G. V. Mavalankar resign his Congress membership, using recent Punjab and Bengal controversies over gubernatorial powers to argue Speakers cannot rule on constitutional legality.

A boxed item reproduces John Chamberlain's Freeman review of James Burnham's "The War We Are In," summarising Burnham's thesis that communists of every persuasion cooperate in practice to hasten the West's collapse despite their mutual rivalries.

"Towards Understanding Madras Politics" carries rebuttal letters from K. Vedamurthy and P. S. Sridhara Murthy defending the DMK government's rice scheme and crediting C. Rajagopalachari, not the DMK, as leader of the anti-Hindi movement, with M. D. Kini's reply maintaining his sceptical view of the DMK's substantive record.

A contributed report describes the March 1968 Warsaw student demonstrations against secret-police rule and censorship, sparked by the banning of "Dziady" and Leszek Kolakowski's expulsion from the Communist Party, and the regime's subsequent purge of twelve intellectuals.

The closing "With Many Voices" column quotes R. K. Narayan on "Stone Age and Glass Age" coexisting in India and Weekend Review warning India is "not many mid-term elections" from public weariness with democracy.

V. B. Karnik's "Unjust and Unfair" protests the Maharashtra government's externment order against missionary Fr. Vincent Ferrer, who ran welfare work benefiting over 10,000 Nasik-district farmers for seventeen years, arguing vague undisclosed charges of "conversions" violate natural justice.

A Special Correspondent's "Exports After UNCTAD" argues both the 1964 and 1968 UNCTAD conferences failed to resolve major trade issues, noting India's exports were just 4.5% of national income in 1966-67 against 40% for the Netherlands, and calls for developing countries to prioritise their own export promotion.

M. R. Masani's piece on the "Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty" supports India's non-nuclear stance while rebutting arguments against signing the NPT, warning that refusal would isolate India alongside Albania, Cuba and North Korea and forfeit US nuclear fuel supply and goodwill.
G. L. Mehta's tribute "Fearless Warrior Of Peace" honours the assassinated Martin Luther King, tracing his explicit debt to Gandhian satyagraha through Thoreau back to the Bhagavad Gita.

A notice announces the newly established Leslie Sawhny Programme of Training for Democracy, a five-year initiative chaired by N. A. Palkhivala with M. R. Masani as Honorary Secretary, to train political workers and party cadres in democratic principles.

An unsigned review of 1967 as "another year of cultural revolution" in China describes the PLA's emergence as the only institution able to restore order, Lin Piao's rise as Mao's presumed successor, and the sustained vilification of President Liu Shao-ch'i as "China's Khrushchev."

A review signed V.B.K. of A. R. Antulay's critique of the Mahajan Commission's Maharashtra-Mysore-Kerala boundary report argues Justice Mahajan applied inconsistent linguistic-majority standards, favouring Mysore's claim to Kasargod while denying comparable Marathi-majority claims to Belgaum.

The "Towards Understanding Madras Politics" exchange continues, with readers Vedamurthy and Sridhara Murthy defending the DMK government against M. D. Kini's earlier criticism, before the editor closes the debate for reasons of space.

A "Without Comment" item reprinted from Swarajya argues Communist parties cannot be treated as ordinary democratic parties since subversion is their "first love," and calls on the Madras and Central Congress governments to free themselves from Communist influence.
The closing "With Many Voices" column quotes Philip Toynbee calling the lie "the worst feature of Soviet society" and notes posters in Calcutta calling for "armed revolution, here and now."

M. R. Pai's "Social Control Over Politicians" itemises the lavish perquisites of Union Cabinet Ministers (Rs. 17,000/month versus a Rs. 2,250 salary) against Norway's leaner system, and proposes a ten-point programme including abolishing perquisites and mandatory wealth disclosure.

Writing as "Atreya," "The Viet Nam Peace Talks" frames Hanoi's stalling over the Paris talks venue as insincere negotiating posture and attacks American liberal critics of the war, including Robert Kennedy and J. K. Galbraith, as amplifying Communist psychological warfare.

The unsigned "Notes" section argues the delay in Assam's reorganisation between hill and plains populations is dangerous, and that "Anti-Congressism" has exhausted itself given Congress's recovery in Kerala and Haryana by-elections.

Chris Cook's "Portugal At War," reprinted from Socialist Commentary, surveys Portugal's colonial wars in Angola, Mozambique and Guinea, detailing 165,000 troops deployed and 42% of the 1966 budget spent, and concludes the war is unwinnable and "both wrong and harmful."

Adam Adil's "Winds Of Change In Eastern Europe" reports on Alexander Dubcek's loosening of party control in Czechoslovakia, including the country's first workers' strike under communism, while contrasting Poland's stiffening resistance to reform under Gomulka.

R. Muthuswamy's "Trends In Recent Elections" analyses Indian municipal and by-election results, finding Congress inroads into Communist strongholds in Kerala and voters increasingly evaluating parties on performance rather than ideology.

The closing "With Many Voices" column quotes Alexander Dubcek wanting "Marks and Spencer, not Marx and Engels" and M. R. Masani comparing Indian attitudes to other nations with Brahmin treatment of Harijans.

V. B. Karnik's "Sheikh Abdulla and Kashmir Problem" argues Abdullah has offered no concrete solution to Kashmir since his release, dismisses plebiscite or independence as impractical, and proposes free and fair elections under the Election Commission as a substitute.

M. R. Pai's "Indo-Soviet Plan Tie-Up" warns against "dovetailing" India's Five-Year Plans with Soviet planning, citing the loss-making Ranchi Heavy Engineering Corporation, mounting Bokaro Steel Plant costs, and Soviet pressure to buy uneconomical Tu-134 aircraft as cautionary examples.

S. Narasimhan's "France In Turmoil" recounts the May 1968 Sorbonne student revolt and general strike of over ninety lakh workers, describing how de Gaulle's dissolution of the National Assembly produced a Gaullist landslide framed as a choice against "totalitarian Communism."

V. B. Karnik reviews Mohammad Ayub Khan's autobiography "Friends Not Masters," correcting Indian misconceptions that Ayub Khan is a military dictator or Pakistan a theocratic state, while sharply criticising his claim that Indian leaders harbour "a deep hatred for the Muslims."

Writing as "Atreya," a report on Indira Gandhi's May 1968 tour of Singapore, Australia, New Zealand and Malaysia describes her cautious avoidance of filling the vacuum left by British defence withdrawal, and Peking Radio's denunciation of the tour as an anti-China plot.

The closing "With Many Voices" column quotes M. R. Masani stating there is "too much politics in India and too little citizenship" and Nirlep Kaur's six-step prescription for transforming India into a foodgrain exporter.

M. R. Pai's "Soviet Aid to Pakistan" argues Soviet arms aid to Pakistan humiliates Indira Gandhi's foreign policy and calls for India to develop independent missile capability and end dependence on both Soviet arms and US PL-480 aid.

A. G. Mulgaokar's two-part "Defections And Their Control" surveys the rise of legislative defections in India, drawing on British precedent on offices of profit, and reports a Committee on Defection's proposals to bar defectors from ministerships and cap ministry size.

An unsigned item warns the Soviet Union may crush Czechoslovakia's liberalising reforms as it did Hungary in 1956, citing dissident physicist Andrei Sakharov's manuscript in support of the Czechoslovak reformers.

Writing as "Atreya", the magazine surveys factional infighting among Indian youth organisations over representation at the Soviet-sponsored World Youth Festival in Sofia, and notes declining festival attendance as evidence of waning Soviet influence.

Adam Adil's essay on "Indian Muslims" responds to A. B. Shah's foreword to S. E. Hassnain's book, arguing Muslims are not inherently backward-looking but that mutual Hindu-Muslim suspicion has entrenched grievance, and calls for closer social contact between the communities.

A review of J. P. Naik's Education in the Fourth Plan praises his incentive-grant proposals while doubting the practicality of his 'Swadeshi' education plea, alongside a report on a Leslie Sawhny Programme training camp whose straw poll found trainees favoured Swatantra, Congress and Jan Sangh, with Morarji Desai the top choice for Prime Minister.

Letters to the editor include S. G. Padalkar's call for a new citizens' party representing the "well-meaning citizen" and the better sort of businessman, and M. R. Masani's anecdote about restoring a Colombian Liberal Party leader's lapsed subscription.
The closing "With Many Voices" column quotes C. Rajagopalachari on illiterate government and a Czechoslovak banner reading "Democratization must become democracy."

M. D. Kini's lead article "Rape of Czechoslovakia" denounces the Warsaw Pact invasion as unprovoked aggression comparable to Hungary 1956, credits Dubcek's liberalising reforms as the true trigger, and condemns India's abstention at the UN and the defeat of Sucheta Kripalani's parliamentary motion condemning the invasion.

Writing as "Atreya", "Schism In Communist Movement" traces the 1964 CPI/CPI(M) split and the 1968 Naxalbari breakaway to a "polycentric" world Communist movement no longer disciplined by Moscow, reading the Czechoslovakia invasion as a symptom of that disintegration.

A. G. Noorani's "Vietnam's Politics And Law" reviews Dennis Duncanson's history of Vietnam and law-focused studies by Richard Falk and by Hull and Novogrod, the latter concluding South Vietnam and the US were legally entitled to use force in self-defence against the North's creation of the National Liberation Front.

Bogaras Bruchman, wife of imprisoned Soviet writer Yuri Daniel, recounts a bureaucratically cruel one-hour supervised visit to him at the Potma labour camp and a written refusal of a private visit from the camp commandant.

The lead article also faults Pravda's justification of the invasion, an alleged NATO subversion plot, as fabricated pretext, framing the episode as evidence of Communism's disintegration as a unified international movement.

The issue closes with reader letters, a review of a book on Communist strategy in India, and a "With Many Voices" compilation of quoted press commentary on the Czechoslovak crisis from world press and public figures.

V. B. Karnik's lead editorial "Hollow Triumph" condemns the Warsaw Pact invasion as pure aggression, describes Czechoslovak passive resistance modelled on Gandhian methods, and argues Russia's occupation is an unsustainable "hollow triumph" that will cost it international standing and push back detente.

An unsigned "Let The World Know" piece documents the Soviet seizure of Czech publishing houses and universities, the underground flight of writers, and the clandestine radio network that smuggled delegates to a secret Fourteenth Party Congress.

G. L. Mehta's "To Sing With The Angels" draws a parallel between the 1968 invasion and the 1938 Nazi occupation, recounting President Masaryk's founding faith in democracy and asserting that Jan Masaryk was "brutally murdered" by Stalin's agents in 1948 rather than having committed suicide.

M. R. Pai's "Press Strike—Its Implications" argues the just-ended two-month Indian newspaper strike let communist-aligned journalists suppress coverage of Soviet arms aid to Pakistan and the Czechoslovak invasion, and calls for journalists to see themselves as a "noble profession" rather than a trade union.

A satirical piece attributed to "Josef Schweik" (translated by Tibor Szamuely) mocks Soviet propaganda by presenting a mock Rude Pravo editorial that "welcomes" the occupying troops as fraternal friends using absurd Leninist double-talk.
The issue reprints extracts from Gandhi's 1938 essay "If I Were A Czech," offering the Czechs "a weapon not of the weak but of the brave": resolute non-violent refusal to submit to force.

Book reviews cover A. B. Shah's Challenges to Secularism and three Czechoslovakia-crisis pamphlets, and the closing "With Many Voices" page quotes Jean-Paul Sartre calling the invasion "pure aggression...a war crime" and Rajagopalachari on the suppression of Czechoslovak liberalisation.

Adam Adil's "Namboodiripad's Defiance" attacks Kerala Chief Minister E. M. S. Namboodiripad for defying the Essential Services Maintenance Ordinance during the September 19 Central Government employees' strike, framing it as a constitutional violation and urging firm Central action against Kerala.

A. G. Noorani reviews Stanley Kochanek's The Congress Party of India, tracing the Prime Minister's growing dominance over the Congress President since the 1947 Kripalani episode and doubting the party has achieved the cohesion Kochanek's book calls for.

An essay on Alexander Dubcek argues he did not originate Czechoslovakia's liberalisation but was driven to it by a pre-existing popular thirst for freedom, and that his capitulation to Soviet pressure left Czechoslovak resistance without leadership.

Writing as "An Observer," V. B. Karnik characterises the September 19 Central Government employees' strike as a Communist-directed political manoeuvre rather than a genuine industrial dispute, criticising the Government's own delay in convening a Pay Commission.

V. B. Karnik's "India And Israel" contrasts the Government of India's pro-Arab pamphlet with Dahyabhai Patel's rebuttal, arguing the Government's stance omits the 1919 Faisal-Weizmann agreement and remains "frozen around initial prejudices," and engages socialist critics Isaac Deutscher and Simha Flapan on Israel's origins.
A reprinted letter from Sgt. Jeffrey A. Davis, killed in Vietnam, explains to his wife why he felt obligated to fight despite disliking the war.
Companion items report a Moscow trial of Soviet dissidents protesting the Czechoslovakia invasion and Soviet pressure on the French Communist Party over its criticism of the occupation.

Writing as "Atreya", "Nixon Wins" surveys the 1968 US election, crediting Nixon's narrow win over Humphrey to Republican unity against a Democratic Party split by Robert Kennedy's assassination and Chicago convention disorder, with George Wallace's segregationist third-party run further dividing the field.

V. B. Karnik's "Reorganisation Of Assam" traces the failure of post-Independence accommodations for Assam's hill tribes, from Naga separatism and the creation of Nagaland in 1963 through the All Party Hill Leaders Conference's push for a "regional federation" sub-State formula.

John Gross reviews Robert Conquest's The Great Terror, summarising the Stalinist purges' scale, an estimated 20 million shot or died in camps from 1930, and noting that purge-era officials like Kosygin and Brezhnev remained in Soviet leadership decades later.

G. A. Abba's "Freedom Of Press, Uses And Abuses" defends the Bombay High Court's contempt conviction of Blitz editor R. K. Karanjia over an article attacking the lower judiciary, rejecting the narrative that Karanjia was a martyr for press freedom.

A. A. Deshpande reports on a Coonoor seminar on "Problems of Democracy and Development," jointly organised by the Indian Liberal Group and the Friedrich-Naumann Foundation, which concluded that developing countries should pursue indigenous forms of democracy rather than imported models.

Reviews cover A. Dasgupta's Tagore and Communism, which argues Communists selectively misuse Tagore's writings, and Andrei Sakharov's smuggled essay Peaceful Coexistence and Intellectual Freedom, alongside an explainer on the Brezhnev Doctrine used to justify the Czechoslovakia invasion.
A short tribute marks the death of industrialist Murarji Vaidya, and the closing "With Many Voices" column quotes Richard Nixon, Andre Malraux and Marshal Tito on contemporary politics.
Marking its 200th issue after sixteen years of publication, the magazine thanks readers and contributors in a brief editorial note.

Writing as "Atreya", "Marxist Contortions in Kerala" traces the fracturing of Kerala's Communist politics, describing a breakaway "Ultra" faction led by Kunnikal Narayanan, Imbichi Bava and Kosala Ramdas that rejects parliamentary participation and has mounted armed attacks on police stations at Tellicherry and Pulpally.

An unsigned piece dismantles the Brezhnev Doctrine of "limited sovereignty" advanced to justify the Czechoslovakia invasion, tracing it to S. Kovalev's September 1968 Pravda article, and reproduces a protest letter signed by some seventy Marxist philosophers at the Korcula Summer School condemning the occupation.

R. Muthuswamy's "Michael Stewart's Mission" frames the British Foreign Secretary's India visit as a fence-mending exercise still inhibited by "ruler-subject" resentments, criticising India's own inconsistency in condemning Britain over Rhodesia while abstaining on Czechoslovakia.

A satirical glossary by "G.L.M." redefines Communist political vocabulary, glossing "Election" as "Nomination by Party bosses for automatic approval by 99 percent members" and "Non-Alignment" as "Turning a blind eye to Communist aggressions."

A. G. Noorani reviews Michael Brecher's India and World Politics, built on interviews with V. K. Krishna Menon, which reveals Menon reflexively condemning "American Imperialism" while treating Soviet actions with near-total leniency.

Reader letters include N. B. Desai's warning about the preacher Acharya Rajneesh's blend of Marxism and religious rhetoric, and S. D. J.'s account of the R. K. Karanjia contempt-of-court case; the issue closes with "With Many Voices" quoting Rajagopalachari calling all factions of Indian Communism "subversionists."

Adam Adil's "Mid-Term Elections" surveys the political churn following the collapse of United Front coalition governments in Punjab, UP, Bihar and West Bengal, highlighting West Bengal's law-and-order collapse and the Naxalbari uprising, and urges voters toward political stability while warning against Communist extremes of right and left.

V. B. Karnik's "Dialogue With China And Pakistan" argues India should pursue sustained dialogue with both neighbours, drawing an analogy to ongoing US-China talks in Warsaw, and finds Pakistan more receptive than China to a "no war" pact.

Ian Tickle's essay on Communist insurgency along the Thailand-Malaysia frontier describes Chin Peng training Malaysian Communist cadres from Thai soil and warns that the winding-down of the Vietnam War could free Communist forces to intensify regional pressure.

B. A. Deshpande reports on a Gandhi Centenary student leadership camp in Trivandrum, and a companion feature collects reader responses to an earlier "Student Unrest" article, with N. B. Desai estimating only 20-25% of student strikes concern genuinely academic issues.

S. S. M. Desai reviews J. K. Galbraith's The New Industrial State, summarising Galbraith's "technostructure" concept and his thesis that capitalist and socialist industrial systems are converging toward similar planning imperatives.

A "Without Comment" feature reprints Madan Mohan Hardat's account of over a decade spent in Soviet labour camps after travelling to the USSR as a young revolutionary in 1940-41, alongside a review of the pamphlet Indo-Soviet Relations with essays by M. R. Masani and M. R. Pai.

The closing "With Many Voices" column quotes Lee Kuan Yew contrasting free-enterprise and socialist Asian economies, and letters mark Freedom First's 200th issue, including N. G. Ranga's memory of a 1951 Democratic Research Service book of parliamentary speeches criticising Nehru's Tibet policy.

Arvind A. Deshpande's "After the Mid-Term Elections" argues the 1969 election results confirmed rather than reversed Congress's 1967 decline, offering four "lessons" including accepting coalition government and checking regionalism.

Writing as "Observer", "Riots In Bombay" holds the Shiv Sena primarily responsible for the February 1969 Bombay riots tied to blocking Morarji Desai's entry into the city, detailing a toll of over fifty deaths from police firing and thousands of arrests.

V. B. Karnik's "Hindu–Muslim Problem" traces the historical roots of communal estrangement and Congress's share of responsibility for Partition, and critically reviews Hamid Dalwai's Muslim Politics in India while endorsing its call for a humanist trend within the Muslim community.

M. D. Kini's "A Communist Tragedy" frames the Soviet invasion of Czechoslovakia as an "Indian Communist tragedy" too, reporting that the CPI banned from its own bookshops a book by party intellectuals, including Rajya Sabha MP K. Damodaran, that used Marx and Lenin's own words to criticise the intervention.

Ramu Pandit reviews T. G. McGee's The Southeast Asian City, summarising its thesis that Southeast Asian urbanisation is "pseudo-urbanization" driven by population pressure rather than industrialisation, with slum dwellers as a potential source of political instability.

G. A. Abba's "Mr. Nath Pai's Bill" argues against the proposed constitutional amendment restoring "parliamentary supremacy" after the Golaknath judgment, contending sovereignty resides in the people and Constitution rather than Parliament, and invokes the Weimar Republic's collapse as a cautionary parallel.
The closing "With Many Voices" column quotes RSS leader M. S. Golwalkar and Home Minister Y. B. Chavan alongside commentary on Stalin's partial historiographical rehabilitation in the USSR.

M. R. Masani's "Plea for Courage and Sanity," an extract from a Parliament budget speech, invokes Gandhi's "talisman" test to attack fertiliser and petrol excise duties as hitting peasants and the urban poor, and calls Bokaro a "white elephant" while urging cuts to defence and non-plan expenditure.

Two unsigned "Notes" condemn the appointment of S. S. Dhawan, a documented pro-Communist sympathiser, as Governor of West Bengal, and warn that Congress's factionalism could cost it its position as India's dominant party.

Adam Adil's "Pakistan In Turmoil" traces Ayub Khan's fall and the imposition of martial law under Yahya Khan to regional resentments and East Bengal's estrangement, concluding the opposition that displaced Ayub is more conservative and anti-Indian than his own regime.

M. R. Pai's "Crisis In Indian Democracy" identifies four threats to Indian democracy -- communist subversion, parliamentary amendment of fundamental rights, inflation from communist-style planning, and civic apathy -- warning that easy constitutional amendment risks a Hitler-style path to totalitarianism.
R. Muthuswamy surveys simultaneous Cold War flashpoints in Berlin, the Sino-Soviet border at Damansky/Chen Pao island, and the Middle East as a single "tension belt" driven by Big Power politics.

Josefa Slansky's reprinted memoir extract recounts her husband Rudolf Slansky's arrest the night of a farewell dinner before his 1952 Prague purge trial, and her own years of forced factory labour and stonewalling by Soviet-bloc officials over promised restitution.
The closing "With Many Voices" page quotes Andre Malraux's remark that both Nehru and Mao told him they had no successor, and Vinoba Bhave's view that parliamentary democracy has not failed in India.

Writing as "An Analyst", "Bengal Preparing for 'Peoples Democracy'" argues the CPI(M) has shifted from one of three leading United Front partners in 1967 to the coalition's dominant force, embedding itself in West Bengal's administration and police and distorting a 25-acre land ceiling policy into a vehicle for forcible land occupation.

Arvind A. Deshpande's "Untouchability - The Indian Apartheid" responds to the Shankaracharya of Puri's defence of untouchability, arguing the practice cannot be legislated away and must instead be worn down by Harijans' own self-respect and achievement, comparing this to the American civil rights movement.

A. G. Noorani reviews Karl Kaiser's German Foreign Policy in Transition, tracing West Germany's shift from Adenauer's "positions of strength" diplomacy to the Grand Coalition's more flexible Ostpolitik under Kiesinger.

Milovan Djilas's "Russia In 1984" offers a speculative counter to Orwell, predicting that by 1984 Marxist-Leninist ideology will be dead in the USSR and a military-bureaucratic regime will replace a fractured Communist Party.

An unsigned note describes a brief, inconclusive Budapest conference of European Communist states, chaired oddly by Alexander Dubcek, at which Romania refused Soviet requests for troop transit rights and further condemnation of China.

Book notices review the Novosti pamphlet "Fire Bell in the Night" on Martin Luther King's murder as one-sided anti-American propaganda, and recommend "Czechoslovakia 1968" alongside D. B. Karnik's The Czechoslovak Crisis.

A "Without Comment" column excerpts P. Kodanda Rao's argument that party discipline makes parliamentary democracy "both undemocratic and anti-democratic," and B. R. Shenoy's data showing Indian unemployment rising from 5.3 million to roughly 10 million across three Five Year Plans.

A. G. Noorani's tribute to the recently deceased President Dr. Zakir Husain recalls his choice of academic vocation and self-effacing public service over inherited wealth, and Jayaprakash Narayan's comparison of Husain's rise to an oak grown from an acorn.

M. R. Pai's "India And Nepal" argues India neglected relations with Nepal under Nehru, credits Lal Bahadur Shastri with recognising its strategic importance as a buffer against China, and warns that a Chinese-built road could open Nepal to Chinese influence.

S. R. Mohan Das's "Harold Wilson's Heartbreaks" praises the British Prime Minister for risking his own popularity to push an Industrial Relations Bill regulating collective bargaining, comparing his stance to Stafford Cripps's earlier imposition of post-war austerity.

M. R. Masani's "A Miserable Plan," extracted from a Parliament speech, demolishes India's draft Fourth Five Year Plan as built on unrealistic growth targets, and names P. C. Mahalanobis, Pitambar Pant, V. K. R. V. Rao and D. R. Gadgil as planners who will be remembered for having "destroyed the economic future" of the country.
Gafoor reviews Shriman Narayan's edited Letters from Gandhi Nehru Vinoba, highlighting a 1955 Nehru letter attacking Freedom First as American-organised and linked to M. R. Masani.

R. Muthuswamy's "The Mirage Of Leftist Unity" argues V. K. Krishna Menon's Midnapore win does not signal genuine prospects for leftist unity, given the deep fragmentation between Communist and Socialist traditions and open clashes within the Kerala and West Bengal United Front ministries.

A. E. Smith's "Subversion In British Universities" describes well-organised New Left and Trotskyist campaigns within British universities, including disrupted meetings addressed by Denis Healey and Enoch Powell.

Adam Adil's "World Communist Congress" recounts the truncated 1969 Moscow gathering, boycotted by Mao, Ho Chi Minh, Tito and Castro, reading its difficulty in convening and its failure to censure China or address Czechoslovakia as proof that Moscow no longer commands a unified international Communist movement.

Writing as "An Analyst," "Violence In Calcutta" catalogues two and a half months of West Bengal turmoil under the United Front government, citing at least 13 political murders and police increasingly ignoring CPM-linked actions.

M. R. Pai's report on Ballygunge documents a season of bombings and stabbings by United Front "goondas" in the constituency of Information Minister Jyoti Bhattacharjee, who declared United Front youths would be armed.
M. R. Pai's "The Leadership Of 1970s" contrasts contemporary leaders' pursuit of perquisites and party-switching with the integrity of past figures like Ram Mohun Roy, Tilak and Visvesvaraiya.

Feroza Seervai's satirical dialogue has the ghosts of Socrates and Lenin debate Soviet equality, with Lenin eventually conceding his classless society is really "State-Capitalism" under a new autocracy.

R. S. Morkhandikar reviews S. P. Aiyar's The Commonwealth in South Asia, crediting British rule with parliamentary institutions, English, and modernisation while noting Britain's own waning Commonwealth commitment as it seeks EEC entry.

Reviews cover a Society for Research in Indian Communist Affairs report on communist infiltration of Tehri Garhwal and Uttarkashi districts, and a collection on secularism in India including essays by the late M. N. Roy.

V. B. Karnik's lead essay "Drift Or Design?" questions whether Indira Gandhi's AICC "stray thoughts" note, the sidelining of Morarji Desai, and the nationalisation of fourteen banks reflect calculated design or directionless drift, warning that further nationalisation of production and exchange would lead to "anarchy and chaos."

Writing as "Atreya," an essay on the CPI(Marxist) cites B. T. Ranadive's London statement that the party's real aim in Kerala and West Bengal is to sharpen class struggle rather than relieve the people, and reports M. R. Masani's parliamentary opposition to the Banking Companies Nationalisation Bill, comparing Indira Gandhi's path to Nkrumah's Ghana and Sukarno's Indonesia.

Writing as "Analyst," a piece surveys a month of administrative breakdown in West Bengal, including an attack on the Ananda Bazar Patrika and Statesman offices by CPM-aligned "student" groups likened to Nazi storm-troopers.

M. R. Pai's "India - An Asian Czechoslovakia?" catalogues alleged Soviet infiltration of Indian press, education and economic planning, naming ministers he considers pro-Soviet including Dinesh Singh, I. K. Gujral and P. N. Haksar, and warns India risks becoming "a Soviet economic colony."
A reprinted extract from Soviet dissident writer Yuri Daniel's prison letter describes the euphemistic "special language" of the Soviet camp system, where starvation rations are called "education."

A reprinted editorial by South African editor Lawrence Gander, convicted for reporting prison brutality, defends the press's duty to publish unwelcome truths, closing with Jefferson's preference for newspapers without government.
A letter exchange between A. B. Shah and V. B. Karnik disputes Karnik's earlier characterisation of Hamid Dalwai's Muslim Politics in India and the roots of Muslim separatism.
A book review covers Strategies of Revolutionary Warfare, connecting its relevance to India via reports that China trained over 1,000 Naga insurgents in Yunnan.

Adam Adil's "Congress in Crisis" surveys the unprecedented Congress crisis after Indira Gandhi backed independent candidate V. V. Giri for President over the party's official nominee Sanjiva Reddy, leading to mass defections and Giri's narrow victory.

An unsigned editorial marks the first anniversary of the Soviet invasion of Czechoslovakia, citing Jan Palach's self-immolation as the year's most notable act of resistance and the replacement of Dubcek by the more compliant Gustav Husak.

A. B. Shah's "The Press and the Present Crisis" invokes Tocqueville to argue there is no half-way house between a free and regimented press, documenting government pressure on editors and mob attacks on The Statesman.
An unsigned piece recounts Soviet writer Anatoly Kuznetsov's defection to Britain while researching a book on Lenin, smuggling manuscripts sewn into his coat lining.

A student report on a Democratic Research Service/Leslie Sawhny Programme seminar at S.N.D.T. Women's University finds participants unanimously critical of strikes over tough exam papers while unable to agree on limits for student involvement in party politics.

Writing as "Analyst," a piece describes clashes between police and CPM/SUC peasant organisations at Haroa and Bharatgarh, and the CPM's shift toward appealing directly to policemen rather than confronting them.

V. B. Karnik reviews Brigadier J. P. Dalvi's Himalayan Blunder, an account of the 1962 war with China that assigns greatest blame to Defence Minister Krishna Menon and Nehru while also holding senior army officers responsible.

K.V.B. reviews J. H. Broomfield's Elite Conflict in a Plural Society on Bengal's Bhadralok elite, showing how the same group that opposed the 1905 Partition welcomed the 1947 Partition rather than face incorporation into a Muslim-majority state.

Arvind A. Deshpande's tribute to Gandhi frames his greatness as accessible moral earnestness rather than exceptional genius, calling his handling of Hindu-Muslim unity a "magnificent failure" while crediting his core teaching that any individual can resist injustice without causing injury.

A. G. Mulgaokar's constitutional essay "P. M. And Party President" argues the Congress organisation cannot legitimately claim directive control over the Prime Minister and cabinet, invoking British precedents where Asquith, Baldwin and Churchill resisted extra-constitutional interference.

Writing as "Analyst," a "Bengal Report" covers Indira Gandhi's Calcutta visit, a Congress attempt to sideline West Bengal leader Atulya Ghosh, and sharpening CPI-CPM conflict within the United Front triggered by the Baranagar beating of CPI trade unionists.

V. B. Karnik reviews J. Bandyopadhyaya's Social and Political Thought of Gandhi, summarising its dispassionate finding that the 1930-32 Civil Disobedience Movement was "practically a complete failure" undone by government repression, and its doubt, via Karl Jaspers, about satyagraha's viability against totalitarian regimes.

A reprint from U.S. News & World Report, "Moscow's Design For Asia," argues the Soviet Union is expanding into the vacuum left by American withdrawal from Asia, citing Brezhnev's June 1969 call for an Asian "collective security" system.

A memorandum presented to Indira Gandhi by Calcutta Congressmen catalogues sixteen "trends" of political violence and breakdown of law and order in West Bengal, including forcible occupation of land and over 1,000 withdrawn criminal cases, and calls for action under Article 356.
An editorial condemns the Ahmedabad communal riots as a national shame in the Gandhi centenary year, and a reader's letter praises A. B. Shah's earlier article on press freedom.

V. B. Karnik's "U. F. Collapse in Kerala" attributes the fall of the Namboodiripad ministry to the CPM's drive to weaken coalition partners using government machinery, a tactic he says is being repeated in West Bengal against the Bangla Congress.

Aziz Madni's "Behind The Rabat Fiasco" dissects India's humiliation at the Rabat Islamic Summit after Yahya Khan reversed course on admitting the Indian delegation, quoting Jayaprakash Narayan's view that India had no business seeking a place at a purely Muslim summit.

Adam Adil surveys twenty years of Chinese Communist rule, tracing the Sino-Soviet split, the Great Leap Forward and Cultural Revolution's devastation, and China's declining international standing with Albania as its only remaining significant ally.

Writing as "Atreya," an essay frames the crises in the Kerala and West Bengal United Front ministries as a deliberate Communist strategy of forming fronts only to isolate and "liquidate" allies one by one.

R. Muthuswamy reviews the Gajendragadkar National Commission on Labour report, the first such commission in independent India, detailing its 299 recommendations including compulsory union recognition and new Industrial Relations Commissions.

Writing as "Analyst," a "Bengal Report" covers the Bangla Congress's resolution threatening a Gandhian satyagraha over law and order, implicitly targeting CPM control of the Home portfolio under Jyoti Basu.

Elbridge Durbrow contributes a satirical imagined monologue by Ho Chi Minh reflecting on how North Vietnamese negotiating tactics and the 1968 Tet offensive shifted the diplomatic and military picture in Hanoi's favour.

Adam Adil's "Congress in Crisis" frames the 1969 Congress split as the worst crisis in the party's 85-year history, tracing it from the Bangalore AICC session through Mrs Gandhi's expulsion from primary membership and the retaliatory dismissal of Nijalingappa.

M. R. Pai's "Prime Minister And The Party" argues the Syndicate-Indicate struggle pits two obsolescent political forces against each other and that India's Constitution, not Congress's dominance, is the real guarantor of democratic stability.

Writing under the pseudonym "Atreya," an essay accuses Indira Gandhi of using power and patronage to smash the Congress party while borrowing Leninist/Stalinist tactics, including a fabricated "Zinoviev letter"-style scandal against C. Subramaniam, Chavan and Sukhadia.

Arvind A. Deshpande's "The German Miracle" frames Willy Brandt's Social Democrat-Free Democrat coalition victory as a hopeful shift comparable to Kennedy's "New Frontier," rooted in German self-confidence rather than anti-Americanism.

An unsigned feature recounts the ordeal of Sukumar Bose, a Bengali student imprisoned in Poland after the Warsaw Pact invasion of Czechoslovakia for writing a satire critical of Polish subservience to Moscow.

V. B. Karnik reviews Victor Fic's Peaceful Transition to Communism in India, tracing CPI tactics from the 1948 Ranadive line of armed revolt to the 1958 Amritsar congress's "peaceful transition" doctrine, and warning that secret directives reveal more revolutionary intent than public declarations.

Book reviews cover S. P. Sathe on the Golak Nath fundamental-rights debate and Kuldip Nayar's Between the Lines, and a reader's letter from E. P. Vargese proposes basing India's franchise on a literacy qualification.

A. G. Mulgaokar's lead essay warns against the campaign, backed by fifty A.I.C.C. members of the Indira Gandhi faction, to delete the constitutional right to property, arguing that once one fundamental right can be abridged by ordinary majority, none remains truly fundamental.

H. R. Pardivala's "The Need Of The Hour" blames professional politicians for corruption and communal exploitation, endorsing a proposal by Khan Abdul Ghaffar Khan and Vinoba Bhave for a new Gandhian political party and appealing to Jayaprakash Narayan to lead it.

M. R. Masani's "Monopolies: State Or Private?" attacks the Monopolies and Restrictive Trade Practices Bill for exempting the only real monopolies in India, government enterprises like LIC and Indian Railways, while targeting private firms, calling the resulting regime "industrial feudalism."

A. G. Noorani reviews two new histories of Partition, R. C. Majumdar's Struggle for Freedom and B. N. Pandey's The Break-up of British India, concluding both point toward greater Congress culpability for the failure to compromise around the 1946 Cabinet Mission Plan.

Moin Shakir profiles Khan Abdul Ghaffar Khan ("Badshah Khan") and the Khudai Khidmatgar movement, recounting how the Muslim League branded him a Congress agent for rejecting the two-nation theory and his post-1947 lament that Pakistan was "founded on hatred."
Writing as "Analyst," a "Bengal Report" covers Chief Minister Ajoy Mukherjee's hunger-strike satyagraha over law and order and his standoff with CPM Home Minister Jyoti Basu.

M. R. Chandvadkar reviews a report on an international colloquium on "Democracy and Development" at Coonoor, which concluded liberal democracy pairs individual liberty with a competitive economy more effectively than dictatorship.

V. B. Karnik's "Rational Politics" blames both the Congress leadership and the Jana Sangh and CPM as the two "irrational" destructive poles of Indian politics, calling for policy built on well-defined, attainable goals.

M. R. Pai's "Why I Oppose Socialism" lays out a four-part case that socialism cannot cure poverty, destroys liberties, produces inequality between rulers and ruled, and introduces class warfare, citing the collapse of small banks after 1969 nationalisation.

Writing as "Atreya," "The Anatomy Of Rural Violence" argues the Home Ministry's dramatic warning about rural violence is "artificially inspired," tracing engineered unrest to Naxalite and CPM strategy rooted in a 1949 Cominform directive.

R. Muthuswamy's "Jamshedpur Strike-Lessons" analyses a 48-day strike across seven Tata-linked industrial units, arguing India's low union-recognition threshold of 15% membership leaves no union commanding enough support to deliver on agreements, and calls for statutory majority-union recognition.

Writing as "Analyst," a "Bengal Report" describes Chief Minister Ajoy Mukherjee's December hunger-strike and subsequent assertion of administrative authority against the CPM's control of the Home portfolio.
Brian Crozier's "The New Left" surveys Che Guevara, Regis Debray, Frantz Fanon and Herbert Marcuse as the intellectual figures behind a fragmented but dangerous Western revolutionary movement.
The issue also reports on the Leslie Sawhny Programme's 1969 training activities and closes with "With Many Voices," quoting N. A. Palkhivala calling socialism "the opiate of the people."

Arvind A. Deshpande's "Political Opportunism" surveys the chaotic state politics of UP, Bihar and West Bengal following the Congress split, singling out Charan Singh's rise to power in UP with 98 MLAs.

A. G. Mulgaokar analyses the Supreme Court's judgment striking down the Bank Nationalisation Act for violating fundamental rights and the compensation guarantee, defending the Court's constitutional role against critics including the Prime Minister.

Adam Adil traces the deteriorating Sino-Soviet relationship from 1956 to the 1969 Ussuri River border clash, noting China's simultaneous talks with the US in Warsaw and urging India to consider its own dialogue with China.

Writing as "Analyst," a "Bengal Report" assesses the first year of the CPM-led United Front ministry, finding over 300,000 acres of land forcibly occupied and CPM membership expanded to roughly 30,000 with a 110,000-strong paramilitary volunteer corps.

Sadhu Singh Dhami reviews C. Seshachari's Gandhi and the American Scene, faulting it for not examining whether Gandhian satyagraha could resolve American racial conflict given Stokely Carmichael's rejection of nonviolence.

Padma Bhavnani reviews Svetlana Alliluyeva's memoir Only One Year, tracing her disillusionment with Communism to her mother's suicide and the Kremlin's refusal to register her marriage to Indian Communist Brajesh Singh.

A reader's letter from N. K. Sane disputes an earlier article on the Jamshedpur strike, arguing it was driven by local "Mastans" (strongmen) rather than ideological Communist factions, with both sides agreeing on the need for statutory secret-ballot union recognition.

M. R. Masani's "Let Us Modernise Our Thinking," a parliamentary budget speech, attacks twenty years of planning for stagnant per capita income and argues state-sector investment returns only 2 paise per rupee against 7 paise in the private sector.

Adam Adil's "Laos & Cambodia" surveys North Vietnamese and Pathet Lao advances on the Plain of Jars and the coup against Prince Norodom Sihanouk, arguing Asian democracies bear primary responsibility for resisting Communist infiltration in South-East Asia.

Jayaprakash Narayan's "Some Suggestions" argues genuine social change requires revived jana shakti (people's power) along Gandhian lines rather than top-down state planning, and proposes a Constitutional Council to bind Centre-state disputes.

B. N. Datar reviews Christopher Mayhew's Party Games on the British Labour Party's shift from 1930s utopian socialism to 1960s pragmatism, and Mayhew's finding that MPs cannot effectively influence the executive.

An unsigned contributed piece catalogues cost overruns and delays at Soviet-aided projects including Bokaro, whose completion slipped from 1968 to 1973 with costs rising to about Rs. 800 crores, and IDPL's "huge loss" from unsuitable Soviet-supplied design.
Arvind A. Deshpande reviews Chanchal Sarkar's Challenge and Stagnation on the Indian mass media, endorsing its harsh diagnosis and proposal to treat newspapers as a public utility.

The closing "With Many Voices" column includes inflammatory quotes from West Bengal politicians Harekrishna Konar and Ajoy Mukherjee and Guru Golwalkar's remark equating secularism with being a "staunch Hindu."

Adam Adil's "Communal Riots" surveys 321 communal riots since Independence, including recent outbreaks in Ahmedabad, Bhiwandi and Jalgaon, arguing an educated elite's failure to modernise its communities is the deeper cause rather than anti-social elements alone.

R. N. Karnik's "Nath Pai's Bill" lays out the legal background to the Golak Nath judgment and the pending Constitution Amendment Bill, giving eight reasons the Prime Minister should not press the Bill given her government's lack of a parliamentary majority.

Writing as "Analyst," a "Bengal Report" surveys Governor's Rule in West Bengal, noting weakening Naxalite violence after police action at Debra and Gopiballabhpur and a failed pro-Soviet CPI proposal to revive the fourteen-party United Front.

A short item quotes C. D. Deshmukh estimating that a quarter to a third of state development funds are wasted through incompetence or venality, illustrated by a public-sector steel plant tender scandal.

A contributed report on a Srinagar seminar on press freedom, organised with the Friedrich Naumann Stiftung and attended by M. R. Masani, Piloo Mody and Khushwant Singh, affirms unanimous support for press freedom while debating whether newspaper monopoly exists.
Reader letters call for coalition among like-minded parties, Swatantra, Jana Sangh, Congress (O), and criticise "Socialism a la Indira" as vote-driven rather than principled.
Book reviews cover Samaren Roy's The Restless Brahmin on M. N. Roy's early revolutionary life, Jamnadas Dwarkadas's Political Memoirs, and Khushwant Singh's India.

A. G. Mulgaokar's "Mr. Dhavan's Imperfect World" attacks the Governor of West Bengal for using a judicial swearing-in ceremony to praise Soviet-style justice, arguing the episode is itself the strongest case for abolishing the office of Governor.

The "Notes" section welcomes the 1970 Ceylon and British elections as proof of democracy's capacity for peaceful change and condemns the murder of communist Maharashtra legislator Krishna Desai as part of rising political violence linked to the Naxalite movement.

Adam Adil's "Situation In Indo-China" surveys the winding-down of the US intervention in Cambodia, phased troop withdrawal from South Vietnam, and a hopeful movement toward negotiation in Laos between Souvanna Phouma and the Pathet Lao's Souphanouvong.

Brigadier J. P. Dalvi's "Meghalaya: Blueprint Of Hope" celebrates the 2 April 1970 inauguration of Meghalaya as a triumph of non-violent constitutional negotiation, tracing the movement from the 1960 Assam Language Bill controversy through the 1966 Mizo rebellion he witnessed as army commander.

V. B. Karnik reviews Angela Burger's Opposition in a Dominant-Party System, arguing the book's framing was overtaken by the 1969 Congress split and speculating about a coming era of regional parties or "politics without parties."
A reader's letter from N. J. Tavaria defends American Cold War interventionism in Asia, crediting Kennedy's 1962 support with preventing India becoming a Soviet satellite.
The closing "With Many Voices" page quotes Abraham Lincoln on the moral case for revolution against denial of constitutional rights.

Writing as "Atreya," "Prospects for Political Consolidation" welcomes the AICC(O)'s resolution to consolidate "like-minded" parties into a Grand Alliance of Congress(O), Swatantra, Jana Sangh and B.K.D. against a perceived Congress-CPI-Moscow axis.

The "Notes" section criticises the Government for hosting NLF representative Madame Binh as an official guest and condemns the CPI's "land grab" movement as a lawless stunt lacking any real redistribution machinery.

M. R. Pai's "Social Market Economy" argues India could adapt West Germany's postwar Social Market Economy philosophy of Walter Eucken and Ludwig Erhard, which combines market competition with state anti-monopoly enforcement while avoiding central planning.

Writing as "Analyst," "President's Rule" assesses over four months of central rule in West Bengal, citing roughly six thousand Naxalite arrests and Durgapur production running at only 10% capacity under trade-union stranglehold.

G. L. Mathur's "National Integration" contrasts Indian societal fragmentation with American civic solidarity and proposes state-incentivised inter-caste and inter-communal marriage, citing the Prime Minister's son's marriage to an Italian woman.
B. N. Datar reviews Murarji J. Vaidya's posthumous Objectives of Planning in India, characterising it as a candid but one-sided free-enterprise critique of Indian planning.
The closing "With Many Voices" column quotes D. F. Karaka warning India is "virtually becoming a colony controlled from Moscow."

V. B. Karnik's "Land Hunger?" argues leftist demands for land redistribution are largely fictional given India's already-fragmented holdings, drawing on economist Michael Lipton's finding that there is little scope for "distributist land reform," and calls instead for rural industry and disciplined enforcement of existing tenancy law.

The "Notes" column marks the second anniversary of the Czechoslovakia invasion, reports the collapse of a CPM-led strike at Durgapur Steel Works after eleven days including the arrest of Naxalite leader Kanu Sanyal, and previews Kerala's mid-term election alliances.

Arvind A. Deshpande's "West Asia-Combat Of Illusions" welcomes the 1970 Nasser-Israel ceasefire brokered through Gunnar Jarring, urging both sides to abandon illusions about force and security while flagging Palestinian refugees and Jerusalem's status as the key unresolved issues.
A. G. Mulgaokar reviews Briton Martin Jr.'s New India 1885, crediting Allan Octavian Hume as the organiser who united regional bodies into the first Indian National Congress session.

Writing as "Analyst," a "Bengal Report" credits Chief Minister B. B. Ghosh's administration, backed by Indira Gandhi, with breaking the CPM-led Durgapur strike without conceding to demands for withdrawal of security forces.

A reader's letter from E. P. Varghese argues Kerala's Land Reforms Act has produced lawlessness rather than reform, criticising the "kudikidappukaran" hutment-dweller provision as enabling squatters to acquire land for nominal compensation.

Reviews cover N. B. Bonarjee's ICS memoir Under Two Masters and Robert Conquest's edited Industrial Workers in the U.S.S.R., alongside a note condemning Japan's refusal to let Czechoslovak Expo-70 hostesses seek asylum.

G. S. Rao's "Skating on Thin Ice" uses the September 1970 Jordan hijacking crisis to warn that small groups of committed "lawless elements" can hold nations hostage, explicitly comparing the Palestinian guerrillas to India's own Naxalites.

Writing as "Analyst," a "Bengal Report" reads the Kerala mid-term election results as encouraging the CPI toward an open alliance with Congress(R), and notes the CPM recalibrating after over-estimating "revolutionary potentialities."

Adam Adil's "Lusaka Conference" surveys the non-aligned movement's history from Belgrade through Cairo to Lusaka, criticising its "abject silence" over the 1968 Czechoslovakia invasion while crediting the conference's call for genuine, internally-driven non-alignment.

M. R. Masani's "Cotton Trade-Government Monopoly," excerpted from a Lok Sabha speech, attacks the proposed Cotton Corporation of India as an unjustified monopoly grab that will hurt farmers, traders and consumers, citing the appointment of a "discredited Gujarat politician" as chairman.

Ludmilla Thorne reviews Anatoli Marchenko's smuggled camp memoir My Testimony, situating it against Solzhenitsyn's One Day in the Life of Ivan Denisovich as unvarnished proof that Soviet labour camps persisted after Stalin's death.
Reviews cover Dimensions of Industrial Relations in India, marking the ILO's fiftieth anniversary, and a survey finding 13-15% absenteeism across thirty Bombay industrial units.

The issue notes a letter from over 300 citizens protesting the government's expulsion of the BBC from Delhi, and closes with "With Many Voices" quoting N. A. Palkhivala warning "Property has become a dirty word today; liberty may become a dirty word tomorrow."

A. G. Mulgaokar's "Heads I Win, Tails You Lose" dissects the 1970 UP constitutional crisis, in which President's Rule was imposed under Article 356 and withdrawn four days later, arguing no genuine breakdown of constitutional government had occurred and that control of UP politics was decisive to Indira Gandhi's own survival.

C. L. Gheevala's "Democratic Socialism - Need For Rethinking" argues doctrinaire nationalisation and central planning have been discredited by experience, endorsing the Socialist Union's view that a mixed economy needs a legitimately recognised private sector as a check on state activity.

A reprinted New Age article by Prabhat Das Gupta catalogues CPM violence against Naxalite and CPI rivals in West Bengal, citing Hare Krishna Konar's own admission of 109 inter-party clashes and 23 deaths in three months, and naming 21 alleged CPM assault-squad leaders.

M. R. Chandvadkar reviews P. V. R. Rao's Defence Without Drift, which argues India neglected defence until the 1962 Chinese invasion exposed "Himalayan Blunders" of complacency, and finds Indian defence spending at only 3.3% of GNP, the second-lowest in the world.

A contributed report on the Liberal International's 1970 Rome Congress, attended by M. R. Masani for the Indian Liberal Group, covers resolutions on European security, Middle East peace, and legal measures against hijacking and kidnapping.

A review of Mrs. P. Chakraborty's Strikes and Morale in Industry finds Indian trade unionism growing more conciliatory rather than militant, with strikes' economic impact "markedly insignificant" compared to unemployment.
A short item reports armed CRP guards assigned around the clock to four West Bengal political leaders under President's Rule, at a daily cost of over Rs. 127 per leader.

S. V. Raju's "The Need for an Alliance" surveys the fractured opposition, arguing the real danger to India's institutions comes from Congress(R)'s toleration of CPI support and attacks on the judiciary, and that a Grand Alliance is necessary to prevent a Communist-backed coalition from taking power.

C. S. Venkatachar's "Article 356 - Use And Abuse" traces the provision to Section 93 of the 1935 Government of India Act, cataloguing nearly a dozen invocations since Independence used to manipulate state party factions rather than resolve genuine deadlock.

Adam Adil's eulogy for Gamal Abdul Nasser credits him with giving the Arab world "a sense of dignity, unity and purpose," weighing the Suez nationalisation and Aswan Dam against the costly, divisive war in Yemen.

V. B. Karnik reviews Robert Payne's The Rise and Fall of Stalin, quoting its verdict that Stalin "killed without compunction and without enjoyment," and tracing collectivisation's roughly ten million peasant deaths and the purges of Old Bolsheviks.

Writing as "Analyst," "Vicious Circle?" warns of a self-reinforcing cycle of political violence in West Bengal in which police repression breeds youth alienation and further recruitment into Naxalite movements, calling for a "positive psychological, healing approach" instead.

A reprinted article by Marcel Body recounts how Lenin's Comintern deliberately split Western European socialist parties in the 1920s, judging Mussolini's fascism "preferable" to Italian socialism and thereby helping clear the path for Mussolini and, later, Hitler.

Reviews cover P. Spratt's D.M.K. in Power, tracing the party's roots to the Justice Party and Periyar's Self-Respect movement, and a study of the Green Revolution's benefits confined to about 20% of irrigated wheat- and gram-growing areas.

Adam Adil surveys Pakistan's first general elections on adult franchise, concluding they entrenched two irreconcilable nationalisms, Bengali autonomy under Sheikh Mujibur Rehman and Zulfikar Ali Bhutto's centralising West Pakistan politics, leaving the question no longer whether Pakistan will survive as a democracy but whether it will survive as one entity.

A. G. Mulgaokar's "Ultra Vires" analyses the Supreme Court's judgment striking down the abolition of privy purses, reading it as reaffirming that no authority, including the Government, stands above the Rule of Law and rejecting the Attorney-General's claim of unreviewable presidential "paramountcy."

S. R. Mohan Das pays tribute to C. Rajagopalachari on his ninety-second birthday, recalling how as Chief Minister of Madras he reformed a lax Secretariat through personal example rather than formal edicts.

V. B. Karnik's "Revolt In Poland" analyses the December 1970 Baltic-coast workers' revolt over food prices, which forced the resignation of Party leader Gomulka despite brutal suppression, situating it within a recurring pattern of communist-bloc unrest from Poznan 1956 to Czechoslovakia 1968.

Anatole Shub reviews Andrei Amalrik's banned essay "Will the Soviet Union Survive Until 1984?," discussing Amalrik's forecasts of anti-Russian nationalist unrest and possible imperial disintegration in the event of a Sino-Soviet war.

K. K. Sinha's "Strategy For Democracy" argues the Indian Right needs a clear ideological platform combining a growth-oriented economy, honest land reform, rule of law and non-aligned foreign policy to unite Congress(O), Swatantra and Jana Sangh against the Left.

A. G. Noorani reviews Archibald Cox's The Warren Court, highlighting its relevance to Indian debates about banning organisations via the Court's protection of dissenting associations' membership lists.
