Reader letters recount repeated Indian government rejections of Israeli agricultural-cooperation offers and protest barring Israel from a World Table Tennis Championship, while a Tibetan refugee's letter condemns Palestinian violence against civilians while comparing the Tibetan and Palestinian causes.

S. P. Aiyar marks the Constitution's 25th anniversary by reviewing N. A. Palkhivala's Our Constitution Defaced and Defiled, endorsing its argument that Parliament's amending power cannot alter the Constitution's basic structure, a position vindicated in the Fundamental Rights Case.

A reprinted Times of London piece warns that Britain's middle class, squeezed by inflation, the Capital Transfer Tax, and comprehensive-education reforms, is becoming dangerously aggrieved and risks a serious political backlash against the Labour government.

Ruzbeh Antia's "Diwali in December" describes a St. Xavier's College student agitation over free expression for student publications, unconditional exam forms, and canteen-committee control, tracing campus unrest to India's Macaulay-designed, clerk-producing colonial education system.

B. P. Singh, President of the Farmers' Federation of India, rejects the government's "no famine" semantics and demands a public enquiry into starvation deaths, arguing procurement pricing policy cost farmers an estimated Rs. 400 crores in a single year and accusing Indira Gandhi of a "subtler" Stalinist-style agricultural collectivisation.

Russell Kirk's "Marx Vs Confucius" contrasts the Cultural Revolution's public burning of Confucian classics at Chufu with Taiwan's revival of Confucian philosophy, arguing Marxism's totalising ethical claims require the extirpation of rival moral systems.

Col. C. L. Proudfoot reviews K. C. Praval's India's Paratroopers as gripping regimental history spanning Burma to the 1971 war, while Rusi J. Daruwala reviews Guruprasad Murthy's Management by Ordinances, which warns India's economy is "tottering on the edge of the embankment" toward possible revolution.

Manjula Padmanabhan reviews a Bombay production of Stoppard's Rosencrantz and Guildenstern Are Dead, praising the leads' witty delivery but concluding the play, unlike Hamlet, has no independent depth of its own.

Jose De Almeida Araujo's first-person account of fleeing Portugal describes the Communist Party's infiltration of the Armed Forces Movement, 300 blank arrest warrants used to jail opponents, and President Spinola's September 1974 resignation, framed by an editorial note comparing it to Lenin's dissolution of Russia's Constituent Assembly.

The "Between You & Me and The Lamp Post" column reads Marshal Grechko's Delhi visit as deepening Soviet leverage over Indian defence policy, criticises the British TUC's invitation to former KGB chief Alexander Shelepin, and reports Sheikh Mujibur Rehman's constitutional coup establishing a one-party state in Bangladesh.

Kirtidev D. Desai's essay on electoral reform identifies misuse of official machinery, unaccounted money, and first-past-the-post vote-seat distortion as India's three central electoral defects, proposing an independent Election Commission and proportional representation.

A verbatim chapter from the Jayaprakash Narayan-appointed Electoral Reform Committee's report tabulates Congress's vote-seat distortion from 1952-1971 (ranging +13.5 to +29.4 points) and recommends studying the West German mixed electoral model.

Zulie Nakhooda's "Whither Child Welfare in India?" argues Indian planning has neglected children in favour of narrow economic development, noting over 60 percent of institutionalised children have living parents driven by poverty rather than orphanhood.

Arvind A. Deshpande reviews a Diebold Institute study on multinational corporations, arguing MNCs and private enterprise will survive current criticism and citing Singapore, Mexico, and Brazil as examples of rapid growth under varied MNC strategies.

Rusi J. Daruwala reviews David Bonavia's Fat Sasha and the Urban Guerilla on Soviet dissidents, outlining an eight-point Soviet propaganda playbook against critics and describing Samizdat's underground publishing network.

C. R. Irani's "Press Freedom in Peril" attacks the government-appointed Fact Finding Committee on newspapers for exceeding its terms of reference under Minister I. K. Gujral's steering, proposing controls on monopoly and selling prices while showing "excessive solicitude" for small and "bogus" newspapers.

James Burnham's "Two Alternatives to Democracy" proposes replacing the democracy-versus-dictatorship binary with Brian Crozier's tripartite scheme of democratic-pluralist, authoritarian, and "totalist" regimes, arguing Chile and Portugal show the real contest was between two kinds of dictatorship.

Ruzbeh Antia's "Fools' Paradise" satirises Indians' disproportionate hockey-victory euphoria after the 1975 World Cup win over Pakistan, criticising the Prime Minister's request to refund customs duties on the team's goods as undermining equality before the law.

George H. Nash's critical appraisal of Amnesty International argues its membership and personnel skew left despite claims of impartiality, though he concludes it does not practice a deliberate double standard, since structural factors simply make repression easier to document in authoritarian right-wing states.
Manjula Padmanabhan's "Sportsday Revisited" is a light satirical sketch of a Junior School Sports Day, centred on the comic "Parents' Race" and a xenophobic remark from one competitive father.

British MP Nicholas Ridley's "How to Denationalise" argues open-ended public-sector wage settlements, not nationalisation itself, are Britain's chief economic defect, proposing to break the Coal Board, Steel Corporation and Airways Board monopolies by allowing private competition.

A. G. Noorani reviews Sakharov Speaks and Solzhenitsyn: A Documentary Record, quoting Sakharov's warning that "detente without democratization" would be dangerous capitulation, and praising both dissidents' courage.

Aziz Madni reviews Alastair Buchan's Reith Lectures collection Change Without War, highlighting Buchan's pessimistic forecast that only the US, USSR and China will retain true strategic capability through the century's end.

Reprinted eyewitness dispatches from Jon Swain in Pnom-Penh and the Daily Telegraph on an alleged massacre of 185 women and mixed-blood children in Nha Trang document Khmer Rouge and North Vietnamese communist atrocities, framed as correcting a "conspiracy of silence" in the Indian press.

The "Between You & Me and The Lamp Post" column condemns India's annexation of Sikkim, eulogises Chiang Kai-shek as a friend of free India, reports Dubcek's and Havel's smuggled protest letters from Czechoslovakia, and excoriates the Lok Sabha and Indira Gandhi's government for celebrating the fall of Saigon.

A. G. Noorani's "The Military Balance" draws on IISS and SIPRI data to compare India's and Pakistan's armed forces, noting India has become a modest arms exporter despite officially citing "self-imposed restraint."

Farok Contractor's "The Young Men and the Sea" recounts an impromptu overnight shark-fishing trip with Karwari Muslim fishermen off Goa, contrasting romantic expectations with an anticlimactic single catch.

M. R. Masani reviews William Buckley Jr.'s United Nations Journal, quoting Buckley's description of the UN as "the densest collection of oratorical bores in the history of the world" and his barbed characterisation of Indian delegates as compromise-obsessed.

A. H. Doctor reviews Rounaq Jahan's Pakistan: Failure in National Integration, summarising its argument that Pakistan pursued state-building without adequate nation-building or Bengali participation, dooming it to break-up.

Rusi J. Daruwala reviews two Asiatic Society of Bombay publications on a 1516-dated illustrated Aranyaka Parvan manuscript, tracing its provenance to Dr. Bhau Daji's collection and its place in a pre-Mughal Lodi school of painting.

The closing "With Many Voices" page quotes "Friedman's Law" that anything the state does costs twice as much as the free market, and describes the Sarvodaya movement as led by "a saint and a politician," Vinoba Bhave and Jayaprakash Narayan.

An unsigned editorial lists nine defining features of fascism -- one-party dictatorship, judicial subservience, press censorship, corporate-state economic control among them -- prompted by leftist mockery of an anti-fascist conference in Patna, quoting Nehru on fascism making "the State a God."

The "Between You & Me and The Lamp Post" column reports Eldridge Cleaver's disillusioned recantation after seven years of exile in Communist states, a Pravda-L'Humanité spat over a Soviet slave-labour-camp documentary, and British NUS secretary Susan Slipman's removal for favouring Communist causes.

Zambian President Kenneth Kaunda tells C. L. Sulzberger the Soviet Union bears primary responsibility for the Angola conflict, while a Daily Telegraph editorial accuses the American liberal establishment of corrosive self-criticism over Vietnam and Watergate.

Nitin G. Raut critiques the PLO's "secular democratic Palestine State" slogan, arguing Article 6 of the 1968 Palestine National Covenant would render more than half of Israel's Jewish population stateless, and calling the PLO's anti-Zionism "a facade for anti-Semitism."

M. R. Masani reproduces his July 1975 letter to Indira Gandhi rebutting her Lok Sabha claim that he and Jayaprakash Narayan had solicited army intervention, tracing the misquotation to a distorted 1974 New Age rendering of his original "Z" magazine interview.

Bernard Levin mocks The Guardian's belated "discovery" that Mozambique's Frelimo government has turned totalitarian, distinguishing "hard-headed liberals" from "soft-headed progressives" whose uncritical enthusiasm for revolutionary movements causes harm.

James Burnham's sequel to "Two Alternatives to Democracy" refines his totalist/authoritarian/democratic classification, arguing modern authoritarianism comes more often and more dangerously from the Left because leftist economic measures build toward totalism.

J. B. H. Wadia weighs whether Hindi commercial films are "cultural flops," answering "yes -- and no" and citing New Theatres of Calcutta and Prabhat of Poona as a minor but real tradition of culturally valuable film alongside the commercial mainstream.

Book reviews cover Philip Mason's biography of Kipling and his complicated relationship with India, Merle Miller's oral biography of Truman quoting his view that "power, money and women" ruin a man, and Lord George-Brown's memoir In My Way.

The Bombay High Court's Division Bench (Justices Madon and Kania) dismissed the Emergency censor's appeal on 10 February 1976, upholding Justice Bhatt's ruling on nine of eleven disputed Freedom First items and issuing a writ of mandamus, holding that Emergency provisions suspend restrictions on state power, not citizens' underlying common-law free-speech rights.

The "Between You & Me and The Lamp Post" column praises Margaret Thatcher's "Iron Lady" anti-Soviet speech, reports Tass's aggrieved response to British "misconceptions" of the USSR, and notes Chinese state media blaming Brezhnev personally for a poor Soviet grain harvest.

A reprinted Bernard Levin column eulogises outgoing US Ambassador to the UN Daniel Moynihan for bluntly calling out regimes like Idi Amin's Uganda as racist and murderous despite Amin's OAU standing, framing liberalism's chief weakness as a shortage of adherents as single-minded as its enemies.

Mehra Masani reviews Collins and Lapierre's Freedom at Midnight, praising its dramatised account of the Gandhi-assassination conspiracy while criticising "gimmicky" digressions on the princes and Gandhi's sex life.

R. Srinivasan reviews Dharma Vira's Memoirs of a Civil Servant, ranking it below classics of the genre but praising its candid account of his governorships of Punjab, West Bengal and Karnataka through the jeep and tractor scandals.
A reader's letter, "The Original Fascist," argues that if corporatism is inherently fascist, the true father of fascism is Lenin rather than Mussolini, drawing the editor's one-word retort "Touche."

"At Last You Can Read This" compiles previously censor-blocked items, including June 1975 Cairo trial testimony branding Nasser a unilateral dictator, an Amnesty International resolution on police duty to disobey torture orders, and the Madras High Court's admission of a Swarajya publisher's writ against a censorship deletion.

M. R. Masani's editorial "Is Solzhenitsyn Right?" treats the writer's 1 March 1976 BBC Panorama warning of the West's "sudden and imminent fall" as vindication of the magazine's own long-standing warnings, noting Lord George-Brown's resignation from the Labour whip in apparent solidarity and dismissing Eurocommunism as a rehash of discredited 1940s promises from Gomulka, Gottwald and Rakosi.

The "Between You & Me and The Lamp Post" column criticises the dismissal of elected state governments in Tamil Nadu and Gujarat as a violation of India's federal structure, gives the March 1976 Union Budget "two cheers," and commends the Swiss proportional-representation model over British-style majoritarianism.

Solzhenitsyn's BBC interview, reported in full, warns the Soviet Union's war-footing economy extracted Western concessions without needing nuclear war, criticises the "spirit of Helsinki" as strengthening Soviet totalitarianism, and argues that free circulation of The Gulag Archipelago inside the USSR would quickly collapse communist ideology.

Lord George-Brown's resignation of the Labour whip over the defeat of Lord Goodman's press-freedom amendment is reported alongside a Glavlit censorship official's fifteen-year black-market book-smuggling scandal and a New York Times item on Kim Il Sung's dynastic promotion of his son as "crown prince" in North Korea.

Thomas W. Lippman reports on a popular Cairo film, based on a Neguib Mahfouz novel, dramatising secret-police torture under Nasser, noting Sadat's own public "corrective revaluation" acknowledging Nasser-era "deviations" and prison camps.

A lengthy reproduction of the Bombay High Court Division Bench's censorship judgement finds the government's objections to nine Freedom First items "fanciful and far-fetched," upholding the Maharashtra Bar Council's right to publish its resolution urging revocation of the Emergency and warning that banning historical material would make it impossible to publish any account of the freedom movement.

S. P. Aiyer reviews Donald Rogowski's Rational Legitimacy, finding its rejection of cultural-determinist theories of government persuasive but its application to a supposedly "pillarized" Indian society overly abstract, leaving him "cold and uninspired."

An abridged Polish Communist journal article by Wieslaw Gornicki, presented as an unexpected echo of Moynihan's UN critique, argues the Group of 77's claimed Third World solidarity is economically incoherent given the vast income gap between Kuwait's $11,000 and Haiti's under $100 per head.

The "Between You & Me and the Lamp Post" column criticises Indian state governors and the CBI for pushing to curb High Court writ jurisdiction under Article 226, contrasting this with a simultaneous British debate over adopting a Bill of Rights, and reports Thai PM Kukrit Pramoj's election defeat by his own brother Seni Pramoj.

Dr. Fredoon P. Antia's "Dying with Dignity" argues for a legal right to die, built around the Karen Ann Quinlan case and a Florida transfusion-refusal ruling, proposing India recognise the right to end one's own life as a Fundamental Right akin to Article 19.

British MP Bryan Magee's "Why Marxism Is Left Behind" reports two prominent ex-Marxists independently telling him Marxism is intellectually exhausted, arguing communist-led national liberation movements succeeded only by concealing themselves under nationalism.

A "World News" digest covers a NATO study warning a Warsaw Pact conventional attack could overrun Western Europe before nuclear response is authorised, Victor Zorza's analysis of the ageing Soviet Politburo, and historian Allen Weinstein's reversal concluding Alger Hiss lied for nearly thirty years.

Nitin G. Raut reviews Golda Meir's autobiography My Life, recounting her clandestine wartime visit to Amman disguised as an Arab woman and Ben Gurion's description of her as "the only man" in his cabinet.
The closing "With Many Voices" page quotes John F. Kennedy arguing Communism has succeeded only as "a scavenger of disruption" caused by war or repression, never as a leader in its own right.

M. R. Masani's "State of the Nation" reprints his letter to Encounter describing Emergency-era detention without trial under MISA, press censorship barring comment on the Prime Minister's own court case, and characterises India's Emergency as a reversible "limited form of authoritarianism" rather than fascism or communism.

A British Royal Commission on the Press report recommends financial assistance for Fleet Street be drawn from the private sector rather than government, warning public funding risks partisan influence over newspapers.

Dimitri K. Simes describes the Soviet Union's permanent, structural "parallel market" in goods and services, arguing the regime has grown more tolerant of it "for a good cause" even as it still prosecutes some speculators, since the official economy may be unable to survive without it.

A. G. Noorani reviews two books on Pakistan's collapse and Zulfiqar Ali Bhutto's rise, detailing the Pakistan People's Party's 1970 manifesto and the authoritarian press curbs Bhutto imposed once in power.

Ernest van den Haag distinguishes "economic desert" from "moral desert" to defend market income distribution, noting the US poverty rate fell from 50% in 1920 to under 11% in 1966 even as resentment of remaining inequality intensified.

Geeta Doctor reviews the Performance Group of New York's immersive, four-hour staging of Brecht's Mother Courage at the Cathedral School, judging it a faithful realisation of Brecht's "Verfremdung" alienation effect.

A news item reports dissident writer Andrei Amalrik's reluctant agreement, after sustained KGB harassment, to accept exile abroad via Israel before travelling to the Netherlands and the United States.

S. V. Raju's "'A Tired Document from Tired Men'" critiques the Steering Committee's draft policy for a new united opposition party merging Congress (O), the Socialist Party, the Jan Sangh and the Bharatiya Lok Dal, endorsing its civil-liberties points but criticising an arbitrary 1:10 income-ratio commitment and vague "total plan" language as Gosplan-like patchwork.

The "Between You & Me and the Lamp Post" column cites a Kultura article showing East Bloc resistance to Third World aid demands at UNCTAD Nairobi and mocks Brezhnev's praise of Congress's public-sector industrialisation policy as responsible for India's economic plight.

Eldridge Cleaver, writing from a California prison cell, attacks the UN resolution branding Zionism as racism, arguing from personal experience that Arab states practice racism toward black Africans including literal slavery.
An extract from Solzhenitsyn's BBC broadcast argues socialism functions as an emotionally satisfying "worldly religion" whose logical expression, not distortion, is forced labour and the Gulag.

A legal correspondent reports Justice Kania's admission of Acharya Kripalani's writ petition challenging the Emergency censor's suppression of a March 1976 opposition-unity resolution, with the maintainability question referred to a Division Bench.

Sujata Manohar reviews Soli Sorabjee's Law of Press Censorship in India, highlighting the Bombay High Court's finding in M. R. Masani vs. Binod Rao that nine of eleven censored Freedom First items were wrongly banned.

Fredoon Antia reviews World of Hunger: A Strategy for Survival, questioning the authors' faith in global redistribution given their own admission that "working adults keep the largest share of available food for themselves" even within families.

A reader's letter by P. L. Mayekar objects to the Swaran Singh Committee's proposal to designate India a "Socialist Republic" in the Constitution, warning the imprecise term would confer unearned respectability and pave the way for enforced ideological conformity.

M. R. Masani's "Oh, The Frivolity Of It!" attacks the Swaran Singh Committee for giving the public only twelve days to respond to its proposed constitutional "Duties of the Citizen," objecting most sharply to the recommendation that courts be barred from testing the validity of laws enforcing them.

The "Between You & Me and the Lamp Post" column praises the Entebbe rescue as proof that deterrent action against terrorism works, and cites Poland's rapid reversal of steep food-price increases after riots as evidence that price controls are no substitute for supply and demand even under a totalitarian government.

"Tass vs. The Times" juxtaposes a Soviet commentator's defence of the Indian Emergency as a response to colonial-era Western press hostility against a Times editorial arguing Western disappointment stemmed from misplaced faith that Indian parliamentary practice extended beyond an English-educated urban elite.

Bernard Levin's bicentennial essay insists America remains "the last, best hope of all mankind" 200 years after independence, contrasting its self-healing constitutional order against France, Italy, Africa, and India under its "seedy dictator."

Resolutions from the Citizens for Democracy annual meeting call for making Emergency proclamations justiciable, for confining suspension of fundamental rights strictly to genuine war or insurrection, and for general elections no later than March 1977.

A "World News" digest reports Swiss voters rejecting an interest-free loan to the International Development Association, a smuggled Granada Television documentary on Soviet ethnic-minority dissent, and a Guardian piece on the political misuse of Soviet psychiatry against dissident Vladimir Bukovsky.
Geeta Doctor's theatre review of the Gujarati play Vaishakhi Koyal praises its unusual lyricism and its heroine's complexity, departing from typical melodramatic Gujarati stage stereotypes.

A. G. Noorani reviews The Anatomy of Communist Takeovers, highlighting Hammond's thesis that only Yugoslavia, Albania, China and North Vietnam saw genuinely indigenous Communist takeovers, with Soviet policy today driven chiefly by Russian national interest rather than doctrinal world revolution.

M. R. Masani's "On Discipline" argues Indian public life suffers chronic civic indiscipline, invoking Walter Lippmann's warning that a public faced with an incompetent representative assembly will choose authoritarian government over freedom instead.

The "Between You and Me and the Lamp Post" column marks the first anniversary of the Helsinki Final Act, names Soviet dissidents monitoring Soviet compliance, and condemns the politicisation of the 1976 Montreal Olympics over Taiwan and South Africa-linked boycotts.

Andrei Amalrik, writing after his forced emigration, challenges Western complacency about Helsinki's effects, describing a KGB shift toward pressuring dissidents into emigration and deniable tactics like staged accidents rather than mass legal arrests.

Sir Keith Joseph argues defenders of the free market have obscured its true moral basis -- the view of humans as rational, choice-making agents -- while socialism denies individuality by treating people as interchangeable productive factors.

Collin Welch praises Israel's Entebbe rescue as a rare complete victory over terrorism, criticising Britain's tepid response despite possessing comparable military capability, and attributing Western timidity to an excess of competing considerations rather than lack of means.

A "World News" digest reports Chinese officials including Teng Hsiao-ping accused of "capitalist roader" privilege, fourteen Soviet political prisoners sending Bicentennial greetings to America, and former Egyptian secret-police chief Saleh Naser's ten-year sentence for torturing journalist Moustapha Amin.

A. G. Noorani reviews Rajeshwar Dayal's Congo memoir Mission for Hammarskjold, highlighting Dayal's paired profiles of Lumumba and Hammarskjold and his balanced verdict that UN failures in the Congo were real but should not obscure its achievements.

M. R. Masani's "The 44th -- And the Last?" recalls his 1975 Bangalore lectures on presidential and gubernatorial discretion and attacks the pending 44th Constitutional Amendment Bill for denying the President a veto and insulating itself from Supreme Court review, arguing the ruling party's 1971 mandate came from under a quarter of the total electorate.

The "Between You and Me and the Lamp Post" column contrasts Indian press adulation of Mao at his death with earlier condemnation of Stalin, citing estimates of 25-80 million killed under Mao's rule, and criticises the Advocates (Amendment) Bill for abolishing the solicitor-barrister division in the Bombay and Calcutta High Courts.

Bernard Levin's essay on Solzhenitsyn's "Live Not by Lies" credo summarises the writer's proposed "key" of personal non-participation in official falsehood as an alternative to active resistance, quoting his catalogue of everyday refusals such as not attending mandatory demonstrations.

A "World News" digest reports Pakistan's fifth constitutional amendment curbing High Court bail powers, unconfirmed reports of Premier Kosygin's declining health, and the pervasive burden of queueing for bread and apartments across the Soviet bloc.

Geeta Doctor's film column "The Poetry of Violence" reflects on Bruce Lee's death, describing how he transformed martial-arts combat into "a strangely compelling dance of death" through fanatical personal discipline.

S. P. Aiyar reviews a sympathetic Scrafe biography of Jayaprakash Narayan, criticising JP's notion of partyless, small-community democracy as romantic but affirming his warnings against state power reducing citizens to "a cog in a vast human machine."

V. B. Karnik reviews the first volume of Sarvepalli Gopal's official Nehru biography, arguing Nehru and Congress leaders' denial of the Muslim League's representative character made Partition's communal violence more likely, and rejecting the book jacket's comparison of Nehru to Mao as "ludicrous."

M. R. Masani's "Prices Are Like Water" argues price controls cannot defeat the underlying laws of supply, demand and money supply, citing a 4.7% wholesale price rise in mid-1976 and Poland's abandoned 1976 price hikes after riots as a cautionary parallel.

The "Between You & Me and the Lamp Post" column recounts the Koh-i-noor diamond dispute (quoting Nehru that "diamonds are for emperors and India does not need emperors"), criticises the Kissinger-brokered Rhodesia settlement as based on "deceit," and welcomes the 1976 Swedish and West German election results as a rejection of socialism.

M. Murlidhar's "Trade Unions as Press Censors" argues British trade unions, especially the NUJ and SOGAT, have begun exercising an insidious form of press censorship, citing disputes at the Financial Times and the Observer.

Peter Sager's "Models of Majority Rule?" surveys deteriorating, Cuban- and Soviet-backed Angola and Mozambique -- industrial production down 70% and agricultural production down 90% in Mozambique -- as a cautionary counter-example to Western pressure for "majority rule" in Rhodesia.

A "World News" digest covers a Guardian editorial accusing Kissinger of deceit over the Rhodesia settlement, the Sri Lankan High Court invalidating emergency regulations used against a Tamil leader, and Soviet pilot Lt. Viktor Belenko's defection with a MIG-25.

A letters exchange between M. Murlidhar and Masani debates whether business malpractice deserves equal blame with labour indiscipline, while N. C. Zamindar alleges communist workers suppressed a Gandhian-literature pushcart in Indore.

S. V. Raju reviews Irving Wallace's The R Document, a thriller imagining a 35th US Constitutional Amendment suspending the Bill of Rights during emergencies, praising it as "a thriller and an educator."

A. G. Noorani reviews Hugo Young's The Crossman Affair on the legal battle over publishing Richard Crossman's Cabinet diaries, highlighting Lord Chief Justice Widgery's balancing of Cabinet confidentiality against the public's right to know how they are governed.

Piloo Mody's tribute "Dum Spiro Spero" memorialises A. D. Gorwala, recounting his resignation from the ICS and the Commodities Prices Board out of conviction that government was insincere, and his sixteen years running the weekly Opinion until the Emergency forced its closure.

The "Between You & Me and The Lamp Post" column argues the 44th Constitution Amendment's postponement of general elections is ultra vires under the Kesavananda Bharati precedent, marks the twentieth anniversary of the Soviet invasion of Hungary, and praises Milton Friedman's Nobel Prize and advocacy of floating exchange rates.

Leo Labedz's "China, Russia and the U.S.A.," based on conversations with Chinese Foreign Ministry officials in Peking, argues Chinese foreign policy is trapped between anti-Soviet and anti-American frustrations and that a Sino-Soviet reconciliation is neither realistic nor in Peking's interest.

Mehra Masani reviews Julian Hale's Radio Power on international broadcasting propaganda, contrasting the BBC's durable wartime credibility with the short-lived effectiveness of Nazi propaganda, and praising Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty for airing dissident voices like Solzhenitsyn and Sakharov.

A letter from F. P. Antia follows up his earlier "Dying with Dignity" article by proposing specific legislative provisions for physician- or next-of-kin-administered euthanasia in India, with the editors noting California's newly signed right-to-die legislation as a model.

M. R. Masani's "Bread or Freedom?" rejects the framing that a nation must choose between elections and economic stability as an antithesis invented by dictatorships, arguing democracies with free elections and rule of law consistently outperform authoritarian states on prosperity.

A reprinted extract from Hedrick Smith's The Russians catalogues the hidden privilege system of the Soviet nomenklatura elite -- closed stores, "certificate roubles," chauffeured Zil limousines, and the rank-contingent dacha system -- presented as vindicating Sanjay Gandhi's claim that inequality is worse in socialist countries.

A "World News" digest cites Brian Crozier's thesis of a slow-motion "Third World War" through Soviet expansionism since 1945, Zhores Medvedev's revelations of two covered-up Soviet disasters, and the founding of the US "Committee on the Present Danger" to warn Carter about Soviet military expansion.

A Bombay High Court ruling in the Sadhana magazine case held that even during the Emergency, strong criticism of government policies and named ministers remains permissible so long as it does not seek to create disaffection toward "Government established by law" as such.
Reader letters debate judicial review's necessity in India, call for dissolving Parliament and holding February 1977 elections, and attribute rising prices to central government deficit financing.

A. G. Noorani reviews B. R. Tomlinson's The Indian National Congress and the Raj, 1929-1942, highlighting Gandhi's unifying but non-partisan role amid Congress factionalism and the contrast between Subhas Chandra Bose's independent Bengal base and the business-funded Gandhian establishment.

Geeta Doctor reviews Pierre Gombin's The Origins of Modern Leftism on post-1968 French "contestation" politics, criticising the ideology's vague, mystical faith in the proletariat as echoing the very Marxist certainties it claims to reject.

M. R. Masani's "Good-Bye to Federalism" argues India effectively ceased to be a federal republic after the December 1976 removal of Nandini Satpathy's Orissa government, quoting Ambedkar's Constituent Assembly warning against over-centralising the Centre, with a Stop Press note announcing the Lok Sabha's dissolution and General Elections.

The "Between You & Me and The Lamp Post" column celebrates Vladimir Bukovsky's release in exchange for Chilean communist Luis Corvalan as a Soviet propaganda defeat, satirises the personality cult around Brezhnev's 70th birthday, and accuses Ho Chi Minh's Western sympathisers, including Nehru and Jayaprakash Narayan, of naivety about his Communist allegiance.

Nitin G. Raut's essay on the Lebanese civil war traces the 1943 National Charter's confessional power-sharing formula and its erosion, arguing Syria's intervention serves pan-Arab strategy against Israel rather than protecting Lebanese Christians, and concluding the country is already de facto partitioned.

M. R. Masani reports as P.E.N. delegate on the 41st International P.E.N. Congress in London, covering Mario Vargas Llosa's election as President, a resolution condemning the imprisonment of writers (including in India) opposed only by East German delegates, and Arthur Koestler's protested keynote address.

A reprinted Times of London editorial welcomes Indira Gandhi's announcement of March elections as a limited step back toward parliamentary democracy while doubting the Emergency's censorship will genuinely relax, noting friction between Sanjay Gandhi's anti-communist rhetoric and the government's pro-Soviet posture.

A "World News" digest covers Jean-Bedel Bokassa's self-coronation as Emperor of the Central African Empire, a Social Democratic Alliance dossier naming 33 Trotskyist-sympathising Labour MPs, and a Rhodesian guerrilla massacre of 26 black tea-estate workers.

Reader letters include Meanjin editor J. H. Davidson's salute to Freedom First's decision to cease publication rather than accept censorship, and K. S. Venkateswaran's argument that the "bread versus freedom" framing used to justify constitutional amendments is a false dichotomy.

A review of Mehra Masani's Broadcasting and the People calls for decentralising Indian radio via low-power local transmitters, while S. S. Bankeshwar reviews Ram Swarup's Foundations of Maoism, endorsing its call for India to develop political-warfare and ideological counter-strategy against China rather than relying solely on territorial defence.

M. R. Masani's "The Lady and the Tiger" welcomes Indira Gandhi's calling of General Elections after eighteen months of Emergency while questioning her motives, recalling a 1975 letter he and other signatories sent urging exactly this course, and criticising India's electoral system for producing landslide seat majorities from minority vote shares.

The "Between You & Me and The Lamp Post" column condemns the supersession of Justice H. R. Khanna for Chief Justice despite his Emergency-era habeas corpus dissent, reporting he resigned within ten minutes of learning of it, and criticises Britain's Bullock Report on industrial democracy for favouring trade-union nominees over employee-elected representatives.

A report on a London press-freedom dispute describes printers' union members refusing to print a David Astor article critical of union censorship of the press, with the Press Council condemning the resulting strike at the Times.

Chief Justice V. D. Tulzapurkar's Nagpur speech defends the Supreme Court's "basic structure" doctrine from Keshavananda Bharati against being dismissed as a mere "Judges' invention," catalogues disparaging remarks by Law Minister H. R. Gokhale about the judiciary, and objects to the Maharashtra Chief Minister's claim that "judges come drunk to Courts."

C. R. Irani of The Statesman receives the 1977 Freedom House Award for resisting Emergency-era press restrictions, though his impounded passport prevents him from attending; the citation places him alongside past recipients Winston Churchill and Willy Brandt.

M. R. Masani mocks the abrupt public rupture between Congress and the CPI after nearly eight years of cooperation, citing his own 1954 book documenting CPI conduct and noting the continuing Indo-Soviet Security Pact as evidence of the contradiction voters are asked to accept.

A "World News" digest reports Ian Smith's rejection of new British Rhodesia proposals, jailed Yugoslav dissident Mihajlo Mihajlov's deteriorating hunger-strike condition, and the Soviet Union honouring Trotsky's assassin Ramon Mercader as a Hero of the Soviet Union.

F. P. Antia's letter renews his case for euthanasia for mentally competent, incurably suffering patients, citing a new California "living will" law and the Archbishop of Canterbury's view that prolonging life "at any cost" is a fallacy, while C. Cardoza's letter defends the fairness of the coming election despite Emergency censorship.

A. G. Noorani reviews Abraham Tertz's (Andrei Sinyavsky's) prison-letters volume A Voice from the Chorus, surveying its eclectic range from essays on Western literary figures to Chechen oral songs and a retelling of an Indian tale from the Mahabharata.

M. R. Masani's editorial "The Lady and the Elephant" allegorises the Indian electorate's endurance of the Emergency and its 1977 verdict against Congress, blaming Indira Gandhi's refusal to resign after the 1975 Allahabad High Court verdict and calling her subsequent actions a "constitutional coup d'etat".

Masani lists five imperative needs for the incoming Janata government: electoral reform through proportional representation, restoration of the rule of law and judicial independence, federalism, identification of foreign supporters of the Emergency, and limited Gandhian government.

In his "Between You & Me and the Lamp Post" column, Masani praises President Carter's outreach to Soviet dissidents Sakharov and Bukovsky, criticises British equivocation over barring Idi Amin from the Commonwealth Conference, and reports on Marxist-led student unrest at Essex and LSE.

M. Murlidhar's essay traces the Soviet campaign against religion from Marx and Lenin through the 1929 League of Militant Godless and a wartime honeymoon for the Orthodox Church, concluding that religion survives privately despite official suppression.

An abridged Free Nation piece, reprinted as "The High-Speed Virgin", accuses British Labour politician Michael Foot and other "Gentlemen Socialists" of using socialist rhetoric to disguise an authoritarian instinct to govern others "for their own good".

N. K. Seetharaman's tribute frames C. Rajagopalachari's entire public life as a struggle for individual freedom, citing his 1959 Swatantra Party warning against a "true Leviathan" state and his defence of Article 19 rights against erosion.

A World News digest reprints Carter's letter to Sakharov, Milovan Djilas's appeal on Yugoslav political prisoners, and an exposé of Spanish Communist leader Santiago Carrillo's role in the 1936 Paracuellos massacres.

Bernard Levin's reprinted Times review marks the 100th issue of Survey magazine, and the issue closes with an obituary of Bertram D. Wolfe, a founder of the Communist International turned resolute foe of Soviet dictatorship and author of Three Who Made a Revolution.

A front-page report, "No Second Derailment", summarises M. R. Masani's address to the Indian Liberal Group proposing a commission of inquiry into the 1975 "constitutional coup d'etat" and a non-partisan "Committee of a Hundred" civil-liberties watchdog, a proposal Jayaprakash Narayan publicly welcomed.

Julius Telesin's essay explains samizdat, the Soviet Union's unofficial uncensored self-publishing practice, distinguishing it from tamizdat and detailing the risks typists and readers face despite its technical non-illegality.

M. Murlidhar criticises the government's retreat on family planning as capitulation to "mass hysteria", invoking A. V. Dicey's distinction between legislative and public opinion to argue population policy should override popular sentiment as the Hindu Code Bill once did.

K. Vedamurthy's essay on the renewed relevance of C. Rajagopalachari likens him to Ralph Waldo Emerson, crediting him with founding the Swatantra Party against "parrot culture" and unquestioning political obedience.

Arnold C. Harberger, in a reprinted Wall Street Journal letter, defends Milton Friedman's 1976 Nobel Prize against criticism of his 1975 Chile visit, stating both economists had no consulting relationship with the Pinochet government and that Friedman refused two honorary degrees to avoid any appearance of endorsement.
Geeta Doctor's film review finds Satyajit Ray's Jana Aranya a weaker retread of Pratidwandi and Mahanagar, criticising its slow pacing and repeated visual motifs.

A. G. Noorani reviews B. B. Misra's The Indian Political Parties, praising its archival Intelligence Bureau sourcing and its account of Nehru's admission to Asaf Ali that the 1939 Congress ministries' resignation had been an error.

A World News digest covers Solzhenitsyn's fund aiding Soviet political prisoners, comparative Soviet-Western worker living standards, and defected MIG pilot Viktor Belenko's astonishment at U.S. military life.

M. R. Masani's lead editorial, "How the People Really Voted", disputes the narrative that Janata "swept the North, lost the South", using Election Commission data to show Congress's southern vote share held only modestly, and blames India's first-past-the-post system for distorting seat-vote relationships.

S. P. Aiyar's "India's Ballot Box Revolution" frames the 1977 election as ending thirty years of Congress dominance, rejecting the "Divine Right Theory" that a dominant party suits a plural society, while warning that political loyalties remain volatile.

Bernard Levin's reprinted Times column mocks Western commentators who dismissed Indian elections as a "pointless farce" while excusing Chinese authoritarianism, and quotes at length Jayaprakash Narayan's final pre-election appeal to "defeat the dictators".

Masani's lamp-post column profiles Ludwig Erhard's post-war economic liberalism and his 1958 warning that Indian statism would delay its escape from poverty, alongside notice of early Janata moves toward broadcast and educational autonomy.

Geeta Doctor's travel essay recounts a drive across the Deccan from Bombay to Hyderabad and Mysore, visiting a Bahmani-era fort at Naldrug and the Srisailam dam, offered as a deliberate contrast to the issue's election coverage.

A World News digest reports India's refusal of a Soviet credit offer for the Bokaro steel plant, Soviet-bloc training of Idi Amin's security forces, and mass detention camps in post-independence Mozambique.

Reader letters from Dinshah K. Malegamvala and N. C. Zamindar call for dismantling the Samachar news monopoly and autonomous broadcasting, while warning that Janata's use of religious campaigners risks repeating the historical "Khilafat mistake".

S. V. Raju's "A Homespun Prime Minister" profiles Morarji Desai's rise from a rural, impoverished upbringing through the Bombay Provincial Civil Service and repeated exclusion from the premiership by Nehru and the Congress "Syndicate", to his 1977 accession, and reviews his two-volume autobiography.

Vladimir Bukovsky's translated Berlin address, "Frontiers of Freedom Within Us", argues that the true frontier of freedom runs within individual conscience rather than at political borders, drawing on his own imprisonment in Soviet labour camps and naming Helsinki human-rights monitors still jailed in the USSR.

Brian Crozier rebuts the "McCarthyite" label, tracing a long left-wing anti-Communist tradition through Orwell, Bevin and Wilson, and his own turn against Communism after reading Victor Kravchenko's I Chose Freedom.

Writing pseudonymously as "Mitradev", a memorandum urges the new Janata government to expose Emergency-era abuses, hold a fair inquiry into politicised intelligence services with blame falling on those who gave orders, and avoid doctrinaire "social engineering", invoking Edmund Burke.

Masani's lamp-post column welcomes reports that the Planning Commission might be abolished as a Soviet-modelled organ of statism, and draws a parallel between British "nepotism" over Peter Jay's ambassadorial appointment and Indira Gandhi's defence of Sanjay Gandhi's business dealings.

A World News digest notes Tanzanian President Nyerere's admission that his country is "neither socialist nor self-reliant", Cuban military advisers arriving in Ethiopia, and Bishop Muzorewa's warning of civil war in Rhodesia.

Nitin Raut reviews Woodward and Bernstein's The Final Days on Nixon's psychological disintegration during Watergate's endgame, while Harold Jackson's review of Sitting Comfortably treats a Cornell study of human evacuation habits with dry humour.

H. P. Ranina's "Has Mr. Patel Missed The Bus?" critiques Finance Minister H. M. Patel's Budget, welcoming rural-development allocations and capital-gains reforms against tax evasion but faulting the unworkable section 72A sick-company provision and a surcharge hike that reverses the Wanchoo Committee's pro-compliance logic, arguing Patel could have become "the Erhard of India".

U.S. Ambassador Andrew Young's reprinted Johannesburg address urges South African businessmen to expand market-economy opportunity to the Black majority as a nonviolent alternative to revolutionary upheaval, citing the economic integration of Black Americans as transforming the U.S. South.

A symposium of clipped international press comment dismisses the new Brezhnev Constitution as cosmetic, noting it grants rights only "as privileges" and that not a single dissenting voice appeared in Pravda's stage-managed public debate.

Masani's lamp-post column praises West Bengal Janata leader P. C. Sen for resigning rather than ally with the CPI(M), and warns that the International P.E.N.'s outreach to a Soviet-aligned centre risks legitimising the persecution of writers like Solzhenitsyn.
A brief news item reports Jayaprakash Narayan chairing the Indian Committee for Cultural Freedom, which resolved to campaign for autonomous broadcasting and repeal of the 42nd Amendment.

World News items cover Lee Kuan Yew's Commonwealth summit warning of a Marxist takeover in post-guerrilla Rhodesia, a London hearing in defence of imprisoned Soviet physicist Yuri Orlov, and newly surfaced "Kaplan papers" describing Stalin's 1951 plan to prepare for a third world war.

Reader letters from D. D. Karve and D. Ghosh debate electoral reform, comparing German proportional representation and the French run-off system, and warn that the Janata Party is already repeating Congress-style factional infighting.

M. R. Masani's lead editorial, "Isn't It Time For JP To Speak Up?", catalogues the Janata government's economic drift, chronic coalition infighting, and broken promises, invokes Lincoln's line on the cowardice of silence, and appeals directly to Jayaprakash Narayan to break his silence.

S. A. A. Pinto opens a two-part essay on torture and preventive detention, arguing custodial abuse is an ancient, universal practice unreliable as an investigative tool, extending well beyond political and Naxalite victims, and noting no magistrate or minister has ever conducted a surprise inspection of police custody.

S. P. Aiyar reviews three rushed Emergency retrospectives, finding Kuldip Nayar's The Judgement vivid but poorly sourced, praising V. K. Narasimhan's Democracy Redeemed as the most substantively reflective, and faulting all for neglecting the RSS's and Citizens for Democracy's roles.
Jal Irani contributes a comic personal essay on the shared Persian origins and diverging fortunes of the Parsi and Irani communities in India.

An unsigned report describes the newly formed "Committee of a Hundred" watchdog group's first intervention, a memorandum on the admissions crisis caused by merging two parallel streams in Maharashtra's medical colleges.
D. M. Kalapesi and S. V. Raju review, respectively, Vadilal Lallubhai Mehta's book on Gandhian trusteeship as an economic model, and a biography of Coimbatore textile magnate G. Kuppuswamy Naidu.

A World News digest reports roughly 30,000 Ethiopians killed or imprisoned under the Dergue junta and Hebrew University's award of an honorary degree to Milton Friedman amid speculation about his advising Israel's new Likud government.

Union Minister Bhanu Pratap Singh's "Democracy and Destitution" argues that restored civil liberties do not solve India's underlying rural poverty, citing falling per-capita food consumption and stagnant agricultural growth, and calls on the Janata Party to make eliminating destitution within ten years its central economic goal.

Writing pseudonymously as "Cato", "Dancing With the Soviet Bear" accuses the Soviet Union and CPI of having fully backed the Emergency and denounced Janata leaders as "fascists", only to pivot to courting the new government, noting the CPI's collapsed 1977 Lok Sabha tally.

K. Vedamurthy's "Rajaji Centenary" reveals Rajagopalachari's true birth date as December 10, 1878 (coinciding with Human Rights Day), recalls his early anti-caste advocacy and 1962 meeting with President Kennedy on nuclear testing, and calls for marking his centenary as an International Year of Human Rights.

S. A. A. Pinto's second instalment on torture and preventive detention argues legal remedies exist on paper under IPC sections 330-331 but are barely enforced, recounting his own eyewitness account of a police beating near Grant Road Station in April 1977.

A report on a Leslie Sawhney Programme seminar, with participants including Achyut Patwardhan, B. R. Shenoy, Piloo Mody and Khushwant Singh, concludes that democracy is only a means to a free society and that continuous grass-roots vigilance, not periodic elections alone, is needed to safeguard it.

A World View digest covers the Indian government's demand that Coca-Cola dilute its equity or leave the country, and Sikkimese politician Nar Bahadur Khatiwada's secret petition to Morarji Desai denouncing India's 1975 annexation of Sikkim as "imperialist and expansionist".

Girish Munshi reviews S. R. Maheshwari's book on President's Rule, noting its 36 documented impositions of Article 356 and questioning why the practice rose sharply between 1971-76 despite Congress's electoral dominance.

M. Savidor, a Member of the Knesset, writes rejecting characterisations of Israel's negotiating stance as intransigent, stating 95% of Israelis would rather be called intransigent than accept Arab preconditions for negotiation.

M. R. Masani's lead editorial demands the Janata Government repeal the 42nd Amendment "lock, stock and barrel" rather than compromise with the Congress opposition, objecting to the anti-democratic manner of its Emergency-era passage and its reduction of the President to a "puppet".

Jayaprakash Narayan's tribute message on Masani's memoir "Bliss Was It In That Dawn" recalls their decades-long friendship since their Nasik Road Central Prison days and praises the book as an objective account of their generation's struggle.

A condensed profile traces Paul Johnson's public break from the Labour Party after his "Farewell to the Labour Party" piece, situating him among prominent Labour defectors and describing his conviction that political freedom is impossible without economic freedom.

Masani's Ahmedabad address, "Not By Politics Alone", argues socialism and secularism both wrongly claim for the State what belongs to God or conscience, and calls for dismantling the "permit-license-quota-raj" in favour of Rajaji's "Farm, Family and Freedom".

A Bombay seminar organised by the Indian Committee for Cultural Freedom criticises the Janata government's plan to replace the Samachar news agency with three new agencies, arguing this merely swaps one government monopoly for three and would run heavy financial deficits.

The Committee of a Hundred's Lawyers Group submits a memorandum demanding total repeal of the 42nd Amendment, backed by a Supreme Court Bar Association statement of "alarm and dismay" at its continued use to deprive citizens of rights.

M. R. Pai reviews Prophets of Freedom and Enterprise, an essay collection on Adam Smith, Keynes, Friedman, Mises and Hayek, arguing it corrects Marxist misrepresentations and flags Mises and Popper as neglected voices in Indian discourse.
David Lamb's reprinted Los Angeles Times feature describes "wawa" ("West Africa Wins Again"), expatriate shorthand for the region's chronic bureaucratic dysfunction and unreliable infrastructure.
The Rajaji Foundation is announced as a registered trust to spread Rajagopalachari's message of Dharma and liberal-society norms, with M. R. Masani and S. V. Raju among its trustees.

M. R. Masani's lead essay "We've Been Through This Before" argues the Emergency was the culmination of a quarter-century of statist planning and weak citizenship rather than a sudden aberration, invoking Croce's warning that democracy needs autonomous social forces and quoting Nirad Chaudhuri's view of Indira Gandhi's rule as an inherited extension of Nehru's authority.
Masani questions whether Jayaprakash Narayan can hold Janata politicians to their pledge of "austerity and honesty", drawing a parallel to Gandhiji being sidelined by Nehru and Patel after 1947.

A "Wisdom from New Delhi" feature reprints Home Minister Charan Singh blaming India's economic troubles on the Second Five-Year Plan's neglect of agriculture in favour of heavy industry, and Industries Minister George Fernandes arguing that true employment requires diffusing purchasing power to rural areas.

S. V. Raju reports on the Indian Liberal Group's absorption into the new Janata Party, crediting the 1977 election with vindicating the liberal view that "bread and freedom are indivisible" and noting Finance Minister H. M. Patel is a former Swatantra Party president.

The lamp-post column praises Sri Lanka's UNP government for liberalising foreign exchange and dismantling import monopolies as a model New Delhi has not matched, and criticises India's blocking of a Zubin Mehta/Israeli Philharmonic concert under Arab-lobby pressure.

A World News digest reports the EEC's criticism of minimal Soviet-bloc development aid, returning Rhodesian guerrilla leader James Chikerema's surprising support for Ian Smith's settlement demands, and an investigation into Yugoslav President Tito's wife Jovanka.

S. P. Aiyar reviews The Press She Could Not Whip, an anthology of foreign press coverage of the Emergency, crediting foreign correspondents like David Selbourne with a courage the domestic press lacked, and recounting Oriana Fallaci's interview in which Mrs. Gandhi called herself "surrounded by a bunch of idiots".

M. R. Masani's editorial "Terrorism on the Home Front" contrasts India's rhetorical support for fighting international terrorism after the Mogadishu hijack with its tolerance of domestic industrial violence, citing gheraos and worker attacks on managers at Brakes India, Mukund Iron & Steel, and Amar Dye Chem, and calling it "Mafia Rule".

M. Murlidhar's "Changing Values of Soviet Youth" surveys Soviet press accounts of youth increasingly prizing material well-being and consumer goods over Marxist ideals, noting declining rural Komsomol membership and resentment of compulsory Marxism coursework.

The seven-point "Delhi Declaration on Press Freedom", drafted by Indian journalists with the International Press Institute and the Friedrich-Naumann-Stiftung, asserts the press's adversarial watchdog role and editorial independence, and calls for competitive news agencies and autonomous broadcasting.

A compilation of press reactions contrasts Jayaprakash Narayan's and Sheikh Abdullah's praise for Anwar Sadat's Jerusalem visit against the Indian Foreign Ministry's evasive, Arab-lobby-conscious hedging.

Ernest van den Haag's "Justice and the Market" argues market outcomes track incentives rather than moral desert, engages Hayek's claim that market distribution is neither just nor unjust, and critiques Marx's "to each according to his needs" ideal using Christopher Jencks's research on inborn ability differences.

An anonymous letter from a white Rhodesian objects to the Anglo-American favouring of the Patriotic Front over Bishop Muzorewa, warning of collapse and violence, and calling instead for a settlement between Ian Smith and Muzorewa.

Geeta Doctor reviews the Theatre Group's Bombay production of Man from La Mancha, and an unsigned TV review recounts Rafiq Zakaria's adversarial but ultimately unsuccessful interrogation of Minoo Masani on his autobiography.

Nitin Raut reviews the Robin Blackburn-edited Explosion in a Subcontinent, faulting its New Left contributors, including Tariq Ali, for a consistent ideological bias in analysing the 1971 Bangladesh crisis.

M. R. Masani's lead editorial defends the Delhi Declaration's affirmation of the press's "adversary role" against Information Minister L. K. Advani's objections, contrasting Advani's stance with Prime Minister Morarji Desai's endorsement of near-absolute press freedom.

The lamp-post column criticises the 44th Amendment Bill for repealing only a fraction of the 42nd Amendment's provisions and condemns the dismissal of the Karnataka government under Article 356 as continuing federal overreach.

K. S. Venkateswaran's "Tackling the Law's Delays" blames High Court backlogs on unfilled judicial vacancies and an inadequate sanctioned strength of judges, criticising a proposed 15/10-minute hearing time cap as ridiculous.

James Burnham's "Why Rhodesia?" argues that only "white racism" is treated as the unforgivable sin driving the global campaign against Ian Smith's government, surveying racism in Japan, southern India, and the Soviet Union to make the point.

Leo Labedz describes a smuggled cache of internal Polish censorship directives from 1974-76, revealing a totalitarian system that dictates content positively as well as banning it, with self-censorship as its most efficient mechanism.

Bernard Levin satirises Mongolia's one-candidate-per-seat parliamentary elections, and David K. Shipler relays testimony from Soviet workers, including coal miner Vladimir Kelbanov, dismissed and psychiatrically confined for protesting unsafe conditions.

An unsigned tribute marks the death of Michael Josselson, longtime chief executive of the Congress for Cultural Freedom, recalling his friendships with Jayaprakash Narayan, Raymond Aron, and Arthur Koestler.

Harry Oppenheimer's address argues U.S. condemnation of apartheid is justified but a simple one-man-one-vote solution is not the answer, while Arnold Beichman's tabulated abstract from Revel's The Totalitarian Temptation contrasts what democracies may not do with what Communist states are permitted.
Letters from K. S. Venkateswaran and Jal Irani criticise a proposed code of judicial ethics as unconstitutional and Morarji Desai's rigid stance on Prohibition, respectively.

H. M. Patel's tribute at the Rajaji Foundation dinner eulogises C. Rajagopalachari as the "Bhishma of Indian Politics", crediting his weekly Swarajya columns for popularising the case against economic controls and the "permit-licence-quota Raj".

Minoo Masani's open letter "Set the People Free", addressed to Finance Minister H. M. Patel ahead of the 1978-79 Budget, urges sharp cuts in direct and indirect taxation and unproductive civil expenditure, citing Wanchoo Committee findings on tax evasion and holding up Ludwig Erhard's postwar German decontrol as the model.

Raymond Fletcher's reprinted Times essay warns that the "totalitarian temptation" is a standing risk in any democracy regardless of party, citing both Nixon and Indira Gandhi as leaders who succumbed to it.

Jo Grimond's reprinted address to the Association of Independent Business argues unchecked bureaucratic growth and monopoly protection are killing small business in Britain, and that competition rather than central direction keeps business efficient.

Victor Perry's piece traces Sadat's 1977 peace initiative partly to Egyptian anxiety over Soviet-backed radical expansion in Africa, including Egyptian moves against Libya and support for Zaire's Mobutu against the Shaba invasion.

A World News digest reports Vladimir Bukovsky's criticism of the West for softening on human rights, an exposé of Spanish Communist leader Santiago Carrillo's Stalinist past, and Soviet miner Vladimir Klebanov's psychiatric committal for organising a workers' protest group.

V. B. Karnik reviews Peace With Horror by John Barron and Anthony Paul on the Khmer Rouge's mass evacuations and killings after 1975, estimated at roughly a million Cambodian deaths, while Geeta Doctor reviews Constantine Fitzgibbon's Secret Intelligence in the 20th Century.

Reader letters criticise Chief Justice M. H. Beg's public remarks as breaching judicial restraint and condemn ongoing industrial terrorism, while a satirical letter by Sheila Sumant mocks opportunist ticket-seeking politicians.

M. R. Masani's valedictory editorial marks his departure from the Freedom First editorship to chair India's new Minorities Commission, recalling the journal's decision to suspend publication during the Emergency rather than submit to pre-censorship, vindicated by a Bombay High Court ruling.

Louella Lobo Prabhu's analysis of the February 1978 Karnataka Assembly election finds the Indira Congress won 149 of 224 seats on 43% of the vote against Janata's 59 seats, attributing the result to vote-splitting and Chief Minister Devaraj Urs's patronage politics via the Havanur Backward Classes report.

Y. Sivaji's analysis of the Andhra Pradesh election finds Janata's vote share collapsed due to organisational disarray, poor candidate selection, and the co-option of discredited Congress defectors, of whom only 12 of 50 recontesting MLAs were re-elected.

S. A. A. Pinto's analysis of the inconclusive Maharashtra election finds Janata the largest single party but far short of a majority, warning that seeking office via Congress(I) support could destroy its leadership's credibility.

Bernard Levin opens a syndicated series on human-rights abuses under unified communist Vietnam, centred on testimony from Nguyen Cong Hoan, a National Assembly member disillusioned after visiting re-education camps holding detainees without trial since June 1975.
K. V. Padmanabhan reviews R. K. Karanjia's admiring biography The Mind of a Monarch on the Shah of Iran, tracing his consolidation of power and "White Revolution" reform programme.

Achyut Patwardhan reviews Madhu Dandavate's Marx & Gandhi, written during Dandavate's Emergency imprisonment, praising its analysis of Gandhi's warning that uncoordinated industrialisation and nationalisation both lead to a "servile society" under a leviathan state.

Sheila Sumant's letter accuses Foreign Minister Atal Bihari Vajpayee of abandoning his own long-held positions on Kashmir, Pakistan, and the Indo-Soviet Treaty simply because he now serves in government.

S. P. Aiyar's "Re-Examining the Federal System" responds to Jyoti Basu's Memorandum on Centre-State Relations, tracing decades of federal centralisation via the Planning Commission and judging its radical decentralist proposals, including abolishing the All-India Services and giving states 75% of central revenue, sound in diagnosis but overstated in remedy.

The "Frankly Speaking" column welcomes Home Minister Charan Singh's announcement that MISA will be repealed outright rather than replaced, and catalogues a wave of March 1978 student violence in Kanpur, Bangalore, and Delhi, contrasting weak police response with West Bengal Chief Minister Jyoti Basu's firmer stance.

A tribute to the late economist B. R. Shenoy by M. R. Pai recalls him as "an economist's economist" ostracized by the profession for his free-market views, believing the poor would never see improvement "unless statism was given up".

V. B. Karnik argues for abolishing the death penalty, citing Amnesty International's December 1977 Stockholm declaration and Arthur Koestler's account of the mental torture of prisoners awaiting execution.

S. A. A. Pinto's "Opiate for the Masses" criticises India's new Drug Policy for forcing foreign pharmaceutical formulators to dilute equity to 40%, arguing the punitive approach will discourage rather than attract the foreign investment needed for bulk-drug manufacturing.

Manohar Malgonkar reviews S. P. Aiyar and S. V. Raju's own book When the Wind Blows, India's Ballot-Box Revolution, praising its account of the Emergency-era resistance movement and its record of the April 1976 Supreme Court ruling abrogating Habeas Corpus rights.

B. P. Adarkar's review of Michael Harrington's The Twilight of Capitalism rebuts its neo-Marxist analysis, arguing that joint-stock ownership, social insurance, and progressive taxation have made 19th-century Marxist capitalism obsolete.

Bernard Levin's satirical column mocks British left-wing figures marching against Soviet involvement in the Ethiopian-Somali war for their selective outrage, closing with an ironic anecdote about "kindly KGB men" handing out soup at a Kremlin vigil.

Mehra Masani's "The Broadcasting Monolith" welcomes the Verghese Working Group's proposal for an independent National Broadcast Trust but warns that concentrating all of AIR's transmitters and future TV stations into one monopoly body would remain unaccountable, calling instead for competition between multiple broadcasting units.

K. S. Venkateswaran defends the constitutional right to property against calls for its deletion, tracing its erosion through Articles 31A, 31B, and 31C, and citing Nani Palkhivala's warning against a "perpetual and deliberate distortion" of the Fundamental Rights chapter.
Geeta Doctor recounts a first-person, wry account of being swept up in a Dawoodi Bohra community protest march in Bombay against the Nathwani Commission.

Bernard Levin's syndicated column on the Taj Mahal describes its perfect symmetry, its illusion of floating weightlessness, and an optical device in its Koranic inscriptions, comparing the emotional effect to Beethoven's Ninth Symphony.

M. R. Masani's "Back to 1967?" argues India's post-Emergency drift mirrors the disillusionment following the 1967 elections, warning the pendulum could swing back toward authoritarianism as it did in 1975, and lamenting that Jayaprakash Narayan's ill health prevents him from leading people "from Rajniti to Lokniti".

S. P. Aiyar reviews Jiri Pelikan's Socialist Opposition in Eastern Europe on Czechoslovak dissent after the 1968 Soviet invasion, drawing explicit parallels to India's own Emergency-era repression and underground press.
K. V. Padmanabhan reviews Paul Erdman's financial thriller The Crash of '79, praising its factual grounding in oil geopolitics and its unusual use of real public figures as characters.

S. V. Raju's "Strangled by Red Tape" and Minoo Masani's own press statement document Masani's May 29, 1978 resignation as Chairman of the Minorities Commission after only three months, citing broken assurances of consultation, statutory independence, staff and premises, and the government's introduction of the Aligarh Muslim University Bill without consulting the Commission.

V. B. Karnik critiques the Bhoothalingam Study Group's wage, income and price policy report, noting its recommended national minimum wage of Rs. 100 rising to Rs. 150 over seven years and concluding it fails to address the core problem of redistributing national income from a wealthy minority to the impoverished majority.

Bernard Levin's syndicated column indicts Western apologists for the Khmer Rouge genocide in Cambodia, naming SOAS lecturer Malcolm Caldwell and New Statesman writer James Fenton for downplaying the killings, and comparing their denial to Holocaust deniers.

Maj. Gen. E. D'Souza writes on the emerging field of sports medicine in India, timed to the opening of a Bombay sports-medicine centre, citing Indian athletes whose careers suffered from the lack of such expertise.
A World News item reports Alexander Solzhenitsyn's June 1978 Harvard commencement address "A World Split Apart", in which he criticised both Western and Soviet societies for spiritual exhaustion.

Muriel Wasi reviews V. V. John's The Great Classroom Hoax, praising his refusal to be taken in by shams in Indian higher education while faulting his impractical proposals on the three-language formula.
Nawaz Mody reviews Rajeev Dhavan's The Amendment — Conspiracy or Revolution, noting his neutral stance on the 42nd Amendment's constitutional validity despite condemning its "moral ineptitude".
A reader's letter from Homeyar Jal Tavaria argues democracies worldwide face a crisis of leadership and calls for "managerial/technocrat" politicians rather than career lawyer-politicians.

S. V. Raju's "Swept Under the Carpet" reads the Morarji Desai-Charan Singh standoff within the Janata Party as evidence of an unresolved ideological split between Nehruvian planning and Gandhian minimum-government instincts, since the coalition was formed only to oust Indira Gandhi rather than around shared economic policy.

Geeta Doctor's "A Kick from the Horse" situates the April 1978 Marxist coup in Afghanistan within two centuries of great-power rivalry, from Peter the Great's Persian ambitions through the 19th-century Great Game to current anxieties in China, Pakistan and Iran.

Prafulla Mohanti's reprinted Times of London piece "A Great Hope Dashed" recounts an Orissa village's disillusionment a year after voting out Congress in 1977, finding prices, unemployment and landlord retaliation against Harijan tenant farmers unaddressed under Janata rule.

The full correspondence between M. R. Masani, as Chairman of the Minorities Commission, and the Prime Minister documents the Commission's paralysis from lack of staff and premises and its resignation, prompted by the Education Ministry drafting Aligarh Muslim University legislation without its input.

Israel Shenker's reprinted piece describes a Kennan Institute gathering analysing Soviet political jokes, with scholar Stephen Cohen arguing they reveal genuine popular attitudes more honestly than official channels.

A World News digest covers Thai birth-control campaigner Mechai Viravaidya's fight to keep contraceptive pills reaching 240,000 women, and Tom Gervasi's study Arsenal of Democracy documenting the scale of US arms exports to Cold War client states.

K. S. Venkateswaran reviews Chandra Shekhar's Dynamics of Social Change, criticising its Marxist-inflected attack on private enterprise and quoting economist Fredie Mehta's view that low growth, not private enterprise, is the real threat to India's poor.
K. V. Padmanabhan reviews Charles Allen's oral-history anthology Plain Tales from the Raj, describing the insulated, hierarchical social world of British colonial administrators in India.

V. B. Karnik's "War Against Dissidents" surveys renewed Soviet repression in 1978, detailing the fabricated espionage trial of Anatoli Shcharansky, the show trial of Helsinki-monitoring founder Yuri Orlov, and psychiatric abuse campaigns, predicting the dissident movement will survive despite state repression.

Bernard Levin's three-part extract on the Shah Commission's Emergency findings dismantles Indira Gandhi's official justifications for the 1975 proclamation, documenting that arrests and press-suppression plans predated the declaration, that electricity was cut to newspaper offices to enforce censorship, and that detainees like Bhim Sen Sachar were jailed merely for writing an open letter.

The "Frankly Speaking" column condemns the Arunachal Pradesh Freedom of Indigenous Faith Bill as illiberal anti-Christian legislation and exposes Emergency-era Indian-edition censorship of passages in Irving Wallace's novel The R Document referencing the Emergency itself.

K. S. Venkateswaran offers a light anthology of courtroom wit from British judicial history, while S. V. Raju's "India's New Princes" itemises Indian MPs' pay and perquisites, totalling roughly Rs. 33,228 a year per member.
Col. H. R. Pasricha argues against prohibition as inherently corrupting to enforce and a "dictatorship" of one man's moral preference imposed on the nation's private habits.
Book reviews cover Yehoshafat Harkabi's Arab Strategies and Israel's Response, H. V. Kamath's The Last Days of Jawaharlal Nehru, and Nayantara Sahgal's novel A Situation in New Delhi.
M. R. Pai gives telephone subscribers practical advice for disputing inflated bills, urging citizens to assert their right to be served by, rather than serve, the Telephone Department.

Meenakshi Rao reviews the Hindi film Des Pardes, criticising Hindi cinema's structural inability to reconcile serious social themes about illegal immigrants with its commercial conventions of music and melodrama.

S. V. Raju's "The Fruits of Compromise" attacks the Janata government for pursuing only a watered-down 45th Amendment rather than fully repealing the 42nd Amendment as promised, a measure the Rajya Sabha then rejected outright.

Zahiruddin Ahmad, a Bengali Muslim who migrated to Pakistan in 1951 and later resigned from its Civil Service, reflects on Partition's thirtieth anniversary, arguing it was a mistake driven by British policy and Gandhi's "blunders" that ultimately hurt subcontinental Muslims more than Hindus by fragmenting their community.

P. G. Mavalankar's Lok Sabha-based piece presses Parliament to act on the Shah Commission's findings, condemning the burning of Commission report copies in several states, including his own Gujarat, as smacking of fascism.

A report on a Srinagar seminar on Third World development, attended by J. R. D. Tata, B. K. Nehru, and M. R. Masani among others, addresses agricultural productivity, technology transfer, and the role of multinational corporations.

Sonal Shah reviews Charan Singh's India's Economic Policy: A Gandhian Blueprint, summarising his argument that Nehru's capital-intensive industrial strategy misallocated resources away from agriculture and produced persistent poverty.

World News carries obituaries of Ignazio Silone, the Italian Communist-turned-anti-Stalinist novelist, and Kenya's Jomo Kenyatta, alongside a note on the Dalai Lama's tentative consultations about reconciliation with Chinese-ruled Tibet.

Geeta Doctor reviews the Kannada film Ghatashradda, calling it unremittingly bleak, and separately reports on the Bhagwan Shree Rajneesh ashram in Poona, framing its provocations as exposing conventional society's "cant and hypocrisy".

Maj. Gen. E. D'Souza argues India lacks a war memorial worthy of its servicemen's sacrifices across the conflicts fought since 1947, criticising the existing small samadhi at India Gate as architecturally insignificant.

S. P. Kotwal, a retired Chief Justice of the Bombay High Court, critiques the Lokpal Bill, 1977 for dropping secretaries and civil servants from the ombudsman's jurisdiction while unprecedentedly including over 5,000 legislators, and for imposing a Rs. 1,000 pre-complaint deposit that bars poor complainants.

The "Of Cabbages and Kings" column analyses Indira Gandhi's Chikmagalur by-election bid against Janata's Veerendra Patil, and defends Foreign Minister Vajpayee's China outreach and the Janata government's cautious response to the Camp David accord.

D. B. Karnik reports on a Yuvak Kranti Dal training camp in Devlali, describing the group's combination of Marxist class-struggle rhetoric with non-violent resistance modelled on Martin Luther King, amid participants' anger over caste atrocities in Marathwada.

James Cameron's reprinted Times column reflects on Londoners' ambivalence toward tourists, while a short item notes 401 official Indian government delegations travelled abroad between August 1977 and January 1978 at a cost of over Rs. 69 lakh.
R. C. Cooper examines Singapore's 1978 budget philosophy of heavily taxing private car ownership to fund mass transit, framing it as a deliberate choice to build "a nation for cars or for ourselves".

V. Krishna Moorthy reviews Nandini Joshi's The Challenge of Poverty, which estimates 800 million people live in absolute poverty in developing countries and calls for a new international economic order.
World News marks the tenth anniversary of the Soviet invasion of Czechoslovakia and warns that Soviet-backed instability in Lebanon and Iran could still threaten the Camp David accord's gains.

A reprinted UPI report describes the Khmer Rouge's decreed "mating periods" in Cambodia, outside which romantic relationships were criminalised, sometimes punished by death, with estimates of up to 1.2 million deaths since 1975.

Shankar Ranganathan's essay, adapted from an All India Radio talk, warns India's forests could disappear within thirty years at current deforestation rates and calls for a reforestation employment programme modelled on the U.S. Civilian Conservation Corps.

S. V. Raju's "A Blessing in Disguise?" argues Indira Gandhi's Chikmagalur by-election win is being overplayed as a national referendum, quoting Jayaprakash Narayan's warning that it was an "isolated event", and suggests the defeat could force Janata's squabbling factions to unite.

A reprint of C. Rajagopalachari's 1963 Swarajya essay "A Dedicated Service, The Only Hope", published for his forthcoming birth centenary, attributes India's corruption to excessive government control over production and appointments, warning that unchecked corruption risks revolution, anarchy, or dictatorship.

The "Of Cabbages & Kings" column covers Indira Gandhi's first post-Emergency trip to the West for her father's 89th birthday celebrations, and the hostile British press reception including a barbed Bernard Levin-Peregrine Worsthorne exchange in the Times.

Margaret P. Joseph surveys the growth of Indian writing in English as an emerging field of literary study, assessing R. K. Narayan, Manohar Malgonkar, Raja Rao, and Kamala Markandaya, and debating whether authentic "Indian-ness" requires writing in a regional language.

A World News digest covers the Soviet Union's status as the world's fifth-largest Muslim power, Poland's Communist leadership managing coverage of Karol Wojtyla's election as Pope John Paul II, and China's post-Mao turn to Japan's economic model.

Manohar Malgonkar reviews the photographic volume Ganga, Sacred River of India, praising Raghubir Singh's photography over Eric Newby's text, while Nitin Raut dismisses Indian Soviet Relations 1947-77 as a biased, propagandistic compilation.

Manjula Padmanabhan reviews Saturday Night Fever and Looking for Mr. Goodbar, finding both films quietly puncture the myth of unrestrained American freedom despite their structurally similar protagonists.
A reader's letter from Ranjan Guha argues India's choice of the Jaguar fighter over the Swedish Viggen was militarily unsound and driven by politics rather than merit.

The unsigned editorial "For This We Stand" reaffirms Freedom First's identity as a journal of "Liberal ideas" rather than an ideology, framed by the Democratic Research Service's founding in 1950 with Sardar Patel's blessing, and explains this Human Rights Special Number as a response to post-Emergency nostalgia for "discipline" and "order".

S. P. Aiyar's "The Urge for Freedom" rejects the view that civil-political rights are a Western luxury developing countries can defer, praises B. R. Ambedkar for centering individual freedom in the Constitution, and critically engages Peter Berger's proposal for a religion-grounded universal human-rights consensus.
