S.V. Raju's editorial "'Stray Incidents' Did You Say, Mr. Home Minister?" rebuts Home Minister S.B. Chavan's dismissal of human-rights abuses, citing playwright Vijay Tendulkar's public-interest petition and specific police-brutality cases to argue Amnesty International's criticism has substance.

Jamshed N. Guzder's biographical tribute traces Dadabhai Naoroji's life from founding girls' schools in 1849 Bombay through his 1892 election as the first Indian MP in the British House of Commons to his mentorship of a young Gandhi in South Africa.

Adi Doctor's "Dadabhai — The Secular Nationalist" contrasts Naoroji's secular, rights-based nationalism against the religio-spiritual nationalism of Tilak and Aurobindo, and explains his "drain of wealth" theory of British extraction from India.

V.S. Srinivasa Sastri's reprinted "Dadabhai in the House of Commons" recounts Naoroji's narrow three-vote 1892 election victory and his parliamentary work on simultaneous ICS examinations and the Welby Commission on Indo-British finances.

Minoo Masani's column praises Captain Lakshmi of the INA for refusing a Quit India commemorative award, supports a separate Jharkhand state for Adivasis, and condemns Iran's persecution of the Baha'i community.

The cover feature on the environment opens with Chief Seattle's 1854 letter and reports on the World Bank's independent "Morse Committee" review finding the Sardar Sarovar Narmada project's resettlement programme inadequate, accompanied by Medha Patkar's "Narmada Action Alert."

The lead feature reports on a January 9, 1993 emergency seminar on secularism held amid curfew and Bombay's post-Babri Masjid riots, with 51 participants questioning whether pre-modern India was ever genuinely tolerant.

M.S. Gore directly disputes that sarva-dharma-samabhava (equal regard for all religions) is consistent with a secular ethic, arguing genuine secularism requires treating religion as irrelevant to individual opportunity.
Minoo Masani argues India should be "non-denominational, not secular," proposing only Republic Day and Independence Day as universal holidays.
Ruchira Gupta's eyewitness account describes the December 6, 1992 demolition of the Babri Masjid, kar sevaks assaulting journalists, and her own near-lynching when identified as Muslim.
The seminar's Uniform Civil Code discussion reproduces a 1986 Indian Secular Society draft proposal, with Justice V.D. Tulzapurkar, recommending abolition of polygamy and unilateral divorce.

Reprinted historical material includes a 1679 letter from Shivaji to Aurangzeb pleading for religious tolerance and Babar's 1529 "secret will" to Humayun urging the same, alongside B.T. Dastur's polemic on India's "relapse into savagery."
A contribution from a Muslim Satyashodak Mandal activist describes the "dilemma of progressive Muslims," accused of teaching Islam when raising reform and of anti-Islamic bias when criticising it.

R. Srinivasan's "The Criminalisation of Politics in India" argues the March 1993 Bombay bomb blasts confirmed a long-recognised trend, tracing it from election-cost financing through the Emergency-era Youth Congress to today's criminal-politician nexus.

S.V. Raju's "Criminal Politicians or Political Criminals?" documents corporators and MLAs across Bombay, Aurangabad and Nagpur facing criminal charges, including alleged links between Vasai-Virar politician Hitendra Thakur's family and Dawood Ibrahim, and favours the 1957 Second Five Year Plan's licence-permit-quota regime as the root cause.

V.C. Phadke's "Keeping the Peace the Bhiwandi Way" explains why Bhiwandi, despite past riots, stayed peaceful during the December 1992-January 1993 violence, crediting mohalla committees and joint Hindu-Muslim patrols as a replicable "Bhiwandi Model."

Mervyn Hiskett's "Democracy or Theocracy" argues a recurring Islamic predisposition against secular pluralism has produced conflict from Partition-era India to 1980s Nigeria and Sudan, citing the Indian Muslim League's rejection of Gandhian secular nationalism.

A.G. Philip's piece under "The Masani Viewpoint" argues Hindutva-style politics is a mobile prejudice that merely finds new targets, comparing the Shiv Sena's shift from south Indians to Muslims with Pakistan's turn against Bengalis after Partition.
The issue also tributes the Sarajevo newspaper Oslobodenje, nominated by the Indian Liberal Group for the Liberal International 1993 Prize for Freedom.

B. N. Mehrish reports on the UN World Conference on Human Rights in Vienna (June 1993), noting the UN Centre for Human Rights received over 125,000 complaints that year, nearly triple 1992's total, and detailing the Vienna Declaration's action programme.

S. V. Raju's obituary for Irene d'Avoine recounts her father Dr. Charles d'Avoine's career as a Bombay rationalist tried and acquitted in 1933 under IPC Section 295, with both father and daughter buried without religious rites.

V. C. Phadke reports on an essay exercise given to 300 Bhiwandi college students on the 1992-93 communal riots, finding many blamed religious fanaticism and opportunistic politicians while also invoking Gandhian universalism.

Adi Doctor reviews Osborne and Gaebler's "Reinventing Government," explaining "entrepreneurial government" that steers rather than rows, citing New Zealand's airline deregulation and Chicago's parent-controlled school councils.

The Dalai Lama's statement on the 34th anniversary of the Tibetan uprising warns that China's new "special economic zone" status for the Tibet Autonomous Region risks accelerating demographic and cultural assimilation.

Minoo Masani's column pays personal tribute to his late sister Mehra Masani, a senior All India Radio official denied the Director-General post, and criticises a Supreme Court decision permitting fee-based reservation of college seats after a student suicide over an unaffordable donation.

A satirical piece by S. S. Bankeshwar "interviews" a suitcase personifying cash-bribe politics after the Harshad Mehta scandal, referencing the Rs. 67 lakh suitcase allegedly delivered to PM Narasimha Rao.

G. Narayanaswamy's Rajaji Birthday Lecture recounts C. Rajagopalachari's Vedantic philosophy of detached duty and his record as Madras Chief Minister opening the Meenakshi Temple to Harijans and pioneering prohibition.

K. S. Ramamurthy's "Kashmir - The Way Out" argues India should honour its 1948 commitment to a free plebiscite, citing N. Gopalswamy Iyengar's UN Security Council pledge and Article 370 as evidence India never treated the accession as final.

A reprinted Swiss Press Review piece, "The Solution: An Independent Kashmir," argues neither the Indian nor Pakistani position serves Kashmiris and recalls Nehru's near-agreement with Ayub Khan on independence with joint neutrality guarantees before his death.

Ashok V. Chowgule's rebuttal defends the Indian Army's conduct in Kashmir against Bernard Levin's earlier accusations, citing the Verghese Committee's finding that reports of Army excesses were "grossly exaggerated or invented."

Minoo Masani's "An Open Letter to My Younger Friends" recalls founding the Swatantra Party with Rajaji in 1959 and appeals to a younger generation to organise a movement keeping economic liberalisation from stalling.

Resolutions of the Fifth Shetkari Sanghatana Convention at Aurangabad blame the Latur-Osmanabad earthquake's toll on anti-farmer housing policy and demand abolition of agricultural pricing controls and restoration of constitutional property rights.

An obituary tribute to H. M. Patel recounts his roles reorganising the armed forces after Partition, founding LIC, and serving as Swatantra Party president and Janata-government Finance and Home Minister.

Yogesh Kamdar's tribute to Justice N.P. Nathwani recounts his defence, then public renunciation, of the Preventive Detention Act, his Emergency-era free-speech victory, and his 1978 inquiry into repression of the Dawoodi Bohra community.

S.V. Raju's explainer defends India's April 1994 signing of the GATT Marrakesh accord against protectionist and sovereignty-based objections, tracing GATT's history since 1947 and its impending conversion into the World Trade Organisation.

Sharad Joshi's essay on "ulti-patti" (reverse settlement), opening with his own experience of being billed rather than paid for cucumbers, estimates Indian farmers' annual loss from unremunerative pricing at Rs. 12,000 crores and links this history of implicit farm taxation to the GATT agricultural negotiations.

Sharad Bailur's "The Great American Bubble" criticises U.S. passage of NAFTA and warns that America's "credit card economy" of proliferating consumer debt underlies a broader fragility in the world economy.

Minoo Masani's column criticises federal overreach in choosing Gujarat's Chief Minister, praises T. N. Seshan's independence as Chief Election Commissioner, and announces the planned launch of the Swatantra Bharat movement in Nagpur.

Tributes mark the deaths of industrialist S. L. Kirloskar, who favoured abolishing the Planning Commission and FERA, and scholar Tarkateerth Laxmanshastri Joshi, who campaigned against untouchability.

S. V. Raju's "The Return of Swatantra" reports on Sharad Joshi's founding of the new political party Swatantra Bharat, prompted by Minoo Masani's appeal, with a thirty-point transitional programme covering law and order, pruning the state, and privatisation.

V. K. Sinha's profile of Taslima Nasreen presents her as a Bangladeshi physician and writer facing a fundamentalist fatwa and bounty over her novel Lajja, arguing, via Philip Green, that free speech is constitutive of democracy while religious sentiment is merely incidental to it.
Gwynne Dyer's "Islamic Feminism" contrasts female heads of government in Pakistan, Bangladesh and Turkey with ongoing fundamentalist violence in Algeria, Egypt and Sudan.

An unsigned report on the Shetkari Mahila Aghadi's Lakshmi-Mukti movement describes the transfer of agricultural land titles to rural housewives in Maharashtra, with over a thousand villages qualifying by February 1992.

Dilip Thakore's "A Testimony of Shame" reviews the UNDP's 1994 Human Development Report ranking India 135th of 173 nations, blaming the "mother of all errors" — the centrally planned socialist model — for entrenching an "amoral" middle class in political power.

Rajesh M. Basrur's essay on Indian national identity, cut off mid-argument, argues the real sources of national unease over Assam, Punjab, Kashmir and Ayodhya lie within Indian society rather than external threats.
"Of Cabbages & Kings" recounts the parable of "Sami," a self-censoring journalist, and the case of Egyptian professor Dr. Nasr Abu-Zaid, blocked from promotion and accused of apostasy.

J. B. D'Souza's cover essay "Privileged Parasites" attacks the perks Indian legislators award themselves, free telephones, air and rail tickets, subsidised housing, while huge numbers of MPs and ministers default on rent and dues owed to the public exchequer, naming three former Prime Ministers as owing the IAF Rs. 8.5 crores collectively.

Madhu Limaye's "The Enemy Within" uses the 1991 Jain hawala diaries seizure, which recovered over Rs. 93 lakhs in unaccounted cash, to argue that corruption has overtaken plague and disease as India's most dangerous scourge, naming Rajiv Gandhi, L. K. Advani and Devi Lal among recipients listed in the diaries and excoriating the CBI for stalling the case for over three years.

Y. D. Altekar's "Making Democracy Work" continues an earlier proposal to separate executive from legislative power as a check on corruption, but concedes the reform can only be enacted by the MPs and MLAs who benefit from the status quo.

Marking Gandhi's 125th birth anniversary, Renuka Sinha's "One Step Towards Gandhi" offers an admiring reading of his autobiography that rebuts caricatures of him as a chauvinist or fanatic, while Nagindas Sanghavi's "Gandhi - His Trials and Triumphs" counters that the autobiography is an inadequate and even misguiding source for understanding his public achievements.

Adi H. Doctor's "Gandhi's Place in Today's Politics" argues for the continuing relevance of Gandhian ideas, including sustainable development over GNP-driven growth, the trusteeship doctrine, and empowering people rather than government, framing Gandhian non-violence as a practical strategy rather than absolute pacifism.

The issue's front matter carries the regular "With Many Voices" quotations column and the "Of Cabbages and Kings" editorial notes, and announces that from January 1995 the magazine would be published directly by the Indian Committee for Cultural Freedom.

The editorial marks the journal's 43rd year and its return to being published directly by the Indian Committee for Cultural Freedom after the Democratic Research Service was required to vacate its Bombay premises, reaffirming Freedom First's commitment to an open society and free-market economics.

S. V. Kogekar's title essay, "The Changing Face of Indian Politics", traces the decline of the disciplined post-Independence Congress System into personality-driven, casteist, populist politics under Indira and Rajiv Gandhi, and surveys regional parties, the BJP and the Janata Dal as each lacking a coherent ideology.

P. R. Dubhashi's "The Purpose of Politics" argues the pursuit of power is not inherently wrong if it serves national progress, and calls for a constitutional code of conduct to separate party from government, citing T. N. Seshan's enforcement of the electoral code as a partial precedent.

Mangesh Kulkarni's "Limits to Politics" surveys custom, theocracy, technocracy and the free market as historical devices for bounding politics, and concludes India lacks the prerequisites for the market alone to do so, proposing instead a welfare-oriented "social market economy" embedded in civil society.

A republished extract from Minoo Masani's 1969 Rajaji Birthday Lecture, "Too Much Politics, Too Little Citizenship", diagnoses the decay of Indian public life through politicians' reluctance to accept opposition, the party becoming an end in itself, the cult of personality, and an illiterate electorate.

Sharad Joshi's "Kicking the Statist-Drug Habit" likens the transition from a statist to a market economy to hard-drug de-addiction, insisting it must be total and uncompromising and warning that bureaucrats and crony-capitalists nostalgic for the license-permit-quota raj will sabotage half-hearted reform.

The issue is built around a twentieth-anniversary retrospective on the Emergency, packaged as "18 Months of Indira's India", covering press censorship, detentions under MISA, and the judiciary's mixed record.

Minoo Masani's "Why the Emergency was not Unexpected" recounts the Allahabad High Court's June 1975 judgment against Indira Gandhi, the midnight arrests of opposition leaders, and his own experience as editor of Freedom First fighting censorship through to the magazine's 1976 vindication in the Bombay High Court.

S. P. Aiyar and S. V. Raju's essay on the battle against the censors details how Masani submitted deliberately provocative material to test the limits of pre-censorship, leading to the Bombay High Court's February 1976 ruling that most objections were "fanciful and far-fetched", and a parallel Gujarati periodical Bhumiputra case in which the Gujarat High Court went further, striking down the censor's guidelines as exceeding statutory authority.

M. A. Rane's "When Lawyers Did Indian Democracy Proud" recounts lawyers led by Chagla, Tarkunde and Jethmalani protesting the Emergency, early habeas corpus successes in several High Courts, and the Supreme Court's Habeas Corpus Case in which a five-judge bench upheld the government with only Justice Khanna dissenting, who was subsequently superseded for Chief Justice.

N. G. Jog's "A Letter to Comrade K. A. Abbas", written during the Emergency, rebuts the claim that the crackdown targeted only smugglers and violent elements, describing the collapse of a free press under Information Minister Shukla and the government's hypocrisy in blacking out foreign criticism while broadcasting praise from Algeria, Libya and Moscow.

Subash C. Kashyap's essay, begun in the rendered pages, opens a discussion of "Socialism and Secularism in the Constitution of India", tracing the constitutional debates on secularism and communalism.

The issue's regular features include a report reprinting the Gummersbach Declaration from a Friedrich Naumann Foundation seminar on deregulation, founding an Asian Association for Environmental Protection, and a birthday tribute to the Dalai Lama on his 60th birthday.

The issue is dominated by a special tribute section, "Minoo Masani 90", marking the 90th birthday of the magazine's founder, opening with a report on the felicitation function at the Royal Bombay Yacht Club where Nani Palkhivala called Masani "one of the noblest Indians" and Sharad Joshi credited the Swatantra Party with shaping his own political thinking.

Ian Tickle's "Two Fighters for Freedom" pairs Masani with Swiss anti-communist publisher Peter Sager, tracing their shared Cold War-era anti-communism and arguing new threats such as ethnic cleansing demand the same vigilance.

An unsigned biographical piece, "From Marx to Gandhi", traces Masani's journey from co-founding the Congress Socialist Party in 1934, through his break with Moscow-directed Communism and his 1942 essay "Socialism Reconsidered", to co-founding the free-market Swatantra Party with C. Rajagopalachari in 1959.

Manuwant K. Choudhary's interview "The Man Who Saw Tomorrow" covers the Swatantra Party's years as the largest opposition party in Parliament between 1967-71 and Masani's resignation from the Minorities Commission chairmanship under the Janata government on principle.

Prakash Arolkar's "The Last Roman", translated from Marathi, gives a full biographical sketch of Masani from his birth in 1905 through Yerawada Jail, the writing of "Our India", and his explanation of the Swatantra Party's eventual decline as stemming from its merger with Charan Singh's "parochial and casteist" Lok Dal.

An unsigned obituary, "Yitzhak Rabin - The Peacemaker", marks the Israeli Prime Minister's assassination by a Jewish extremist, drawing an explicit parallel to Gandhi's killing by a Hindu nationalist and recounting the Oslo peace process and 1994 Nobel Peace Prize.

Paresh Vasa's "Robbing the People" attacks the new Employees' Pension Scheme, arguing it silently confiscates workers' provident fund contributions by pooling accounts and reverting unclaimed corpora to government rather than heirs.

Ranga Kota's "The Reforms and the Poor", opening in the rendered pages, defends the Narasimha Rao government's economic reforms against the charge that they harm the poor, rebutting arguments based on self-reliance and employment.

An unsigned obituary marks the death of jurist H. M. Seervai, tracing his 65-year Bombay Bar career, his 17-year tenure as Advocate General, his treatise on the Constitutional Law of India, and his decade as president of the PUCL, Bombay.

The cover package "The Communications Revolution" opens with S. V. Raju's "Changing the Way We Live", a nostalgic survey of India's shift from valve radios and manual telephone exchanges to computers, mobile phones and the internet.

T. H. Chowdary's "Communications Satellites" argues India's ban on domestic uplinking to foreign satellites is self-defeating and costs foreign exchange, calling for de-monopolising the spectrum and privatising INSAT's commercial functions.

Amita Malik's "Doordarshan: Responding to Competition" surveys the broadcaster's history from the SITE satellite experiment through Emergency-era subordination to government control, criticising its delayed coverage of Indira Gandhi's assassination and its imitative response to satellite rivals like Zee TV.

Namita Unnikrishnan's "Children and The New Information Environment" summarises a Delhi study finding that migrant labourer families prioritise renting a TV over adequate meals, that a "silent family" phenomenon replaces conversation, and that 75% of surveyed children aged 8-15 wanted products they saw advertised.

A special section marks Minoo Masani's 90th birthday with Zareer Masani's "A Son's Tribute", recalling his father's formative anti-communism and belief in federalism including a right to secession, and Khushwant Singh's "Walk Alone", invoking Tagore's "Ekla Chalo" to praise Masani's independence of mind.

J. B. D'Souza's "Delusions of Progress", cut off mid-argument in the rendered pages, critiques GNP and the Human Development Index as measures of well-being, citing a "genuine progress indicator" study showing a roughly 45% decline in genuine American progress since 1970 despite rising GDP.
The "Of Cabbages and Kings" column mounts a sharp critique of Mother Teresa's homes for the dying, drawing on The Missionary Position and a Lancet report describing primitive medical conditions.

The issue leads with Geeta Lal's report on the Convention on Liberal Values held in New Delhi in January 1996, attended by roughly 200 economists, scientists and journalists, at which speakers including Vice-President K. R. Narayanan and Sir David Steel affirmed liberal principles and called for a "slim and strong state, not a fat one".

The Convention's concluding consensus statement on "Basic Liberal Principles" distinguishes liberalism from laissez-faire, holding that the state must uphold rule of law and provide education, healthcare and infrastructure while otherwise keeping markets open and competitive.

Otto Graf Lambsdorff's "Protectionism the Modern Face of Imperialism" traces the anti-imperialist roots of Manchester free-trade liberalism and argues that today's "fair trade", eco-imperialist and WTO "social clause" advocates repeat the coercive imperial logic under moralised cover, blaming the Smoot-Hawley Tariff Act of 1930 for deepening the Great Depression.

Sharad Joshi's essay on the Beijing Fourth World Women's Conference argues it marginalised grassroots activism in favour of a professionalised NGO class, contending genuine gender inequality lies in differential degrees of freedom rather than power or wealth, and that liberalisation rather than state intervention is the true antidote.
P. R. Dubhashi's essay covers the Emergency-era experience in a southern Indian state.

The issue carries an open letter from international PEN protesting the imprisonment of Chinese dissident Wei Jingsheng, alongside the regular "With Many Voices" and "Of Cabbages and Kings" columns on corruption, democracy and civil liberties.

The cover feature "Right to Information" anchors the issue: essays by R. Srinivasan, S. P. Sathe, M. S. Srinivasan and V. M. Tarkunde argue from constitutional, administrative and democratic-theory angles that access to government information should become a fundamental right, with the Official Secrets Act, 1923 identified as the chief obstacle.

R. Srinivasan's "Towards an Open Government" cites James Madison's warning that "a popular government without popular information...is but a prologue to a farce or a tragedy, or perhaps both" and surveys the US Freedom of Information Act, 1966 and comparable laws in Australia, Canada and Britain as models for a Union-level Indian FOI act.

S. P. Sathe's "Access to Information: The Constitutional Position" traces information monopolies historically as tools of hegemony, analyses Supreme Court cases including the Judges Case and the LIC v. M. D. Shah 'Yogakshema' ruling, and concludes courts have treated the right to information only as collateral to free speech rather than a freestanding right, recommending a constitutional amendment and a Freedom of Information Act to supersede the Official Secrets Act.

M. S. Srinivasan's "Right to Information" argues that withholding information from citizens amounts to a form of tyranny, cites the 1975 Emergency censorship as a cautionary precedent, and proposes state-subsidised information centres and a duty on media to present raw, factual information.

Justice V. M. Tarkunde's "Right to Information and Accountability of the State" surveys M. N. Roy's and Jayaprakash Narayan's partyless-democracy ideas, credits public interest litigation and the National Human Rights Commission with extending accountability between elections, and calls for a comprehensive people's-right-to-know statute modelled on the US Freedom of Information Reform Act, 1986, plus repeal of the Atomic Energy Act's secrecy provisions.
The editor's note ties the Right to Information theme to the recent Eleventh Lok Sabha elections and the end of one-party dominance, and previews a seminar report on coalition politics.

The regular "With Many Voices" column collects quoted extracts on Indian and world politics, while "Of Cabbages and Kings" covers endocrine-disrupting chemicals, the public beheading of an Indian expatriate in Saudi Arabia, Aung San Suu Kyi's Burma boycott call, and a critique of India's VIP security culture.

The cover package "CTBT and all that..." debates India's refusal to sign the Comprehensive Test Ban Treaty: Rajesh M. Basrur argues the treaty's collapse reflected the nuclear powers' own lack of genuine commitment to disarmament rather than Indian obstruction, faulting the Entry Into Force clause for making India, Pakistan and Israel scapegoats.

E. D'Souza (Maj. Gen., Retd.) defends India's refusal to sign, arguing the CTBT is not truly comprehensive since it exempts laboratory and sub-critical testing while letting the five declared powers keep upgrading arsenals, and praises Ambassador Arundhati Ghose's firmness at Geneva.

S. S. Bankeshwar calls nuclear disarmament efforts an exercise in futility since weapons technology cannot be disinvented, and argues India faces only three choices, fatalism, a foreign nuclear umbrella, or self-reliant deterrence, endorsing the third.

Sharad Joshi's "Liberalism in India - Awaiting a Hitler?" argues that Vedantic thought anticipated liberal individualism but that seven centuries of conquest and colonial rule, followed by Nehruvian statism, suppressed this inheritance, warning that economic disillusionment could produce an Indian Hitler exploiting communal and caste grievances.

A report on the Second International Conference of Tibet Support Groups in Bonn covers the Dalai Lama's keynote framing the Tibet struggle as pro-justice rather than anti-Chinese, and China's retaliatory shutdown of the Friedrich Naumann Foundation's China offices after the Foundation proceeded with the conference.

The regular "Of Cabbages and Kings" column mourns Swatantra Party colleague N. C. Zamindar, reports on a decade-old broadcasting-licence writ petition tied to Minoo Masani's Emergency-era censorship fight, and comments on executions of Indian workers in Saudi Arabia and the CIA's Cold War "Operation Jakarta" in Indonesia.

S. S. Bankeshwar's "Gowda and the Press" recounts his frustrated attempts to interview then-Chief Minister, later Prime Minister, H. D. Deve Gowda, arguing Gowda mistakes ignorance of national affairs for humility and contrasting him unfavourably with Rajaji and Morarji Desai.

Shyam Ashtekar's account of Anna Hazare's Maharashtra anti-corruption crusade traces its escalation from complaints against state ministers through a hunger strike and public clashes with Shivsena and BJP figures, criticising the movement for lacking a systemic diagnosis and tacitly endorsing the same statist welfare logic that breeds corruption.

Arun Shourie's companion profile credits Anna Hazare's Ralegaon Siddhi model village, transformed through water-harvesting, a communal grain bank, and abolition of liquor and tobacco sale, as the product of sustained voluntary community labour rather than government schemes.

A two-part symposium on reserved constituencies for women opens with an open letter opposing the rotational reservation system as disenfranchising, proposing permanent three-seat multi-member constituencies instead, followed by an essay tracing the Shetkari Mahila Aghadi's campaign for full women's panels in panchayat elections.

The "Of Cabbages and Kings" column criticises continuing sati-glorification at Jhunjhunu, a Janata Dal-Sunni political alliance in Kerala, and the government bailout of Indian Bank as socialising losses from politically directed lending.
The regular "With Many Voices" column collects press quotations on foreign-investment fatigue, the Deve Gowda coalition's improvisational style, and Congress's dependence on the Gandhi family name.

The cover feature "Dams and the Environment" opens with A. K. R. Hemmady summarising the geological case, drawing on Roger Billham's research, that the Himalayan belt is overdue for a major earthquake near the Tehri Dam site that could affect 100-200 million people, and reviewing evidence of siltation and ecological damage from dam-building generally.

M. Ramakrishnan of the Geological Survey of India counters that environmental objections to dams are sometimes exaggerated, arguing small dams cannot collectively replace large dams' storage and flood-control capacity and calling for a mixed strategy alongside better seismic data.

Shahnaz Anklesaria Aiyar's piece on the Narmada Valley Project, an estimated Rs. 15,000-crore scheme that will submerge 350,000 hectares and about 237 villages, argues both Gujarat's proponents and displaced-community activists overstate their case, coining opponents' extremism "ecofundamentalism".

Justice K. S. Puttaswamy argues dam construction should be decided by expert investigation rather than judicial intervention, supporting completion of the Tehri Dam given sunk costs while criticising the Supreme Court's involvement in the Narmada Dam case.

A second feature, "The Making of the Indian Constitution", marks the Constitution's fiftieth year with reprinted extracts from framers including B. R. Ambedkar, whose closing Constituent Assembly address warns that political democracy is incomplete without social and economic democracy and cautions against both hero-worship of leaders and abandoning constitutional methods for grievance.

The issue also carries a talk by Martin Lee of Hong Kong's Democratic Party on Hong Kong's 1997 handover from British colony to Chinese province, alongside the regular "With Many Voices" and "Of Cabbages and Kings" columns.
The golden-jubilee cover story "Fifty Years After..." reprints a Project for Economic Education seminar taking stock of fifty years of Indian independence with a marked lack of celebratory tone.

Sadanand Varde questions the moral authority of the "freedom fighter" label given how many holders have since been implicated in corruption, quoting Achyut Patwardhan's despairing verdict that neither British departure nor socialism delivered on freedom's promise, and arguing development has bypassed the majority the freedom struggle claimed to serve.

Indumati Parikh argues formal political freedom in 1947 was never matched by a social revolution against caste and gender hierarchy, citing declining female-to-male sex ratios and persistent mass illiteracy as evidence that Phule's and Ranade's nineteenth-century reform demands remain unmet.

Jiban K. Mukhopadhyay lays out a statistical balance sheet of fifty years of centralised planning, citing the "Hindu rate of growth" of 1.5% annual per-capita GDP growth from 1950-79, a loss-making public sector, and a stark India-China comparison on growth, literacy and foreign investment that finds India lagging.

The issue's regular editorial and miscellany sections frame the golden jubilee against contemporary concerns including founder Minoo Masani's health and tributes to Dadabhai Naoroji award winner Nani Palkhivala.

The cover feature "A Question of Values" reproduces Abe Solomon's draft "Universal Declaration of Human Values", eleven articles grounding rights in freedom, truth, reason and compassion, produced in association with the Project for Economic Education, arguing the 1948 UN Declaration of Human Rights rests on unstated values that need their own explicit codification.

A transcript of the accompanying Mumbai seminar records eighteen named participants debating whether values or rights are logically prior, the Maharashtra government's new compulsory school values-education policy, and the public's emotional response to the deaths of Princess Diana and Mother Teresa.

Nani Palkhivala's acceptance speech for the Dadabhai Naoroji Memorial Prize sketches Naoroji's vision of a free India built on universal education and secular equality among religions, closing on a pessimistic note about India's corruption fifty years after independence.
V. C. Viswanathan's "Ethics as Business Strategy" profiles Alacrity Foundations and Body Shop as businesses built on ethical codes.

The "Of Cabbages and Kings" column criticises politicians occupying AIIMS guest-house rooms meant for visiting scientists, a Karnataka legislators' rest-house built with jacuzzis and imported tiles, and Uttar Pradesh Chief Minister Kalyan Singh's defector-heavy cabinet, sixteen of whose ministers face criminal charges including murder and dacoity.
The issue opens with a tribute extract from the Dalai Lama marking the 38th anniversary of Tibetan resistance, alongside the regular "With Many Voices" column of press quotations.

The cover symposium "Stability in Diversity" examines coalition politics, federalism and constitutional design on the eve of the 12th Lok Sabha elections, with Lionel Fernandes arguing genuine democracy must be participatory rather than a periodic ritual of casting ballots, listing alertness, concern, sensitivity, openness, honesty and courage as its requirements.

Nagindas Sanghavi argues the rise of coalition politics reflects a genuine and welcome democratisation of the party system, crediting state-level coalition experience since the 1950s with building administrative maturity and channelling the Communist Party into democratic participation.

Writing pseudonymously as "Deepak", a contrary essay argues coalitions are a symptom of divisive social forces rather than political maturity, proposing a two-round national election in which only the top two vote-getting parties would contest a run-off to force single-party majorities.

Santishree D. N. B. Pandit traces the strong unitary bias built into the Constitution and Article 356's repeated misuse to dismiss non-Congress state governments, recommending binding status for Inter-State Council decisions and fairer revenue-sharing to make India a genuinely federal polity.

A republished interview with Minoo Masani argues the Indian President is not a mere rubber stamp but holds real reserve powers under Articles 74 and 75 to decline Cabinet advice, attributing Presidents' failure to exercise these powers to personal timidity rather than constitutional constraint.

Jiban K. Mukhopadhyay traces GDP growth from 3.5% annually before 1979-80 to roughly 7% before 1997-98, crediting the United Front coalition's Common Minimum Programme and Finance Minister P. Chidambaram's 1997-98 "dream budget" with sustaining reform momentum despite coalition instability.

The cover feature "Understanding the Verdict of 1998" summarises a thirty-participant Mumbai seminar debating why the 12th Lok Sabha elections again produced a hung parliament, covering proposals such as proportional representation, a fixed election calendar, and postal ballots for soldiers, plus a boxed argument that political power is shifting from caste Hindus toward Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes and Other Backward Classes.

Amit Dholakia's "A Turning Point" reads the hung parliament as evidence of party fragmentation and the "end of ideology", describing Congress's fall to just one actor among many and predicting satellite television will become a decisive, potentially trivialising, factor in future elections.

V. Krishnamachari's "She Came, She Waved, but Failed to Conquer" offers a critical post-mortem of Sonia Gandhi's 1998 campaign debut, arguing the "Sonia magic" was overstated since Congress's 142-seat tally barely exceeded Narasimha Rao's uncharismatic 1996 result, and documenting losses in symbolically important seats including Rae Bareilly.

The "Of Cabbages and Kings" column reports the 1997 closure of the Harold Laski Institute of Political Science, an obituary for Freedom First Advisory Board member Aziz Madni, and a polemical item accusing Nobel laureate Gabriel Garcia Marquez of being an apologist for Castro, Stalin and Pablo Escobar.

The regular "With Many Voices" column compiles press soundbites on the corruption and criminalisation surrounding the 1998 elections, including Chief Election Commissioner M. S. Gill's remark that booth capturing is "the reality of India".

The issue is dominated by a memorial tribute, "Minoo Masani - Journey's End", marking the founder's death on May 27, 1998, at age 92, opening with a poem by Dr. Louella Lobo Prabhu eulogising him as a fearless dissenter unafraid of being "a minority of one".

S. V. Raju's obituary "The Quintessential Dissenter" traces Masani's arc from Congress Socialist Party leader disillusioned with Soviet communism to co-founder of the Swatantra Party, Lok Sabha opposition leader, and Emergency-era editor of Freedom First who fought censorship in court.

A condensed record of tributes from a June 12, 1998 condolence meeting includes N. A. Palkhivala praising Masani's Constituent Assembly membership and advocacy for deregulation, and Masani's son Zareer Masani giving a frank tribute describing his father's impatience and total refusal to compromise principle for office.

A reprinted personal credo, "I Believe", lays out Masani's humanism grounded in the "Brotherhood of Man" independent of religious belief, his rejection of chauvinism, and his debt to Stoic philosophy, particularly Marcus Aurelius, for resisting unpopularity.

A transcript recorded by K. R. Malkani of a 1934 conversation between Gandhi and Masani has Gandhi arguing that a socialist programme imposed by a minority amounts to violence if the majority lacks genuine desire for it, while Masani counters that land nationalisation is intelligible and acceptable to ordinary peasants.

The rendered pages also open a symposium of four articles on the ethics and politics of India's May 1998 Pokhran-II nuclear tests, which the editor's note says the magazine condemns despite running dissenting pro-test pieces for balance.

The cover feature "Sliding into Chaos?" frames population explosion, rising prices, a weakening economy, and erosion of the rule of law as the issue's central concerns, with the editorial citing Bombay's crime wave and gangster impunity as evidence of a breakdown in law and order.

Deepak's "The Crippling of the Indian Mind" argues India remains physically crippled by population growth and mentally crippled by inadequate education, predicting "sanguinary chaos" within two decades absent reform, and crediting rising living standards and female education, citing Kerala's literacy record, as the real solvents to high birth rates.

Jiban K. Mukhopadhyay's "Must We Remain a Destitute Economy?" argues India needs sustained growth above 9% annually, not the customary 5%, to meaningfully reduce poverty, noting 53% of over 965 million Indians live below the World Bank's poverty line, and blames lack of political will for stalled reforms in PSU privatisation and labour law.

J. B. D'Souza's "The Indian State Vs. Its Citizens: An Unequal Contest" surveys human-rights violations including bonded and child labour and caste oppression, arguing state violations by the army, paramilitary and police under laws like TADA are more severe than societal ones because they occur under colour of law and go unredressed.

The "Of Cabbages and Kings" column comments on politicians' shared superstitions around astrologically timed swearings-in, a controversy over a Delhi church serving wine, and a tribute to the late Swatantra Party stalwart S. S. Mariswamy.

The issue reproduces a "Joint Statement Against Nuclear Tests and Weapons" issued on Gandhi's birth anniversary by retired Pakistani, Indian and Bangladeshi armed-forces personnel calling for both countries to renounce nuclear weapons.

The cover symposium "The Bureaucrat: Public Servant or Government Servant?" assembles former civil servants examining the decline of professionalism and independence in the Indian bureaucracy since Nehru's time.

J. B. D'Souza, a retired Chief Secretary of Maharashtra, argues bureaucratic complicity with politicians, not just bad policy, explains why land reform failed, recounting his own resistance to ministerial pressure over a road realignment and a Backbay land-lease rate hike, and insisting officials must see themselves as public servants first.

Ashok V. Desai contrasts the careers of I. G. Patel and Manmohan Singh at the RBI, including the BCCI licensing episode, to argue that ministers' historic deference to bureaucratic judgment collapsed under Indira Gandhi, who began promoting "malleable" bureaucrats over independent-minded ones.

A. D. Moddie, a retired ICS officer, recounts witnessing entrenched corruption from his 1949 Bihar posting onward, including a police officer who personally committed an armed dacoity, and describes resigning from the ICS after finding no colleague could justify staying on.

Marina Pinto traces the civil service's arc from the British-era "steel frame" ethos of neutrality through Nehruvian-era respect for that neutrality to its decline from the late 1960s as a doctrine of "committed" bureaucracy rewarded compliant officials, citing the Shah Commission's findings on Emergency-era subservience.

The cover feature "Coping with Coalitions" debates whether coalition government is viable for India: Subhash C. Kashyap argues coalitions succeed only with pre-election alliances and ideological affinity, criticising India's first-past-the-post system and proposing a constructive vote of no-confidence.

Seetha Parthasarathy argues a fractured mandate reflects genuine social churning as OBCs, Dalits, women and regional communities outgrew Congress's old umbrella coalition, and that coalition government handled with sagacity could mature Indian democracy.

Nagindas Sanghavi describes the 1999 elections as the "Keralisation" of national politics, marking a shift from post-election parliamentary coalitions to pre-election electoral fronts, with no clear successor to Congress's dominant-party role.

S. R. Kelkar defends the parliamentary system against calls for a presidential model, pointing to unstable presidential regimes elsewhere and arguing that coalition ministries under the 11th and 13th Lok Sabhas still delivered reasonable economic management.

Major General (Retd.) E. D'Souza's essay on the Kargil war argues Pakistan deliberately exploited high-altitude terrain and Indian complacency after Lahore bus diplomacy, with at least six months of pre-planning, and calls the episode an intelligence failure at every level despite shepherd reports of unusual activity reaching the Cabinet.
The issue also carries a memorial tribute to J. M. Lobo Prabhu, a former ICS officer and Swatantra Party parliamentarian, written by his widow Louella Lobo Prabhu.

The cover package "Are the Armed Forces being Politicised?" opens with Major General (Retd.) E. D'Souza's "A Storm Warning", which traces the Army's tradition of political neutrality from Field Marshal Cariappa onward and warns against creeping political interference, citing General Thimayya's near-resignation and the non-appointment of Lieutenant General P. S. Bhagat as troubling precedents.

A second cluster, "Coping with Coalitions", debates whether India should adopt a presidential system tailored to its federal diversity, with P. R. Dubhashi's contribution noting only Congress governments have completed full terms since independence and recalling Gandhi's advice, unheeded by Nehru, that Congress should disband after independence.

R. Srinivasan's "Alzheimer in the Nation's Brain" surveys the long history of libraries as repositories of collective memory, from ancient Mesopotamian archives through the burning of the Library of Alexandria to the 1998 destruction of a research centre in Guinea-Bissau's civil war.

J. B. D'Souza's obituary tribute to Pesi Masani, Minoo Masani's mathematician brother who died in Pittsburgh in October 1999, recalls their shared boyhood and Pesi's quiet decades-long support of a homeless-women's charity.

The regular "With Many Voices" and "Of Cabbages and Kings" columns compile press quotations on the Kargil war and Pakistan coup, and satirise VIP security disruptions alongside a critical comment on the Pope's 1999 visit to India.

The cover symposium "THE Mature Indian Democracy", retitled from "maturing" after contributors disputed whether India even qualifies as a democracy, assembles roughly two dozen contributors: J. B. D'Souza argues fifty years of franchise have changed little for India's rural poor, using the recurring figure of a tribal woman named Somiya, and catalogues institutional decay including police encounter killings and impunity for criminal-politicians.

Arvind Deshpande and Nagindas Sanghvi argue Indian society itself remains fundamentally undemocratic beneath its political institutions, citing persistent caste and rising communal xenophobia, while V. K. Sinha and K. F. Rustomji take a more optimistic view, citing halved infant mortality and doubled life expectancy.

N. Namasivayam and Mohamed Jaffar invoke Ambedkar's 1949 warning that mere political democracy is meaningless without social and economic democracy, and tabulate defaulting ex-prime ministers' unpaid Air Force dues.

A companion symposium, "Of Elections and Electioneering", analyses the 1999 Lok Sabha elections, covering caste- and money-driven candidate selection in Maharashtra and the NDA's Kargil-driven mandate against the "videshi" (foreign-origin) controversy around Sonia Gandhi.

The "Of Cabbages and Kings" column, titled "Mobocracy on the Rise", criticises the Hindu-fundamentalist mob that drove filmmaker Deepa Mehta from Varanasi during the shoot of "Water" despite official clearance, and the NDA coalition's muted response.
A translated Rabindranath Tagore poem, "False Religion", also appears in the rendered pages.

The cover feature "The Kashmir Question: Many Options, Few Takers" reports on Freedom First's third organised discussion on Kashmir, tracing the 1947 accession and the unfulfilled plebiscite promise via a V. P. Menon extract and Nehru's 1952 parliamentary pledge, and debating whether Kashmiris resent Indian rule.

Maneesha Tikekar's account of a February 2000 Islamabad seminar presents the Pakistani elite's framing of Kashmir as "shahrag" (jugular vein) against India's "atoot ang" (inseparable part), while the feature warns Kashmir has become entangled in a transnational Islamic fundamentalist "grand design" associated with Hasan al-Torabi and Osama bin Laden.

The feature surveys proposed solutions including freezing the Line of Control, a phased plebiscite, and Ayesha Jalal's "Sovereignty Association" idea, closing on the hopeful note of the Indian army's announced phased troop withdrawal from Kashmir.

M. A. Rane's tribute to Justice B. R. Lentin of the Bombay High Court, who died in April 2000, recalls his 1981 intervention halting the forcible eviction of Bombay pavement-dwellers and his enquiry into the Antulay cement-permit scandal that led to Chief Minister A. R. Antulay's resignation.
The regular "Of Cabbages and Kings" column covers the 1999-2000 drought and the Sri Lankan civil war.

The cover feature "The Enemy Within: Corruption - The Enemy of Dharma" opens with S. S. Bankeshwar's "The Monster of Corruption", arguing India ranks among the world's ten most corrupt countries, distinguishing predictable "organised" corruption from more destructive "chaotic" corruption, and citing South Korea's swift prosecution of corrupt former presidents as a model India cannot match.

A footnoted transcript of the magazine's June 24 Mumbai seminar on corruption records panelists invoking Sudhir Kakar's research on authoritarian Indian child-rearing as a root of official venality, and calling for stripping politicians of their power to transfer bureaucrats at will.

Seminar participants critique the Prevention of Corruption Act's sanction-to-prosecute clause as a structural enabler of impunity and ground the discussion in first-person anecdotes of everyday bribery, from an RTO clerk to capitation-fee medical admissions.

Proposed remedies discussed include computerised land records, decentralisation to the panchayat level, simplified laws, contested value-education proposals, and the Indian Liberal Group's plan to publicise honest role models starting with Raja Rammohun Roy.

The front matter carries a tribute to the late industrialist S. P. Godrej and an "Of Cabbages and Kings" column touching on Count Otto von Lambsdorff's Holocaust-compensation work and press freedom in Kashmir and Sri Lanka.
The discussion explicitly continues into the next issue as part two of a two-part treatment of corruption.

An obituary opens the issue for Dr. Usha Mehta, the Gandhian scholar-activist who ran the Gandhi Smarak Nidhi in Bombay and built one of the city's best libraries on the Mahatma and the national movement.

S. V. Raju's "Liberalism: A Contemporary View" traces liberalism's roots in Bentham, Mill and T. H. Green through the Swatantra Party's founding against Nehruvian statism to Minoo Masani's 1985 view that socialism's aims of freedom and equality are good even though its methods produce tyranny.

A second-part corruption symposium, "The Enemy Within - II: Containing Corruption", distinguishes tolerable "petty corruption" from systemic corruption bred by the permit-licence-quota raj, reprinting a Jayaprakash Narayan passage that corruption is a moral, not merely economic, failure.

K. K. Pathak's reprinted 1964 letter to Union Home Minister Gulzari Lal Nanda blames socialist permit-licence-quota policies for debasing society and calls for dedicated corruption courts, open trials, and civic-education reform.

J. B. D'Souza's "Corruption in Education" surveys rampant corruption in schooling, from black-money admissions and leaked exam papers to fake-degree "certificate factories", citing the Misa Bharati medical-college admission case.

Prem Vaidya's tribute "J. R. D. Tata - A Pragmatic Visionary" recounts filming JRD Tata for a 25th-independence-anniversary documentary, JRD's insistence on stressing continuing mass poverty over industrial statistics, and his pioneering 1932 airmail flight and long tenure as Air India chairman.
M. R. Pai's "Bandit, not Robin Hood!" argues sandalwood bandit Veerappan's operation is sustained by corrupt politicians, bureaucrats, police and forest guards profiting as silent partners.

The cover feature "Thank God for the Armed Forces But..." was built around three news pegs, a terrorist attack on the Red Fort army post, the Gujarat earthquake, and the Mumbai International Fleet Review, to examine the Indian Armed Forces' expanding and politically fraught role.

Maj. Gen. Eustace D'Souza's "Don't Politicize the Army - Please!" surveys the forces' unsustainable range of duties, criticises the National Security Council's structure and the delayed Chief of Defence Staff post, and reviews historical politicisation episodes from the Krishna Menon era to Operation Blue Star.

R. V. Chari's "The Samba Spy Case" recounts the 1975-1980 espionage frame-up of over fifty army officers, including a soldier's death in custody, through to their full exoneration and reinstatement by the Delhi High Court in December 2000, drawing an explicit parallel to the Dreyfus Affair.

A. K. R. Hemmady's essay on the Gujarat earthquake surveys the region's seismic history, reports over 15,000 deaths in Bhuj and Anjar, criticises fatalistic religious explanations for disasters, and details disaster-management failures including absent officials and relief flights turned away from Bhuj airport.
The "With Many Voices" column compiles press reactions to the January 26, 2001 earthquake, recording 16,480 deaths and roughly Rs. 3,500 crores in estimated property loss as of early February.

The "Of Cabbages and Kings" column opposes a proposed tobacco-advertising ban, criticises both Kerala's CPM-literature panchayat mandate and Gujarat's RSS-weekly school circular, and defends the BALCO privatisation against opposition attacks.

The cover feature "WTO - Yes! But Let's Proceed Carefully" opens with A. Mohamed Jaffar's primer explaining the WTO's origins from GATT and stressing that its agreements do not require dismantling India's Public Distribution System or food subsidies.

L. S. N. Prasad examines how globalisation and falling global commodity prices have exposed Indian agriculture's structural weaknesses, citing Kerala farmer suicides linked to collapsing produce prices, and calls for freeing agriculture from state control and unifying India's fragmented internal market.

Dana R. Dillon, a Heritage Foundation policy analyst, argues the Bush administration should build on WTO commitments with a comprehensive US-India bilateral trade agreement, citing India's high average tariffs and restrictive foreign equity caps.

Ashok V. Karnik's "The Tehelka Tapes - An Analysis" defends due process against a political and media rush to judgment following the defence-bribery sting, questioning the tapes' editing and the ethics of publicising secretly recorded, unverified boasting as proven fact.

Obituary tributes mark the deaths of columnist Behram "Busybee" Contractor and B. K. Desai, Secretary of the Democratic Research Service and Freedom First's publisher from 1959 to 1963, who later helped found the Shiv Sena before drifting away.

S. S. Bankeshwar's "Using Surplus Food Stocks Profitably" laments the government's silence on a Delhi School of Economics letter about India's rotting foodgrain surplus, arguing the stocks should fund drought-relief income-generation schemes.

The cover feature on voter apathy, prompted by the 2001 Tamil Nadu and West Bengal elections, opens with R. Srinivasan's "Do We Really Care Who We Elect?", which frames Indian elections as a "gladiatorial sport" driven by caste loyalty and patronage, and argues political corruption is a "global phenomenon" citing scandals touching Western leaders' families too.
C. Narendra's "Democracy on the Decline in Tamilnadu" condemns the newly elected government's night-time arrest of former chief minister M. Karunanidhi as an act that "would do fascism proud".

Seetha's "Rewarding the Corrupt" argues Indian voters share the blame with corrupt politicians, citing the repeated re-election of Jayalalitha, Neelalokahitadasan Nader, and Rabri Devi despite serious charges, contrasting this with the 1989 anti-Bofors backlash.

S. S. Bankeshwar's "A Great Leap Backwards" warns India's legal framework lets convicted candidates become chief ministers through gaps between the Representation of the People Act and gubernatorial discretion, and proposes minimum educational qualifications for candidates and voters.

The issue's centrepiece, Subroto Roy's memoir "Encounter with Rajiv Gandhi", claims his "perestroika" manuscript and an unpublished 1955 Milton Friedman memorandum shaped the Congress economic-reform group that drafted the March 1991 manifesto he says was the true template for the 1991 liberalisation.
The issue reproduces the Dalai Lama's March 2001 statement on the 42nd anniversary of the Tibetan uprising and his August 2001 clarification affirming Jammu and Kashmir as an integral part of India.

A planned Bollywood cover feature was scrapped after September 11, 2001, and replaced with "How Dare You! America's War Against Terrorism", opening with a reprinted World Forum on Democracy statement condemning terrorism to which Freedom First is a signatory.

S. V. Raju's lead essay argues Indians should not invest the United States with moral superiority after 9/11 given its history of self-interested policy including arming both the Taliban and Pakistan, framing the real confrontation as with fundamentalist Islam rather than Islam itself, and urging India and Pakistan to use the moment to discuss Kashmir.

Minoo Adenwalla's "We Shall Not Sleep", written within days of the attacks, surveys al-Qaeda's prior record from the 1993 WTC bombing to the USS Cole attack and predicts a war of covert strikes and economic attrition rather than conventional battle.

Dr. Prasenjit Maitri's "The WTC Tragedy and After" argues US foreign policy bears some responsibility for breeding anti-American terrorism, citing Cold War-era coups in Chile and Central America and calling Osama bin Laden "a Frankenstein created by America itself".

S. S. Bankeshwar's "The USA's Double Standards" accuses Washington of treating terrorism against itself as a global crime while dismissing Kashmiri terrorism, which he says has killed over 80,000 people, as a matter for mere "restraint and patience".
The "Of Cabbages and Kings" column addresses the Prevention of Terrorism Ordinance (POTO) and carries an obituary for Professor G. N. Sarma.
Marking the magazine's 50th year, the issue is dedicated to the birth centenary of Jayaprakash Narayan, honouring him as "Loknayak" ahead of Sarva Seva Sangh centenary observances.

An unsigned biographical feature traces JP's life from his 1902 birth through his American education and reading of Marx, repeated imprisonment by the British including torture at Lahore Fort, his post-Independence turn from Marxism to Gandhian Sarvodaya, the 1966 Bihar drought "Free Kitchen Movement", the 1974 Total Revolution call, and his death in 1979.

Arvind Deshpande's personal tribute recalls meeting JP through the Indian Committee for Cultural Freedom in the early 1960s, defends him against charges of political "failure", and recounts a 1969 episode in which JP reacted with sorrow rather than anger to Sheikh Abdullah's harsh treatment over a Kashmir miscommunication with Indira Gandhi.

Prem Vaidya's first-person account of filming Bihar's 1966 drought relief documents systemic distribution fraud and missionary organisations outperforming government agencies, then follows JP's arc through the 1974 Bihar agitation, Emergency detention and declining health, and the 1977 Janata Party victory.

The issue reprints JP's December 1975 "Testament of Protest", an open letter to Indira Gandhi written from Jaslok Hospital and originally suppressed in the Indian press, in which he denies plotting to paralyse the government and defends the Bihar movement's constructive aims.
The regular "Of Cabbages and Kings" column comments on English-language enrichment, the national flag, and cable-operator censorship.

This special issue, under the cover theme "Mera Bharat Mahan?", is devoted almost entirely to the 2002 Gujarat riots, opening with a dedication to a Hindu woman killed in Ahmedabad for helping a Muslim man escape a mob.

Editor S. V. Raju's editorial declines to call for Narendra Modi's removal as Gujarat chief minister given his electoral mandate, but calls the violence an "organised massacre" bordering on genocide and argues the BJP is "a creation of and controlled by" the RSS.

Kusum Choppra's "Gujarat: The Beginning of the End?" narrates the Godhra train burning that killed 58 people and the ensuing organised mob violence using voter lists to target Muslim homes and businesses, coining the term "Jehadi Hindus" for Hindutva militants.

Nagindas Sanghavi examines the psychology of ordinary, otherwise moderate Gujaratis endorsing the violence as necessary "cleansing", citing over 800 killed and 30,000 houses or shops burnt, and identifies NRIs as the VHP's chief financiers.

Cyrus Guzder's "Is Secularism Good for Business?" argues communal disorder damages the economy, invoking Milton Friedman and Peter Drucker alongside 19th-century Gujarati poet Narmadashankar Lalshankar's inclusive vision of Gujarati identity.

The cover feature "The Citizen's Right to Know" centres on the Supreme Court's May 2002 judgment compelling candidates for public office to disclose their criminal, financial and educational antecedents.

Jagdeep S. Chhokar, a petitioner in the case, lays out the electoral-reform case for disclosure, reviews decades of unimplemented reform reports, and cites the MKSS-led Right to Information campaign in Rajasthan as a model for citizen-forced change.

Sharad Joshi offers a libertarian counter-argument that mandatory disclosure could weaponise criminal charges against agitation leaders like himself, drawing on his own record of over 700 cases in 22 years of farmer activism, and argues the deeper fix is withdrawing the state from economic life so money power in elections withers.

Thomas Sowell's obituary tribute to development economist Lord Peter Bauer credits him with rejecting the orthodoxy that Third World poverty could only be escaped through foreign aid, noting Hernando de Soto's later research vindicated his thesis.

Documentary filmmaker Prem Vaidya argues 15th August 1947 should be remembered as a day of Partition and atonement rather than untroubled celebration, detailing Gandhi's absence from official celebrations and the mass migration that followed.
The "Of Cabbages and Kings" column covers the V. B. Karnik birth centenary and the POTA/Vaiko controversy, alongside tribute notices for Professor P. G. Mavalankar and litterateur Durga Bhagwat.

This 50th Anniversary Commemorative Issue is a retrospective anthology assembled by guest editor Dr. Mary Thomas, who read every issue from the magazine's June 1952 founding through July 2002 to select articles spanning its half-century for republication.

Mary Thomas's own essay traces Freedom First's evolution from a monthly organ fighting Communism to its 1985 conversion into a quarterly Liberal journal, naming past editors and contributors including Minoo Masani, Dinkar Sakrikar, V. B. Karnik and Nissim Ezekiel.
A reprinted 1952 M. R. Masani essay rebuts the relativist claim that non-Western peoples care only about bread and not liberty, invoking Gandhi's spiritual self-control against Communist materialism.

A reprinted 1953 C. Rajagopalachari address, "True Freedom", grounds a distinctively Indian answer to both Soviet-style state regulation and unrestrained Western liberty in the Isa Vasya Upanishad's and Bhagavad Gita's teaching of self-control.

Sampurnanand's 1953 address diagnoses a "neurosis" in the Indian intelligentsia caught between democracy and Communism, citing ancient India's historic tolerance of heterodox thought as against Communist orthodoxy.

Malcolm Muggeridge's "The Art of Non-Conforming", originally published in Vogue, argues the mid-twentieth century is marked by exceptional ideological credulity and presents the "Non-Conforming Man" as a necessary resistance figure against mass orthodoxy.
The issue is dedicated to the First National Convention of the Indian Liberal Group in Hyderabad, billed as the first Liberal political convention in 75 years.

An unsigned editorial reprints the founding June 1952 "The Open Society" editorial marking the journal's 51st year, reframing India's fight against totalitarianism and communism as today's fight against religious fundamentalism and communalism.

A "Going By Instinct" editorial on 9/11, Godhra, and the looming Iraq war argues the "war on terrorism" rhetoric enabled both India's POTA law and the Gujarat pogrom, while taking the position that Iraq bears responsibility for defying UN disarmament resolutions.

Nagindas Sanghavi opens the "Only Politicians, No Statesmen" symposium by arguing the BJP's December 2002 Gujarat win (127 seats, 51% vote) was a continuation of a trend visible since 1995 rather than a post-Godhra landslide, faulting the Congress's outsourced campaign under Kamalnath and the media's failed pre-poll predictions.

Ashok Karnik's "A Wake Up Call From Gujarat" argues the result was a defeat of how secularism was practiced, not of the principle itself, criticising the Congress's "soft Hindutva" temple-visit campaigning and unsubstantiated post-Godhra conspiracy theories blaming the VHP.

A. D. Moddie poses nine pointed questions to Hindutva ideologues, contrasting "cultural nationalism" with Rajaji's self-control and Amartya Sen's account of a "receptive and creative" Indian culture, and challenging the movement to address corruption and land-grabbing at pilgrimage sites.

Cyrus Guzder's "Bridging the Communal Divide: 1" argues uncompromising constitutional citizenship, applied equally regardless of religion, is now the only workable ideology, citing the Shiv Sena's unpunished arson of a Muslim-owned hospital in Thane.

Satish Sahney's companion piece argues the Hindu-Muslim divide will keep spreading unless both communities' fundamentalism is checked, urging that the word "secular" be retired since it is read as anti-Hindu code, and that reconciliation efforts should focus on youth.

The issue also carries a "With Many Voices" digest of press quotations on Gujarat and communalism, and a tribute by Minoo Shroff to Nani Palkhivala, the constitutional lawyer and Forum of Free Enterprise stalwart who died in December 2002.
Freedom First No. 457 (April-June 2003), edited by S. V. Raju, runs a three-part "Only Politicians No Statesmen" symposium framed through "The Bihar Perspective."

Shanker Prasad Tekriwal's "Laloo's Lathi Raj" catalogues failures in education, welfare and rural electrification under the Laloo-Rabri Devi government, and accuses it of corruption including the fodder and bitumen scams.

Manuwant Choudhary's "Living Dangerously in Bihar" gives a first-person account of the state's decline after the Jharkhand bifurcation, covering CARE-India's exit, endemic kidnapping-for-ransom, and naxal violence, and argues Nitish Kumar is no credible alternative to Laloo.
Manoje Nath's "The Bihari: Prisoner of his Own Image" argues the self-effacing "Bihari" stereotype is a psychological trap that keeps Biharis from demanding their fair share of national resources.

Major General E. D'Souza's "Captains Courageous" profiles Field Marshal Cariappa, General K. S. Thimayya, and Field Marshal Sam Manekshaw as evidence that India has in fact produced genuine military statesmen, rebutting the magazine's own framing question.
The issue carries obituary tributes to P. R. Brahmananda, S. Ramakrishnan, and K. F. Rustamji, alongside a report marking the V. B. Karnik birth centenary.

Arvind Deshpande contributes a short piece giving a liberal view on the Iraq War, and Prem Vaidya opens a longer feature on General Sir Arthur "Maharishi" Cotton, the East India Company engineer credited as father of Indian irrigation in the Godavari and Cauvery deltas.

Freedom First No. 459 (Oct-Dec 2003) is dedicated to Satyendra Kumar Dubey, the NHAI engineer murdered in Gaya, Bihar after exposing corruption on the Golden Quadrilateral project; an unsigned piece details the bureaucratic mishandling of his complaint and calls for "hundreds of Satyendra Dubeys."
The issue concludes the year-long "What India Needs" cover series, drawn from a September 2003 seminar at St. Xavier's College, Mumbai.

A. D. Moddie's keynote argues India inherited and perpetuated a colonial administrative architecture, citing a Fraser Institute/Centre for Civil Society study ranking India 86th of 123 countries on economic freedom, and calls for a coalition to build countervailing power against an unaccountable political class.

Jiban K. Mukhopadhyay makes the economic case for a feasible 7% growth rate led by agriculture, citing China's post-1978 reform sequencing, and argues full engagement with WTO negotiations gives India more leverage than the IMF or World Bank.

Nagindas Sanghavi diagnoses corruption, criminalisation and communalism as intertwined diseases, citing India's shortage of judges relative to Western democracies, and admits he has no solution to offer for communalism.

Sadanand Varde argues social justice requires equalising real opportunity, not just formal legal equality, recounting caste-based violence in rural Maharashtra and proposing a constitutional "right to recall" non-performing elected representatives.
The Indian Liberal Group's election appeal opening the issue calls for clean candidates, transparency, and continued economic liberalisation tempered by equity.

Freedom First No. 460 (Jan-Mar 2004) marks the birth centenary of freedom fighter Yusuf Meherally with two tribute essays, while the editorial notes the issue was delayed and cut to 44 pages for lack of advertising.

S. V. Raju's "Of Cabbages & Kings" recounts a Delhi workshop to draft "A Liberal Strategy for India: 2004 and Beyond" that collapsed into factional manoeuvring, closing by invoking Masani's and Rajagopalachari's insistence that a liberal party pursue principle rather than chase power.

Kisan Mehta's reminiscence recalls Yusuf Meherally's tenderness toward fellow prisoners at Yeravada jail, their secret correspondence under aliases, and Meherally's late-life work organising a freedom-struggle exhibition from his sickbed.

G. S. Bhargava's tribute narrates Meherally's life from his 1928 leadership of the "Simon Go Back" protests through his break with his guardian M. A. Jinnah, his Congress Socialist Party co-founding, and his death in 1950 at 47 from a lathi injury sustained years earlier.

A. D. Moddie's "India's First 21st Century General Elections" surveys the eve of the 2004 poll, describing a "600 million schizophrenic" electorate and assessing a maturing BJP/NDA, a dynastically-trapped Congress, and a Left overtaken by history.
Manuwant Choudhary's open letter reproaches Sharad Joshi for allying the Shetkari Sanghatana with the NDA, invoking Minoo Masani's vision of a "Swatantra Bharat Party" as a betrayed liberal dream.

Former Prime Minister Chandrashekhar, interviewed by R. Rajagopalan, criticises opportunistic shifts among India's political leadership and calls for cross-party unity on shared national-interest questions such as agriculture.
Amitabh's short story "Pad (Carrion)," introduced as a depiction of pre-Ambedkar Mahar community life, opens with a shanty town's frantic, unresolved scramble to butcher a dead cow found at dawn.
Freedom First No. 461 (April-June 2004) opens with an obituary tribute to Justice V. M. Tarkunde, extracted from an address by Attorney General Soli Sorabjee.
The cover feature reports a May 2004 Mumbai discussion on "India's Festival of Democracy - Elections 2004," organised with the Indian Liberal Group and the Project for Economic Education.

S. V. Raju warns the Election Commission's autonomy is at risk from government dependence for manpower and funds, citing the 720-fold rise in election costs since 1967 and instances of the EC straying beyond its mandate.

Nagindas Sanghavi argues the 2004 campaign again failed to surface substantive issues, framing the BJP's retreat from militant Hindutva toward "India Shining" and the Congress's revival as personal validation of Sonia Gandhi's dynastic leadership.

Ashok Karnik argues the narrow BJP-Congress seat gap reflected no decisive ideological verdict, warning that anti-incumbency and demand for "instant delivery" risk pushing governments toward short-termist populism.

Uttara Sahasrabuddhe contends only six states effectively determine national power, reframing India's run of hung parliaments as a reflection of social diversity rather than instability, and identifies an emerging bipolar Congress-BJP polity.
Floor discussion at the meeting covered disputes over criminal-record disclosure for candidates, electoral-roll disenfranchisement, and the politicisation of Sonia Gandhi's foreign origin.
Freedom First No. 462 (July-Sept 2004) is dedicated to Abe Solomon, the magazine's longtime patron and fundraiser, alongside an obituary for Radical Humanist Dr. Indumati Parikh.

The cover feature, "The Liberal Budget - Building an Equitable Society," presented by S. V. Raju as a joint Indian Liberal Group/Project for Economic Education effort, offers the first liberal alternative to the government's annual Union Budget.

Raju's essay grounds the Liberal Budget in Ludwig von Mises's distinction between liberalism and socialism as a matter of means not ends, setting nine numeric human-development targets for 2007 and 2012 and calling for abolishing discretionary tax search-and-seizure powers.

The Liberal Budget summary argues disinvestment should be tested by whether the state belongs in an activity at all, calls for lifting agricultural land ceilings and internal trade barriers, and for genuinely independent regulators.

Major General E. D'Souza's "Indian Troops in World War II" argues the contribution of Indian soldiers, who won 37 Victoria Crosses, has been erased from British and American memory, crediting Baroness Sheila Flather's campaign for the Hyde Park Corner Memorial Gate.

Prem Vaidya reviews the Eighth Mumbai International Film Festival, including a tribute to Leni Riefenstahl and documentaries on youth suicide in Kerala, a 1971 war rape survivor in Bangladesh, and forced tribal-marriage settlements in Pakistan.

Louella Lobo Prabhu's satirical column comments on M. F. Hussain's controversial career, a Supreme Court ruling that the right to strike is not fundamental, and the forcible shutdown of screenings of the film "Girl Friend" over its lesbian subject matter.
"Of Cabbages and Kings" welcomes Manmohan Singh's appointment as Prime Minister while criticising the politicisation of Governors' appointments under successive governments.

Freedom First No. 463 (Oct-Dec 2004) is built around a birth-centenary tribute to founder Minoo Masani, reprinting his essays "Leadership" and "I Believe" alongside S. V. Raju's retrospective "Minoo Masani - The Principled Politician."

Raju traces Masani's journey from founding the Congress Socialist Party in 1934 through his break with its Moscow-directed wing, his 1944 "Socialism Reconsidered," and his 1959 co-founding of the Swatantra Party with C. Rajagopalachari.

In "Leadership," Masani argues India suffers a shortage of genuine leadership due to cultural deference and political "tailism," contrasting Churchill and de Gaulle's conditional leadership with Indian equivocation and quoting Walter Lippmann's warning about authoritarian temptation.
In "I Believe," Masani professes a humanist Brotherhood of Man ethic grounded in Stoic philosophy, tracing how contact with Gandhi's linkage of ends and means led him to renounce State Socialism.

"Of Cabbages and Kings" comments on sycophantic press coverage of Indira Gandhi, calls Yasser Arafat "the father of modern terrorism" on his death, and warns of Bush's re-election implications for civil liberties.

R. M. Lala's "Three Great Liberals" profiles Dadabhai Naoroji, Pherozeshah Mehta, and Jamsetji Tata as London-shaped founders of Indian liberalism, crediting Naoroji as the first Indian elected to the British Parliament.
V. Balachandran explains U.S. Electoral College mechanics to rebut Indian media claims that the Supreme Court "elected" Bush in 2000, drawing a parallel to the 1961 Hawaii electors dispute.
The editor's note announces the postponement of the Indian Liberal Group's Second National Convention to February 2005 and notes the death of Times columnist Bernard Levin.

Freedom First No. 464 (Jan-Mar 2005) is a Convention Special issue for the Indian Liberal Group's Second National Convention in Mangalore, opening with an excerpt from Minoo Masani's autobiography "Against the Tide" recounting the Indian Liberal Group's 1965 founding.

Masani describes distributing the Swatantra Party's 21 principles to the Liberal International's Executive Committee at Gardone in 1959, and names Sophia Wadia, Khushwant Singh, B. R. Shenoy, and H. V. R. Iengar among the ILG's founding executive committee.

A. D. Moddie argues coalition management and accountable governance will define India's 21st century, using Bihar's decline and rising unorganised-sector unemployment as case studies, and proposes renaming the Ministry of Labour a Ministry for National Employment and Productivity.

Moddie proposes multi-party youth committees, naming figures like Rahul Gandhi, Jyotiraditya Scindia, and Milind Deora, to tackle population planning, panchayati raj reform, and employability training.

S. P. Sathe treats accountability as a moral concept, tracing the Supreme Court's closure of a chief-minister reappointment loophole, its mandated candidate disclosure of assets and criminal records, and the growing institutional legitimacy of the Election Commission under T. N. Seshan.

Sathe cites Public Interest Litigation, liberalised after the Emergency, as a key civil-society accountability tool exposing ordinance abuse and corrupt cement-allotment practices, and credits the National Human Rights Commission's intervention in Gujarat carnage cases.

Ajit Karnik surveys India's post-1991 economic liberalisation, crediting it with a fall in poverty from 37% to about 26% while warning of worsening state government finances, and invokes Hayek's "Fatal Conceit" to critique the planning-era state.

Freedom First No. 465 (April-June 2005) devotes its cover feature, "From Tibet to TAR," to five essays marking the 46th anniversary of the Tibetan National Uprising Day and the Dalai Lama's March 10, 2005 statement.

Ajay B. Agrawal's "The Annexation of Tibet — India's Shameful Role" argues Tibet was fully independent until 1950, and that Nehru's government conceded a "vague suzerainty of China" it could not later escape, quoting Sardar Patel's prescient 1950 warning letter.

Claude Arpi's "The Irony of the Bandung Conference" argues the 1955 Bandung Conference's anti-colonial rhetoric masked Tibet's abandonment, citing Acharya Kripalani's description of the Panchsheel Agreement as "born in sin."

The Dalai Lama's own March 10, 2005 statement reaffirms the Middle Way Approach seeking genuine autonomy rather than independence, while acknowledging Chinese economic development in Tibet alongside continued human-rights concerns.

Aspi Mistry rebuts press coverage claiming the Dalai Lama "gave up" the demand for a free Tibet, and Pema Thinley's reprinted Tibetan Review editorial argues global commercial self-interest, from the EU's arms-embargo debate to US retreat from UN pressure, leaves China facing no real accountability.

Tenzin Tsundue, writing as a second-generation exile, describes the 20,000-member Tibetan Youth Congress's generational impatience with the "Genuine Autonomy" compromise and its demand for full independence.

A reprint of Minoo Masani's 1956 essay "Why I Oppose Communism," marking his birth centenary, traces his journey from socialist sympathies to anti-Communism grounded in Lord Acton's axiom that liberty is the supreme good.

"Of Cabbages and Kings" comments on India's UN Security Council ambitions, a Supreme Court ruling permitting caste-exclusive housing societies, and criticises the Maharashtra government's dance-bar ban as moral posturing.

Freedom First No. 466 (July-Sept 2005) was delayed after Mumbai's unprecedented flooding destroyed the editor's papers and computer, forcing abandonment of a planned cover feature on India-Pakistan rapprochement.

S. V. Raju's tribute to C. R. Irani, the late Statesman editor, credits him with preserving the paper's independence during the Emergency and recounts his history in the Swatantra Party at Minoo Masani's invitation.
